stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for murder. The prosecution case is that the victim (a security guard) died in a factory fire that the defendant started for the sake of making a false insurance claim. The defendant admits starting the fire but denies having wanted to kill the victim, which the prosecution accepts. How must the judge direct the jury in relation to the mens rea for murder in a situation like this?
correct: They may find the mens rea proven if they are sure that death or serious harm was virtually certain, and that the defendant realised that it was.
why: Oblique intent (Woollin): the jury MAY find intention only if (1) death or serious harm was a virtual certainty from D's act (barring an unforeseen intervention) AND (2) D appreciated that it was. It is evidence from which intention may be found, never a rule that it must be (Matthews & Alleyne). Your pick wrongly treats D's foresight of a mere risk as enough: D must appreciate the virtual certainty itself.

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for criminal damage. The prosecution case is that the defendant, who was renting a property, damaged the flat by removing wall brackets on which a TV was fixed, ruining them in the process. The defendant claims not to have committed the offence because both the wall brackets and the TV were bought by the defendant. Will the defendant be guilty of criminal damage in such a situation?
correct: Yes, if the prosecution prove that the defendant realised that the wall brackets might no longer belong to them.
why: s 10(2) CDA 1971: fixtures become the landlord's property, so the brackets probably did 'belong to another'. But the mens rea covers that element too. D must intend or be reckless (subjectively, R v G) as to the property belonging to another, and an honest belief that it is your own negates mens rea (R v Smith [1974]). B states the civil-law position and ignores mens rea.

stem: Defendant A has been charged with causing grievous bodily harm with intent to cause grievous bodily harm on a victim and Defendant B is charged as an accessory. Both defendants were at a protest rally and the victim was a counter-protestor. Defendant A attacked the victim and Defendant B threw A a piece of wood with which A beat the victim. The defendants had never met each other before. Can Defendant B be convicted as an accessory to causing grievous bodily harm with intent on the victim?
correct: Yes, if Defendant B intended to assist Defendant A to intentionally cause grievous bodily harm on the victim and realised that Defendant A was not acting in self-defence.
why: Accessory to s 18 (Jogee): B must intend to assist A to commit the offence WITH its mens rea, i.e. intend to help A to intentionally cause GBH, and know the essential facts, including that A was not acting in self-defence (i.e. that the force was unlawful). Intending to assist only 'some harm' would fit a lesser offence (s 20/s 47), not s 18. No prior agreement or acquaintance is needed for assistance.

stem: Defendant A is being prosecuted as an accessory to wounding a victim with intent contrary to s 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861. The wound was caused by Defendant B using a knife that Defendant A had been told by B to leave by the back door of the restaurant where A is a cook. A knew that B is a significant figure in local gang crime but claims to have had no idea what the knife was going to be used for. Can Defendant A be convicted as an accessory to the wounding on these facts?
correct: No, Defendant A does not have the intention to assist Defendant B to cause serious harm to the victim.
why: Accessory mens rea (Jogee): D must intend to assist the principal to commit the offence and know the essential matters. At a minimum, D must contemplate the type of crime (Bryce; Maxwell). Realising that the knife might help 'a crime' is foresight, not intention, and A had no idea what it was for. So A is not an accessory to the s 18 wounding (Serious Crime Act 2007 offences aside).

stem: A defendant has hired someone to give her partner a “severe beating” having found out that the partner was having an affair. The hired person confronts the partner and asks for a bribe instead, but the partner reacts violently and the hired person kills the partner in reasonable self-defence. What can the defendant be convicted of?
correct: No offence because the defendant has not encouraged the commission of an offence.
why: Secondary liability is derivative: there must be a principal offence. The hired man never carried out the beating, and the killing was lawful self-defence, so no offence was committed for D to be an accessory to. D is not a principal to manslaughter either: her encouragement is not the unlawful, dangerous act that caused death. (Inchoate liability under the Serious Crime Act 2007 is not among the options.)

stem: The defendant is charged with theft of a £2,000 ornament that the defendant has now sold. The defendant has been looking after the victim as a carer and they have formed a close relationship. The victim appears to have given the ornament freely as a gift by having someone else leave it at the defendant’s house. The defendant sold the vase once the defendant had received it. There is evidence the defendant had asked the victim for the vase on a number of occasions. Which defence might be arguable in this case?
correct: There was no dishonesty in receiving the vase.
why: Hinks: receiving a valid gift CAN be an appropriation, and consent does not prevent appropriation (Gomez). So 'no appropriation because it was a gift' (your pick), and the consent options, fail. The arguable defence is dishonesty (Ivey: D's actual belief, then the standards of ordinary decent people). Accepting a genuine gift may well be honest, although the repeated requests cut the other way.

stem: The defendant sneaks onto a parking lot outside a garage and drives off with the defendant’s own car. The defendant did not want to pay the garage for work they had done. What offence might have been committed in this situation?
correct: Theft, but only if the defendant’s actions were dishonest.
why: s 5(1) TA 1968: property 'belongs to' anyone having possession or control of it, or a proprietary interest in it. The garage had possession and a lien, so taking back your own car can be theft (R v Turner (No 2)). It is not burglary, because a parking lot is not a building. Dishonesty is the live issue and must be proved (Ivey), so 'theft because dishonest' assumes what has to be decided.

stem: The defendant has been charged with theft from their neighbour. The defendant was paid an amount of cash to invest in Company A on behalf of the neighbour. Instead, the defendant invested it in Company B, made a profit, which was then used to buy a larger number of shares in Company A than would have been possible with the original amount of cash from the neighbour. Can the defendant be convicted of theft in these circumstances?
correct: Yes, if the court decides that the defendant’s conduct was dishonest.
why: The cash was received under an obligation to deal with it in a particular way, so s 5(3) treats it as still belonging to the neighbour. Using it for another investment is an appropriation, and dealing with it as your own satisfies s 6 (intention to permanently deprive). Lack of loss is irrelevant. Appropriation alone does not convict, though: the decisive question is dishonesty (Ivey). That is why the key is 'Yes, IF dishonest' and not your 'Yes, because appropriation'.

stem: A defendant is charged with aggravated arson having set fire to rubbish piled up outside their own flat in a block of flats. The defendant was drunk at the time and said, while doing so “See this, it is a fire hazard and people might die if it catches fire,” at which point the defendant set the rubbish on fire. The defendant denies having intended to put any lives in danger and says that the offence was committed in a moment of drunken rage about the failure to collect rubbish. Can the defendant be convicted of aggravated arson on these facts?
correct: Yes, because the defendant seems to have foreseen the risk that lives could be endangered.
why: Aggravated arson (s 1(2)/(3) CDA): D must intend, or be reckless as to, life being endangered by the damage. His own words show he actually foresaw that risk, so subjective recklessness is proved whatever his intoxication. It also applies to his own property. 'Basic intent' only tells you that voluntary intoxication is no excuse. It is not why he is guilty here.

stem: The defendant is being prosecuted for wounding with intent to cause grievous bodily harm and claims not to have realised what they were doing at the time because the victim had slipped a drug into their drink. Will the defendant be able to avoid conviction on this basis?
correct: Yes, unless the prosecution prove they in fact intended to cause grievous bodily harm.
why: s 18 is a specific-intent offence, and the PROSECUTION bears the legal burden of proving intent beyond reasonable doubt. Evidence of (involuntary) intoxication goes to whether intent was actually formed. D carries no burden to prove the spiking. If D nonetheless formed the intent, intoxication is no defence ('a drunken intent is still an intent': Kingston).

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for murder and wishes to raise the defence of self- defence on the grounds that the victim attacked them while they were walking home. It is not clear on the evidence whether the victim was going to attack them, and the prosecution allege that the defendant irrationally assumed the victim was attacking them. Can the jury conclude that the defendant was acting in self-defence on this basis?
correct: Not if the prosecution prove that they did not believe use of force was necessary or their use of force was unreasonable in the situation as they believed it to be.
why: Self-defence: once the defence raises it (evidential burden only), the PROSECUTION must disprove it to the criminal standard. D is judged on the facts as D honestly believed them, even if that belief was unreasonable or irrational (Williams (Gladstone); s 76(3)–(4) CJIA 2008). The question is whether force was reasonable in that situation. Your pick wrongly puts the burden of proof on the defence.

stem: The defendant is charged with manslaughter, having killed a person who was trying to take the defendant’s car in a public car park. The defendant is alleged to have hit the person repeatedly with a carjack even as the person was running away. Will the defendant be able to rely on self-defence in this case?
correct: Yes, but only if, based on the defendant’s perception of the situation, it was reasonable to use force and the force used was proportionate.
why: Not a householder case (a car park), so s 76 CJIA 2008 applies: was force needed, and was the force used reasonable in the circumstances as D believed them to be? Disproportionate force is not reasonable (s 76(6)). The 'grossly disproportionate' test is for householders only. The fact that the person was running away bears on reasonableness but is not an automatic bar. E omits D's own perception of the situation.

stem: A defendant is on trial for shooting a man who, the defendant says, was threatening the defendant’s child. The fighting took place inside the victim’s house after the defendant went there to warn the victim off and the victim threatened to kill the child when they next saw them. Is the defendant likely to be able to rely on the defence of prevention of crime or defence of another in these circumstances?
correct: No, because it is not likely to be reasonable to have used force in these circumstances.
why: s 3 CLA 1967 / defence of another: force must be necessary and reasonable. The threat ('when I next see them') was not imminent, and D went to the victim's house, so shooting him is unlikely to be reasonable. The 'not grossly disproportionate' householder test (s 76(5A)) protects an occupier in his own dwelling, not someone who goes to another's house. Your pick applies the wrong test.

stem: The defendant has been prosecuted for murdering a victim the defendant found in their house. The victim was unarmed and turns out to be homeless and seems to have broken into the kitchen to steal some food. The defendant is alleged to have grabbed a sword and beaten the victim a number of times as the victim was trying to escape out the door. How should the jury decide whether the defendant was acting in self- defence in these circumstances?
correct: They must decide whether the use of force was reasonable and may decide it was not if the force used was disproportionate but not grossly disproportionate.
why: Householder case (s 76(5A) CJIA 2008; R (Collins) v SoS for Justice): force that was GROSSLY disproportionate can never be reasonable. Force that was disproportionate but not grossly so MAY still be reasonable, and the jury decides on all the circumstances. Your pick says the jury 'may' reject grossly disproportionate force, but in fact they MUST.

stem: A defendant is accused of murder and says, in evidence, that they got into such a rage when taunted by the victim about their mental illness that they could did not think about what they were doing and just lashed out with the pickaxe they were then holding. They wanted to hit the victim but did not think about what hitting them would do. The victim died from the wounds. Which offence is the man likely to have committed based on such an explanation?
correct: Unlawful act manslaughter.
why: Loss of control is only a partial defence to MURDER, so murder must first be proved. D 'did not think about what hitting them would do', so there is no intention to kill or cause GBH, and murder fails. Hitting someone with a pickaxe is an unlawful and objectively dangerous act (a battery) that caused death, which is unlawful act manslaughter (Church; Newbury).

stem: The defendant is being prosecuted for fraud, having sold the victim a chandelier. The prosecution evidence is that the chandelier was listed in a catalogue as ‘Arguably a Louis XIV’ and that the victim who bought the chandelier asked the defendant whether he had the authenticity of the chandelier checked to which the defendant said that she had. The defendant had been told by an expert that it was probably not a Louis XIV and was probably a replica (which is what it turns out to be). If the prosecution proves these facts, are they likely to have established the actus reus of a fraud?
correct: Yes, because the defendant’s representations overall gave a misleading impression that it was more likely to be a Louis XIV chandelier than not.
why: Fraud by false representation (s 2 FA 2006): a representation is false if it is untrue OR misleading (s 2(2)). It can be express or implied, and can be about a state of mind or opinion (s 2(3)). 'I had it checked' was literally true, but in context it gave the misleading impression that it was authentic, when the expert had said it was probably a replica. No actual gain or loss is required.

stem: A person is being prosecuted for fraud. They allegedly managed to secure funding for housing improvements by failing to disclose their age. The government had initiated an initiative called the “Pensioners Solar Heating Fund”. The person was not old enough to be a pensioner but applied. There was no question on the form that asked the age or pension status of the applicant but there was a free text box, “Basis of the Application”, which the person left blank. Is the person likely to be found to have committed the actus reus of any fraud offence?
correct: No, because the person is likely to be found to have been under no duty to disclose their age or whether they were a pensioner.
why: Fraud by failing to disclose (s 3 FA 2006) needs a LEGAL duty to disclose (statute, contract, fiduciary relationship or trade custom). The form never asked for age or pension status, so there was no duty. Leaving a free-text box blank is not a false representation either. So the actus reus is not made out. Dishonesty (option C) is mens rea, not actus reus.

stem: The defendant has been charged with theft of a rail season ticket which permits travel from 1st May of one year to 1st May of the next year. The defendant denies stealing it and claims only to have borrowed it from August of that year to the end of April. Can the defendant claim not to have intended to deprive the owner of the season ticket on this basis?
correct: No, because the defendant has intended to keep the ticket until it had lost practical value.
why: s 6(1) TA 1968: borrowing counts as an intention to permanently deprive where it is 'equivalent to an outright taking', i.e. the thing is returned with its goodness or practical value exhausted (R v Lloyd). A season ticket handed back days before expiry is practically worthless. Temporary deprivation of use (your pick) is not enough on its own.

stem: A defendant is on trial for theft for finding used car parking tickets with time still to run on them and selling them to new users of the car park. The defendant claims to have believed there was nothing wrong with doing this. How should be the magistrates determine whether the defendant was being dishonest?
correct: They should determine whether selling the tickets was objectively dishonest taking into account the defendant’s understanding and beliefs.
why: Ivey v Genting / R v Barton & Booth: first find D's ACTUAL knowledge or belief as to the facts (the genuineness of the belief matters, not its reasonableness). Then judge objectively by the standards of ordinary decent people. There is no second limb asking whether D realised it was dishonest. The Ghosh test is gone, and options A and B are Ghosh-style tests.

stem: A person realises they have been cheated out of £200 by a conman. When they see the conman a couple of days later, they punch him and, when he is lying on the ground, they reach into his wallet and take out £200. When confronted by police about this, the person says that the conman was a criminal who needed to be stopped. They took the £200 back as it was theirs. Will the person be convicted of robbing the conman?
correct: No, because they are unlikely to be found to be acting dishonesty.
why: Robbery is theft with force (s 8), so no theft means no robbery. Under s 2(1)(a) TA 1968, a belief in a legal right to the property is not dishonest, even if it was obtained by force and even if the belief is mistaken (R v Robinson). She believed the £200 was hers. The force alone does not make it robbery. She may still be liable for the assault.

stem: A defendant is accused of inflicting grievous bodily harm on a victim. The victim has a serious psychiatric reaction to a campaign of harassment and silent intimidation by the defendant. In what circumstances can the defendant be guilty of an offence under s 20 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861?
correct: The defendant can be guilty if the defendant realised there was a risk of some harm to the victim at some point during the campaign of harassment.
why: Psychiatric injury can be GBH, and s 20 'inflict' needs no assault (R v Burstow). Mens rea is foresight of SOME harm (Mowatt; Savage), so mere assault mens rea (your pick) is the s 47 rule, not s 20. With a continuing course of conduct, foresight arising at any point during the campaign suffices.

stem: A person is accused of setting fire to their own car during a dispute with his ex-partner. The person did so because he did not want their ex- partner to get ownership of it in a divorce settlement. The person has been charged with basic arson contrary to s 1(3) of the Criminal Damage Act 1971. Has the man committed criminal damage to the car?
correct: Yes, if the partner had a share in the car and the man realised that this might be the case.
why: Basic arson is just s 1(1) criminal damage by fire, so the property must 'belong to another' (s 10(2): anyone with a proprietary interest) AND D must intend or be reckless as to that (Smith). Fire does not remove that requirement (your pick). Damaging your own property only becomes an offence under s 1(2) aggravated damage (danger to life).

stem: A person is being prosecuted for causing grievous bodily harm, with intent to cause grievous bodily harm contrary to s 18 of the Offences Against the Person Act 1861 but denies having intended any such harm because they were too drunk to think clearly after spending a number of hours drinking with friends. How should the jury be directed in relation to the defendant?
correct: If the person did not intend to cause serious harm, they may convict the person of s 20 GBH whether or not the person realised some harm might occur.
why: Majewski: for a specific-intent offence (s 18), voluntary intoxication is relevant evidence on whether intent was formed, so the jury must consider it, not ignore it (your pick). If there was no intent, acquit of s 18 but convict of s 20 (basic intent). For basic intent, voluntary intoxication is no defence and actual foresight need not be proved.

stem: A defendant is charged with murder of a victim as an accessory to a second defendant. There is evidence that the first defendant had suggested that the second kill the victim and that the first defendant wanted the victim dead but they have produced evidence that the second defendant had been talking about doing so anyway. Can the first defendant be an accessory to murder of the victim on this basis?
correct: Yes, if the first defendant intended to encourage the second to kill the victim and knew that what was said might do so.
why: Encouragement (Jogee; Giannetto): the accessory must INTEND to encourage the principal to commit the offence, knowing the essential matters. There is no need to prove the encouragement made a difference, and the principal's prior plan does not matter as long as the encouragement was communicated. Your pick adds a causation requirement and settles for foresight ('realised it might'), which Jogee rejected.

stem: The defendant has been charged with aggravated burglary. The defendant was invited into the victim’s flat to agree a payment of the defendant for work they have done as a drug courier. The two argued and the defendant decided to take all the money the victim had. The defendant pulled out a knife to stop the victim from resisting and ran off with the money. What offence most accurately reflects what the defendant has done on these facts?
correct: Robbery.
why: Aggravated burglary (s 10) requires a burglary, which requires entry as a TRESPASSER (s 9). D was invited in. Deciding to steal after a lawful entry does not make D a trespasser. Using or threatening force (the knife) at the time of stealing, in order to steal, is robbery (s 8).

stem: A defendant throws a stone at a victim wanting to hurt them but misses and breaks a window of the victim’s house. Could the defendant be guilty of criminal damage in such circumstances?
correct: Yes, if the defendant realised there was a risk of missing and damaging the window.
why: Transferred malice does not work across different offences (Pembliton): intent to hurt a person cannot become intent to damage property. D can still be guilty if reckless as to damage. Recklessness is SUBJECTIVE (R v G [2003]), so D must have actually realised the risk. 'Obvious risk' (your pick) is the old objective Caldwell test, which has been overruled.

stem: Four friends wish to set up a business in partnership and so enter into a written partnership agreement that specifies:- All of them have contributed an equal amount of capital to the business.- Interest is paid on their capital contributions at 5% pa.- All of them share profits and losses equally.- One of the partners is paid a salary of £10,000 pa.Which statement best reflects the friends’ position under the Partnership Act 1890?
correct: They have excluded the default provisions under the Partnership Act 1890 in relation to the payment of interest on capital and the payment of a salary.
why: The PA 1890 s 24 defaults are: share capital and profits equally; NO interest on capital (s 24(4)); NO salary (s 24(6)). The agreement's equal sharing simply mirrors the default. Interest on capital at 5% and a salary for one partner both depart from it, so those two defaults are excluded, not just the salary (your pick).

stem: A partnership operates under a written agreement that specifies that the partnership will continue for a fixed period of 5 years. After 3 years have elapsed, one of the partners would like to retire from the partnership. Which statement best reflects the partner’s position?
correct: The partner cannot leave the partnership during the fixed term without the consent of their fellow partners to vary the agreement to permit retirement.
why: A fixed-term partnership is not a partnership 'at will', so no partner can retire or dissolve it by notice during the term (ss 26 and 32 PA 1890 apply only to partnerships at will). But it is not locked shut either (your pick): the partners can all consent to vary the agreement (s 19) to permit retirement.

stem: A private limited company is a small family-run business with all of the four shareholders living in the same postcode district. Three of the shareholders each own 30% of shares entitling them to attend and vote at a general meeting. The fourth shareholder owns the remaining 10%. A couple of company matters require an urgent shareholder meeting and they ask your advice on whether they can shorten the notice needed for this meeting. Which of the statements below best describes your advice?
correct: A majority in number of members owning not less than 90% of the voting shares need to consent to short notice; so the three shareholders who each own 30% of the shares all need to consent.
why: CA 2006 s 307(5)–(6): in a PRIVATE company, a general meeting can be held on short notice if a majority in NUMBER of members holding at least 90% of the voting shares agree (the articles may raise this to 95%, but no higher). The three 30% holders are 3 of 4 members and hold 90%, which is enough. 95% (your pick) is the public company threshold.

stem: A company with unamended model articles of association has decided to obtain a loan and grant a security in respect of the loan to the bank. Which of one of the following best describes the procedure that the company needs to follow?
correct: The company’s board of directors must approve the loan and the granting of the security.
why: Under the Model Articles (art 3), the directors manage the business and may exercise all the company's powers. That includes borrowing AND granting security, so both are board decisions. No shareholder approval is needed unless the articles restrict it. Your pick covered only the security, but the loan itself is also a board decision.

stem: A private limited company is to be incorporated with two classes of shares, A shares and B shares. The B shares will carry 3 times the number of votes on all matters, compared to A shares. The new company’s share capital will be as follows: A owns 10 B shares B owns 40 A shares C owns 20 A shares D owns 5 B shares E owns 25 A shares Who will be persons of significant control in the new company? Which answer best reflects the position?
correct: B only.
why: PSC threshold: MORE than 25% of shares or of votes. There are 100 shares and 130 votes (85 A shares × 1, plus 15 B shares × 3). B has 40% of shares, so B is a PSC. A has 10 shares (10%) and 30 votes (23%): no. E has exactly 25% of shares, which is not MORE than 25%, and 19% of votes: no. So B only.

stem: A promoter is incorporating a new private limited company and is investigating the statutory requirements for share registration. The articles of the company will provide for one class of share and no pre- emption rights. There are two subscribers to the new company and the plan is then to allot shares to a new shareholder within 6 months of incorporation. Which statement best describes when the two subscribers and the subsequent shareholder will become members of the company?
correct: The two subscribers will become members on registration of the company when their names are entered in the register of members. The subsequent shareholder will become a member when their name is entered in the register of members.
why: CA 2006 s 112: subscribers are deemed to agree to become members and become members on registration (incorporation), with their names entered in the register of members. Anyone else becomes a member when they agree to AND their name is entered in the register. Filing at Companies House and allotment resolutions do not confer membership.

stem: A company is incorporated with the Model Articles as its articles of association. There are four shareholders of the company, each holding a 25% share. One of the directors has now retired and the board is seeking advice on the appointment of a replacement director. Which statement set out below most accurately reflects the procedure the board should follow under the Model Articles to appoint a new director?
correct: The new appointment can be made by ordinary resolution of the members or by a majority decision of the directors.
why: Model Articles art 17: a new director can be appointed EITHER by ordinary resolution of the members OR by a decision of the directors. So the board does not have sole authority (your pick), and no special resolution or share qualification is needed.

correct: The company’s board of directors must approve the loan and the granting of the security.
why: Same rule as the loan-and-security card: under the Model Articles (art 3), the directors exercise all the company's powers, including borrowing and granting security. Both the loan and the charge are board decisions.

stem: Which one of the following will appear in a profit and loss account?
correct: Wages.
why: The profit and loss account records INCOME and EXPENSES for a period, and wages are an expense. Premises and cash are assets, and an overdraft and creditors are liabilities, so all four belong on the BALANCE SHEET.

stem: A company with an accounting reference date of 31 December is preparing a balance sheet. Which one of the following best describes the period for which the balance account will be produced?
correct: The balance sheet will be a snapshot of the business on 31 December.
why: A balance sheet is a SNAPSHOT of assets, liabilities and capital at one date, here the accounting reference date (31 December). It is the profit and loss account that covers the 12-month period (your pick).

stem: Which one of the following measures a business’s profitability?
correct: Return on capital employed.
why: Return on capital employed (profit ÷ capital employed) measures PROFITABILITY. The current ratio (your pick) and acid test measure LIQUIDITY, while debtor days and stock turnover measure efficiency.

stem: You are acting for the liquidator of a private limited company, who was appointed 3 months ago. The liquidator is seeking to avoid a number of floating charges granted by the company prior to liquidation. It would appear no fresh consideration was given for these charges. Therefore, the liquidator wishes to check the correct periods of time within which such transactions taking place prior to liquidation can be challenged and if there are any related solvency requirements. Which statement most accurately sets out the relevant period and solvency requirements for the liquidator to avoid a floating charge?
correct: If the transaction was with an unconnected person and it took place within 1 year of insolvency, a charge can be avoided provided that the company was insolvent at the time of the charge or became insolvent due to the transaction.
why: IA 1986 s 245: a floating charge granted to an UNCONNECTED person is avoidable if it was created within 12 months before the onset of insolvency AND the company was unable to pay its debts then, or became so as a result. For a CONNECTED person the period is 2 years and insolvency need NOT be shown. In both cases the charge stands to the extent of fresh consideration. Your option said insolvency must still be proved for connected persons, which is wrong.

stem: A sole trader who runs a painting and decorating business is unable to work for the foreseeable future after an accident. The sole trader owes £800 to a paint supplier and the amount has been outstanding for 5 months. Although the sole trader is planning to sell some business premises, the paint supplier needs to recover the amount quickly to enable it to pay its own creditors.Which one of the following statements provides the most accurate advice to the paint supplier?
correct: The paint supplier cannot serve a statutory demand because the debt is less than £5,000.
why: Serving a statutory demand is a route to a bankruptcy petition, and an individual can only be petitioned against for a debt of at least £5,000. £800 is far below that, so a statutory demand is pointless. The supplier should sue in the County Court instead. £750 (E) is the threshold for COMPANY winding-up.

stem: A holiday homeowner gifted the property to their sibling 18 months ago when their business started to encounter financial difficulties. The original owner has now been made bankrupt and the trustee in bankruptcy intends to set aside the transfer of the holiday home.Which one of the following statements offers the most accurate advice to the trustee?
correct: It will not be necessary to prove the bankrupt was insolvent at the time of the gift because it was made within 2 years of the bankruptcy.
why: Transaction at an undervalue by an individual (IA 1986 ss 339, 341): the relevant time is 5 years before the bankruptcy petition. Within 2 YEARS, insolvency need not be proved at all. Between 2 and 5 years it must be proved, but it is PRESUMED for a gift to an associate. Your pick confuses that presumption with the 2-year rule. The gift was 18 months ago, so no proof is needed.

stem: A trade creditor with whom an entrepreneur has good relations received payment for an outstanding invoice shortly before the entrepreneur became bankrupt. The trade creditor is aware that other creditors did not receive any payments and has become concerned that their payment may be set aside. Which one of the following statements offers the most accurate advice to the trade creditor?
correct: The payment will be a preference if it is proved that the entrepreneur became insolvent because of the preference or that they were already insolvent and there was a desire to prefer.
why: Preference (IA 1986 s 340): the payment must be within the relevant time (6 months, or 2 years for an associate), the debtor must have been insolvent then or become so as a result, AND the debtor must have been influenced by a DESIRE to prefer the creditor. Timing alone (your pick) is not enough, and this is not a transaction at an undervalue because a debt was paid at full value.

stem: A post-graduate student who works as a part-time shop assistant has accumulated credit card debts of £8,000 and a student loan of £20,000. The student has applied for a debt relief order.If the debt relief order is granted, which one of the following statements is correct?
correct: The student will be freed from repaying their credit card debts after 12 months.
why: A debt relief order gives a 12-month moratorium, after which qualifying debts are discharged. STUDENT LOANS are excluded debts and survive the DRO. So the credit card debt goes after 12 months but the student loan does not. Your pick wrongly says no debts are freed.

stem: A private limited company incorporated in 2014 with unamended articles of association has an issued share capital of 200,000 ordinary £1 shares. It intends to offer a further 50,000 ordinary £1 shares to its existing shareholders pro rata to their existing shareholding. One of the shareholders may not be in a financial position to take up the offer but a third party (acceptable to the board and all existing members) would invest if shares were available. Which one of the following statements describes the best step(s) to be followed to achieve the company’s intentions?
correct: The company should make the offer to all its shareholders pro rata to their existing shareholding.
why: s 561 CA 2006 (pre-emption) is satisfied by offering the new shares to ALL existing shareholders pro rata. Once the offer period (at least 14 days) expires, any shares not taken up can be allotted to the third party (private company with one class of shares: s 550 authority). So no disapplication resolution (C) and no individual waiver (D) is needed.

stem: A start-up company has no assets and requires a loan to purchase stock. Which one of the following describes the most realistic option for the company to secure the loan?
correct: A term loan secured by a floating charge and directors’ guarantees.
why: A lender will not lend unsecured to a start-up with no assets (your pick). A fixed charge needs specific, identifiable assets, which the company does not have. A FLOATING charge can attach to the stock it is about to buy (circulating assets), and because that security is weak, the bank will also want personal guarantees from the directors.

stem: Which one of the following best describes a limited liability partnership?
correct: A corporate body with a separate legal personality formed by two or more members.
why: LLPA 2000: an LLP is a body corporate with legal personality separate from its members (s 1). It must be incorporated by TWO or more persons associated for carrying on a lawful business with a view to profit (s 2). One member (your pick) is enough for a company, but not for an LLP.

stem: A partner retires from an ongoing partnership. The partner wants to ensure that they will not be liable, after their retirement, for any future partnership debt incurred with the partnership’s many suppliers. The retiring partner has already asked that their name is removed from all the firm’s publicity materials, invoices and other documents. Which statement best describes what other action (if anything) the retiring partner should take to minimise any further liability to the partnership’s suppliers?
correct: The retiring partner should ensure that each supplier has had actual notice that they have left the partnership.
why: PA 1890 s 36: a retiring partner stays liable to people who DEALT WITH THE FIRM BEFORE the change until they have ACTUAL notice of it. A Gazette notice is enough only for people who had no previous dealings. The suppliers are existing creditors, so each needs actual notice. An indemnity (your pick) only shifts the cost between partners. It does not stop the suppliers suing the retiring partner.

stem: All the partners in a trading partnership unanimously vote that, until they all agree otherwise, they will not make any new purchases with a value over £10,000 due to cash-flow difficulties. A month later one of the partners is offered a “bargain” item of equipment for £15,000 by one of the partnership’s regular suppliers. That partner bought it immediately, claiming there was no time to consult the others, and justified the purchase by stating it would help the partnership generate greater profits. Did the partner have actual authority from their fellow partners to make this purchase and which statement best reflects the position?
correct: No, because of the unanimous decision setting a spending limit.
why: Actual authority, both express and implied, comes from the agreement between the partners. A unanimous decision capping purchases at £10,000 REMOVES actual authority above that limit. 'Implied authority' (your pick) is a kind of actual authority, so it goes too. What may survive is APPARENT/usual authority under PA 1890 s 5, which binds the firm to a supplier who does not know of the restriction (s 8). That is a different question.

stem: A former partner would like to be discharged from their pre-retirement partnership liabilities, which have been incurred under various contracts with the partnership’s existing suppliers. The partnership is continuing with the remaining partners. Which statement best describes who would need to agree to novate these contracts to achieve the former partner’s goal?
correct: The former partner, the ongoing partners and the existing suppliers.
why: Novation replaces one contract with a new one, so everyone affected must agree: the creditor (supplier) releases the retiring partner, the continuing partners take on the liability, and the retiring partner is released (PA 1890 s 17(3)). People who happened to be partners at the date of retirement (your pick) are not the relevant group.

stem: Two businesspeople are forming a private limited company. They have decided it will adopt the Model Articles for private limited companies in their entirety and without amendment. Which of the following must be supplied to the Registrar of Companies (at Companies House) to complete the registration process?
correct: Memorandum and Form IN01.
why: CA 2006 s 9: registration requires the application (Form IN01) and the MEMORANDUM of association (plus statements of capital and of officers, which are part of IN01). Articles need only be filed if the company is NOT simply adopting the Model Articles unamended. Unamended Model Articles apply by default (s 20).

stem: If a private limited company was incorporated in March, what will be the date of its accounting reference date (ARD) annually?
correct: 31 March.
why: For companies incorporated since 1 April 1996, the first ARD is the LAST day of the month in which the anniversary of incorporation falls (CA 2006 s 391(4)). Incorporated in March, the ARD is 31 March.

stem: Two entrepreneurs have just acquired a private limited company “off the shelf” from a company formation agency. The company was incorporated last July. They would now like to change the company’s accounting reference date to 31 December annually. They have approved the change at the company’s first board meeting. What best describes what else would be required?
correct: Form AA01 filed at Companies House.
why: s 392 CA 2006: the company changes its ARD simply by giving notice to the registrar on Form AA01. The board can decide it, and no members' resolution is needed. The board minute stays in the company's own records and is not filed (your pick).

stem: Your client is keen to invest in a new private limited company. They have been offered a number of shares in the company and wish to understand the significance of a shareholder’s role in a private limited company. Which one of the following statements best describes your client’s role as a shareholder?
correct: They will be one of the owners of the company involved in certain key decisions and rewarded by way of dividend, if profits allow.
why: Shareholders own the company. They are rewarded by dividends (if profits allow) and decide the matters reserved to members, such as amending the articles, removing directors and authorising certain transactions. Day-to-day running belongs to the directors. 'No ability to influence' (your pick) ignores those voting rights.

stem: A private limited company adopts the Model Articles as provided by the Companies Act. Special notice of a general meeting to remove a director has been given and a general meeting is being held to vote on the resolution to remove the director. Exactly 50% of the votes cast in the meeting are cast for the resolution, the other 50% against. Which of the following summaries best describe the outcome of the vote?
correct: A majority (over 50%) of shareholder votes cast at the meeting is needed to pass the resolution. As this threshold has not been reached, the director remains in office.
why: Removing a director (s 168) needs an ORDINARY resolution: a simple majority, i.e. MORE than 50% of votes cast. A 50:50 tie fails, so the director stays. The Model Articles for private companies give the chair NO casting vote at a general meeting (only at board meetings, art 13).

stem: The board of directors of a private limited company has recently received training from their company solicitors on their roles and responsibilities, following a major governance report on the company conducted by independent consultants. The training drew their attention to the duties owed under the Companies Act 2006 and the protection they provide to those who invest in and deal with the company. Which of the following correctly describes to whom the directors of the company owe these duties?
correct: The company.
why: CA 2006 s 170(1): the general duties are owed to the COMPANY, not to shareholders, employees or fellow directors. Only the company can enforce them, with shareholders limited to derivative claims.

stem: A private limited company produces fresh organic fruit. There is a board of six executive directors. A year ago, a second company approached the board and offered to sell the first company a plot of land adjoining one of the first company’s principal market gardens. Due to financial uncertainty and a large debt burden, the board of the first company rejected the proposal. Subsequently, two of the six directors of the first company acted independently and acquired the plot of land for themselves for £250,000. Owing to the recent fall in interest rates and optimistic economic forecasts by the UK Government, the board of the first company regrets its failure to acquire the plot of land and intends to purchase it for the offer price of £350,000. The board of directors of the first company has not been informed who owns the land. If the new sale of the plot of land goes through, which statement best summarises the directors’ duties that will be primarily engaged by the behaviour of the two directors?
correct: The two directors will be in potential breach of their duties to avoid conflicts of interest and not to accept benefits from third parties.
why: Taking for themselves a property opportunity they learned of as directors breaches s 175 (avoid conflicts of interest). It does not matter that the company rejected it (s 175(2); Bhullar; Regal (Hastings)). Their £100k turn on a deal reached through the directorship is also caught by s 176 (benefits from third parties) in the course materials. Nothing suggests acting outside the constitution or for an improper purpose (s 171, your pick). The resale will also need a s 177 declaration.

stem: A public limited company is planning to hold an Annual General Meeting (AGM) next month. Which of the following best explains the calculation of the notice period for the company’s AGM?
correct: The AGM must be called on at least 21 days’ notice, excluding from this notice period the day of giving the notice and the day of the meeting itself.
why: A PUBLIC company's AGM needs at least 21 days' notice (s 307(2)(a)). Notice periods are CLEAR days, excluding both the day the notice is given and the day of the meeting (s 360). 14 days (your pick) is for other general meetings.

stem: A private limited company is holding a general meeting. The resolutions being proposed are to amend the articles and to authorise directors to allot shares. Which of the following statements best summarises the filing requirements for documents from the meeting following the passing of the resolutions?
correct: Both resolutions require filing with the Registrar of Companies, but the minutes of the meeting do not.
why: Copies of special resolutions (e.g. amending the articles) must be filed within 15 days (ss 29–30). So must an ordinary resolution giving directors authority to allot under s 551 (s 551(9)). Minutes are kept by the company and never filed.

stem: A newly incorporated company with unamended articles and one class of shares requires further capital to expand. The directors have decided to allot further shares to an existing shareholder, the consideration for which will be the acquisition of plant and machinery. Which one of the following statements offers the best advice to the directors?
correct: Neither an ordinary resolution to allot nor a special resolution to disapply pre-emption rights will need to be obtained from the shareholders.
why: A private company with ONE class of shares: the directors may allot under s 550 without shareholder authority, unless the articles prohibit it. Pre-emption (s 561) does not apply where the consideration is wholly or partly NON-CASH (s 565), and plant and machinery is non-cash. So no ordinary or special resolution is needed.

stem: A company with ordinary and preference shares has an existing authority from its shareholders to allot further ordinary shares. It is proposing to allot ordinary shares, but it is not yet clear to whom. Which one of the following statements is correct?
correct: A special resolution may be required.
why: With two classes of shares, s 550 is unavailable, so a s 551 authority is needed, but the company already HAS one. Pre-emption (s 561) applies to ordinary shares allotted for cash. If they will not be offered pro rata to existing holders, a SPECIAL resolution disapplying pre-emption may be needed (s 570/571). No further ordinary resolution is required (your pick).

stem: All three partners in a new partnership agree to make initial capital contributions as follows:A = £30,000B = £35,000C = £25,000In addition, B will loan the partnership an additional £10,000. They have not yet entered into a written partnership agreement. Which statement best reflects the partnersʼ position?
correct: A written partnership agreement could provide for both interest on capital and on the loan at a rate chosen by the partners, but in default Partner B would be entitled to interest of 5% on the loan.
why: PA 1890 s 24 defaults: no interest on CAPITAL (s 24(4)), but a partner who advances money BEYOND their agreed capital (a loan) is entitled to 5% interest on it (s 24(3)). These are only defaults, so a partnership agreement can provide for interest on capital and set a different rate on the loan. 'Not permitted' (your pick) is wrong: it is simply not paid unless agreed.

stem: A solicitor in a sole practice has been found with a small amount of Class A drugs at a house party. The solicitor has accepted a caution for the offence. Which of the following best describes the professional conduct implications in the circumstances?
correct: The solicitor is in breach of the conduct regulations as the solicitor has failed to uphold public trust and confidence in the profession.
why: The Principles reach conduct outside practice where it affects public trust (Principle 2: uphold public trust and confidence in the profession). Accepting a caution for possessing Class A drugs does that. It is not a breach simply because 'an offence was committed' (D). The breach lies in the conduct and its effect on trust. A caution must also be reported to the SRA promptly (Code for Solicitors 7.6–7.7), so A and B are wrong.

stem: You are an office manager with a background in working for online digital service companies. You started work 3 months ago at a law firm at their Manchester city centre office as their office manager. After a month, the managing partner of the firm asked for money to be transferred from the client account to the business account as a temporary short-term loan to the business. You were worried about the request as it didn’t seem in line with normal business practice, however, you did not object and the transfer took place. The Solicitors Regulatory Authority (SRA) have now announced they are investigating the firm for breaches to the Code of Conduct for Firms, breaches of the Code of Conduct for Solicitors, and breaches of the relevant Principles. Is the office manager bound by any of the Codes or the Principles?
correct: Yes, regardless of qualification, the office manager is bound by the Code of Conduct for Firms and the Principles.
why: The SRA Principles apply to everyone in an SRA-authorised firm, including non-lawyer managers and employees. The Code of Conduct for Firms also binds the firm's managers and employees in relevant respects. So the office manager is bound by BOTH the Principles and the Code for Firms, regardless of qualification. Your pick leaves out the Principles. Only the Code for Solicitors is limited to individual authorised persons.

stem: A solicitor in an SRA-regulated firm is having an extra-marital relationship. The solicitor wishes to marry their new lover but is too embarrassed to go through a divorce. The solicitor travels to another part of the country and goes through a ceremony of marriage with the new lover, without the knowledge of their first spouse. The deception is later discovered by the first spouse, who reports the matter to the police. The solicitor is convicted of bigamy and sentenced to 12 months' imprisonment. Which of the following statements best describes the professional conduct implications of the solicitor’s actions?
correct: The solicitor has breached the professional conduct regulations as they have acted dishonestly.
why: Going through a marriage ceremony while concealing an existing marriage is a deliberate deception of the new partner and the registrar. That is DISHONEST (Principle 4), the most serious and specific breach. A conviction is not in itself the breach (your pick): the regulator looks at the underlying conduct. Public trust (C) is engaged too, but dishonesty best describes it. Private-life conduct is caught when it reflects on honesty.

stem: You are an assistant solicitor in a medium-sized law firm. You are working for a partner who is also the firm’s appointed Compliance Officer for Legal Practice (COLP). They ask you to consider how Principle 4 (the duty to act with honesty) may affect the practice. Which of the following scenarios falls outside the scope of Principle 4?
correct: A solicitor is chatting to a potential new client at a networking event. The client tells the solicitor that they have a box at Manchester City and invite the solicitor to watch a game with them. The solicitor indicates they are a Manchester City fan and would enjoy that. In fact, the solicitor supports Chelsea.
why: The Principles apply outside practice only where the conduct realistically reflects on a solicitor's fitness or on public trust. A trivial social white lie about a football team does not. Inflating your degree and experience on a CV (your pick) is plainly dishonest and squarely within Principle 4, as are borrowing client money, backdating a letter and misleading a client about their case.

stem: A solicitor is the managing partner of a medium-sized high street law firm specialising in family law. A junior solicitor of the firm represents a client in an acrimonious divorce in which the client is ordered to give their spouse half of the family assets. The client is outraged and blames the firm for failing to robustly defend their interests in the proceedings. The client makes a formal complaint to the partner claiming that the solicitor who represented them was negligent, incompetent, and rude. The partner reads the complaint and “dismisses” it as baseless without speaking to the solicitor in question or the client. The firm’s complaints procedure requires a formal inquiry into all complaints. The client is not satisfied and wishes to escalate matters, but the partner tells them that the matter is “closed”, and they should move on. Which of the following statements is correct regarding the professional conduct implications in the scenario?
correct: The firm has breached its professional conduct obligations by failing to deal with the complaint in line with its internal procedures and informing the client of their right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman and the SRA.
why: Code for Solicitors 8.2–8.4 / Code for Firms: complaints must be dealt with promptly, fairly and free of charge, under the firm's procedure. The client must also be told IN WRITING, at the outset and at the end of the procedure, of the right to complain to the Legal Ombudsman (with time limits and contact details) and, where relevant, to the SRA. Your pick covers only half the breach: telling the client 'the matter is closed' also withholds the escalation route.

stem: A solicitor is acting for a client in a litigation matter. At the hearing, the client loses the case and is ordered to pay £5,000 towards the opponent’s costs. Outside court the solicitor says to their opponent, “Don’t worry. I’ll make sure that the £5,000 will be paid within the next 14 days.” Fourteen days have now elapsed, and the client has still not provided the solicitor with any funds to pay the costs. Who can force the solicitor to comply with the promise?
correct: The court.
why: 'I'll make sure the £5,000 is paid within 14 days' is an unequivocal oral UNDERTAKING, binding personally on the solicitor whether or not the client provides the funds. The COURT can enforce it under its inherent supervisory jurisdiction over solicitors as officers of the court. The SRA and SDT can discipline a breach but cannot compel performance, and the Legal Ombudsman deals with service complaints.

stem: A staff member in a large firm of solicitors steals money from a client account. The firm makes good the loss, dismisses the staff member, informs the police and puts in place procedures to ensure that the situation does not arise again. Should the matter still be reported to the SRA?
correct: Yes, there is a need for the firm’s compliance officer to record the incident and report it to the SRA as this amounts to a material breach.
why: Theft of client money by staff is a serious breach and is reportable as MATERIAL even after the loss is made good and the employee dismissed. The compliance officer (COLP, or COFA for the Accounts Rules) must record it and report it promptly to the SRA (Code for Firms 9.1–9.2). The Legal Ombudsman deals with service complaints, not regulatory breaches.

stem: A defendant has been prosecuted for a non-imprisonable summary offence relating to food standards. The court has adjourned the matter for trial and is considering bail. The defendant has said certain things to the food standards officers during the inspection that cause the magistrates to think that the defendant might commit further offences before trial. In what circumstances can the court refuse bail in this situation?
correct: It cannot because the defendant has not been convicted.
why: For a NON-imprisonable offence, the only grounds for refusing bail are in Bail Act 1976 Sch 1 Part II: a previous failure to surrender plus a belief that D would fail again; D's own protection; D already serving a sentence; or D arrested in these proceedings for absconding or breaching bail. The risk of committing further offences is NOT a ground, so bail cannot be refused on that basis. (Note: the key's stated reason, 'not convicted', is a loose way of putting this. The real point is the absence of a Part II ground.)

stem: A police officer arrests a suspect, having seen him as a part of a crowd during an affray seemingly engaged in threatening unlawful violence. The suspect is taken to the police station to be detained. What reason could the officer provide to the custody officer for the arrest?
correct: They had reasonable grounds to suspect that the arrestee has committed an offence and that they had reasonable grounds for believing the arrest to be necessary.
why: PACE s 24(2) and (4)–(5): a constable may arrest without warrant someone they have reasonable grounds to SUSPECT has committed an offence, provided they have reasonable grounds to BELIEVE that arrest is necessary for a s 24(5) reason (Code G). The offence need not be indictable: that limit applies to a citizen's arrest (s 24A). 'Arrestable offence' is an obsolete concept.

stem: A defendant is unrepresented in a summary trial, in which they rely on an alibi defence. The defendant gives evidence in their own defence and calls two alibi witnesses. The defendant does not know what the position is in relation to closing speeches and asks the court legal advisor for help. How should the court legal advisor respond?
correct: The prosecution and the defence can make closing speeches.
why: CrimPR 24.3 (magistrates' court): the defence may always make a closing speech. The prosecution may make one only if the defendant is represented OR, whether represented or not, has called evidence other than their own. Here D called two alibi witnesses, so both sides may make closing speeches.

stem: A defendant is on trial for the murder of their parent. The defence is diminished responsibility. The defendant has produced evidence to show that a history of poor treatment substantially impaired their capacity to make rational judgements. The jurors retired to consider the case but have returned to ask what should happen if they think it unlikely that the defendant’s capacity for rational judgement was substantially impaired but cannot be sure that it was not so impaired. How should the judge direct the jury about when they should conclude that diminished responsibility is established?
correct: They should only find diminished responsibility if they conclude it was likely that the defendant’s capacity was substantially impaired.
why: Diminished responsibility is one of the rare defences where the burden is on the DEFENDANT, on the balance of probabilities (Homicide Act 1957 s 2(2)). The jury must find it 'more likely than not', so if they think impairment unlikely, the defence fails. Your picks wrongly put the burden on the prosecution.

stem: A person has been arrested and detained on suspicion of criminal damage by daubing a £1,000 political advertising board with red paint (a summary offence). A police officer saw the person commit the offence and arrested them immediately. The person wishes to receive legal advice but a superintendent at the station has authorised a delay of legal advice on the basis that they have reasonable grounds for suspecting that exercising the right to legal advice will interfere with evidence. The detainee subsequently confesses during their Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 interview. The admissibility of the confession is challenged at trial. Which of the following is the best argument for the defence to exclude the confession?
correct: This offence was summary only so there was no basis for preventing legal advice.
why: PACE s 58(8): access to a solicitor can be delayed only for an INDICTABLE offence, on a superintendent's authority, with reasonable grounds for BELIEVING one of the s 58(8) harms will result. This offence is summary-only, so there was no power to delay at all. 'Believing, not suspecting' (your pick) is also a true flaw, but it is secondary: the threshold condition was never met. A true statement that is not the strongest answer is your recurring trap.

stem: The defendant is charged with burglary. At the trial in the Crown Court, officers give evidence to the effect that, upon their arrival at the burgled house, they noticed that the kitchen glass window had been smashed and then saw the defendant hiding down a rear alleyway close to the burgled. The defendant was breathing heavily, sweating profusely and his trousers had a jagged tear. The evidence from the police officers at the scene is that they reasonably believed that the tear was a result of the defendant’s commission of the burglary. They also said that, in interview, after the standard caution about the right to silence, they had told the defendant of their belief that the defendant was down the alleyway because they had committed the offence and asked the defendant to account for his presence at the scene but the defendant refused to tell them. No other caution was administered. May the court draw such inferences as appear proper from the defendant’s refusal to account for the condition of their clothing?
correct: No, the court may not draw inferences from the refusal to account for the condition of their clothing.
why: s 36 CJPOA 1994 allows inferences from a failure to account for objects, substances or MARKS (including the condition of clothing). But only if the officer tells the suspect of the belief, asks them to account for the specific mark, and gives the special warning (Code C 10.10–10.11). Here they asked only about presence (a s 37 issue) and gave no special warning, so no inference can be drawn about the torn trousers. Your pick is wrong because s 36 does cover clothing; its conditions just were not met.

stem: Two defendants are being prosecuted for murder. Allegedly, both carried out a sustained attack on the victim that caused multiple injuries that caused death. The evidence shows that one or the other or both (and no one else) caused the injuries. Defendant A claims to have tried to stop defendant B and wishes to adduce evidence of two of defendant B’s convictions for grievous bodily harm with intent to show their violent nature. Will the defendant A be able to prove defendant B’s convictions?
correct: Only if the court decides that the convictions have substantial probative value in proving defendant B’s propensity towards violence.
why: Co-defendant's bad character: gateway s 101(1)(e) CJA 2003 requires SUBSTANTIAL probative value in relation to an important matter in issue between the defendant and the co-defendant. The s 101(3) 'unfairness' exclusion does not apply to gateway (e) (it protects the defendant against the prosecution). That is why your pick, with its 'unless unjust' qualifier, is wrong.

stem: A defendant has been convicted of an offence contrary to s 5 of the Public Order Act 1986; a non-imprisonable offence. Which of the following accurately represents the possible sentences that the court can impose?
correct: A discharge or a fine.
why: A community order can only be imposed for an offence punishable with imprisonment (Sentencing Code s 202). Custody is obviously impossible too. For a non-imprisonable offence such as s 5 POA, the options are a discharge or a fine (plus ancillary orders).

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for burglary of a shop and has elected trial in the magistrates’ court. The prosecution case is that the defendant broke in through the back of the shop after it had closed. The defendant says that the shop owner has made up the allegation after the defendant accused them of sexually inappropriate behaviour and the defendant claims to have been at the cinema with a witness at the time of the burglary. What obligation is the defendant under to set out the details of this defence?
correct: The defendant must provide the name and details of the witness but is not obliged to provide any other details.
why: In the magistrates' court a defence statement is VOLUNTARY (CPIA 1996 s 6). But s 6C requires every defendant to serve notice of intended defence witnesses (names, addresses, dates of birth), not just alibi witnesses (your pick). The alibi particulars requirement lives in the defence statement, which D need not serve here.

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted in the magistrates’ court for five counts of theft from the owners of a golf club where they had been allowed to do some casual gardening work by the owners. The defendant is homeless, otherwise unemployed, in receipt of benefits, has a significant number of previous theft convictions and is currently released on licence in relation to two other theft counts. Which statement reflects the likely outcome of an application for a representation order?
correct: The defendant may be automatically eligible on the means test and likely to succeed on the merits test.
why: Means: defendants on passporting benefits (e.g. universal credit, income-based JSA/ESA, income support, guarantee pension credit) are automatically eligible. Merits (interests of justice, Widgery criteria): a likely loss of liberty is the key factor. With many previous theft convictions and being on licence (risk of recall), custody is a real risk, so the merits test is likely passed.

stem: A defendant has been excluded from the magistrates’ court after shouting abuse at court staff and jeering loudly at the start of proceedings. The court is scheduled to decide whether to send the case (two counts of grievous bodily harm) to the Crown Court. In what circumstances can the Magistrates’ Court proceed in the defendant’s absence at this point?
correct: It can proceed to plea and allocation so long as the defendant is legally represented and it is not practicable to proceed with the defendant present.
why: MCA 1980 ss 17B/18(3): the court may proceed with plea before venue and allocation in D's absence ONLY IF D is legally represented and D's disorderly conduct makes it not practicable to proceed in their presence. Your pick omits the representation requirement.

stem: A defendant has been convicted of burglary of a shop late at night and assault occasioning actual bodily harm on a security guard while they were attempting to escape. Under the relevant sentencing guidelines, the judge decides that, if these offences were being sentenced separately, a 2-year sentence for the burglary and a 9-month sentence for the assault occasioning actual bodily harm would be appropriate. Having regard to the principle of totality, which of the following most accurately reflects how the judge is likely to impose sentence?
correct: 2 years and 3 months for the burglary and 9 months for the assault occasioning actual bodily harm to be served concurrently.
why: Totality (Sentencing Council guideline): offences arising from the same incident usually get CONCURRENT sentences, with the lead sentence increased so that the total reflects all the offending. So the burglary goes up to 2 years 3 months, with 9 months concurrent. Your pick makes the sentences concurrent without the uplift, which under-punishes the overall criminality.

stem: A defendant has been convicted of theft and the court is considering a 2- year conditional discharge. The defendant wishes to know more about this sentence. How should the defendant’s solicitor advise them about the sentence?
correct: The discharge means that they have no further punishment but will be subject to be resentenced if they commit an offence within the next 2 years.
why: Conditional discharge (Sentencing Code s 80): no punishment is imposed and there are no requirements. The only condition is committing no offence during the period (up to 3 years). If D reoffends within it, they can be resentenced for the original offence. Requirements belong to community orders and suspended sentences.

stem: An adult defendant is charged with racially aggravated common assault and criminal damage. The defendant, on impulse, became embroiled in an argument with the staff in a Chinese restaurant over their perceived failure to provide free prawn crackers. During the argument, the defendant slapped a member of staff in the face using highly derogatory, racist and hostile language about the Han Chinese before pushing over a tropical fish tank. He then stormed out of the building still making offensive racist remarks about the Chinese. The definition of both of the charged offences includes the words “demonstrating towards the victim a hostility based upon their membership or presumed membership of a racial group”. The defendant, who was on bail at the time and has many recent convictions for similar offences, is due to be sentenced today. The defendant has not shown any remorse. Which of the following statutory aggravating features must be taken into account and which mitigating factors may be considered when moving the sentence starting point?
correct: The previous convictions, that the offence was committed on bail and that the offence was impulsive.
why: Statutory aggravation: previous convictions (Sentencing Code s 65) and offending on bail (s 64). Racial hostility (s 66) cannot be added on top, because it is already an element of the racially aggravated offences: no double counting. A guilty plea is a separate reduction, not mitigation, and none is mentioned here. Acting on impulse (lack of premeditation) is genuine mitigation.

stem: A defendant was charged with theft. At the first appearance, the defendant did not enter a plea and the issue of plea before venue was adjourned to a second hearing, where the defendant pleaded guilty. The case was then adjourned to a Newton hearing at which the judge accepted the defence version of the facts of the offence. How much discount when passing sentence is the court likely to allow for the guilty plea?
correct: A one-quarter discount, given that the plea was tendered at the adjourned plea before venue hearing.
why: Guilty plea guideline: the full one-third is given only for a plea indicated at the FIRST stage of proceedings (normally the first hearing). D entered no plea then, so the maximum is one quarter. A Newton hearing reduces the credit only if D's version is REJECTED. Here it was accepted, so the quarter stands.

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for robbery but denies any involvement. He was arrested after the victim pointed him out on a nearby street when the police drove her around to find the robber. The police had earlier taken and recorded a description from the victim. The defendant requested an identification procedure, but the police refused to hold one. Which of the following is the most accurate reflection of the victim’s ability to identify that it was the defendant who robbed her in her evidence in court?
correct: She will be able to do so because she had previously described the robber and an on-street identification was appropriate in this case.
why: The street identification was proper: the description was recorded first and there was no known suspect at that stage (Code D 3.2). Arguably a later procedure should have been held once D disputed the identification (Code D 3.12). But a Code D breach does NOT automatically exclude the evidence. It goes to the s 78 discretion and usually to a jury direction. So 'will be excluded' (your pick) overstates the position, and the victim can identify D.

stem: An adult faces trial for an offence of affray. The affray took place in a crowded street. A witness claims to have seen the defendant throw a bottle at the police. The defendant admits that he was present in the street at the time of the affray but was an innocent bystander and did not throw a bottle. The trial judge is about to sum up. Which of the following options is the best approach for the trial judge to take in relation to the issue of identification in the case?
correct: If there is any doubt about the defendant’s participation in the affray, a Turnbull warning should be given as part of the summing up.
why: Turnbull applies wherever the case depends substantially on the correctness of an identification, including where PRESENCE is admitted but the witness may have mistaken who did the act, as with a crowded street (R v Slater; R v Thornton). Admitted presence (your pick) does not remove the risk of misidentifying the participant.

stem: A defendant is facing trial for actual bodily harm on an adult male following a violent attack at a demonstration. The male victim tells the police that he thinks he knows who it was and describes someone matching the defendant’s description. Based on other intelligence they have, the police suspect the defendant, so they drive the victim to another demonstration that they believe the defendant will be at. There, the victim identifies the defendant. The police refuse to hold any further identification procedure deeming it to be unnecessary. What is the most likely way in which this identification evidence will be dealt with at the defendant’s trial?
correct: It may be excluded as evidence and the victim will only be able to describe the person who committed the attack.
why: Once the police have a KNOWN suspect who disputes identification, Code D requires a formal procedure (normally a video identification). Taking the victim to a demo to 'spot' him is an informal confrontation-style ID and a serious breach. It may be excluded under s 78 PACE. If so, the victim can only describe the attacker; a first-time dock identification is not allowed.

stem: A witness has just finished testifying for the prosecution in a defendant’s trial for robbery during which the witness confidently claimed to have seen the defendant leaving the property in question at the relevant time. The witness was challenged about being very short sighted but denied the fact. Can the defence produce independent evidence of the witness’ short- sightedness?
correct: Yes, because it relates to a medical disability.
why: Answers on collateral matters of credit are normally final. One exception is evidence of a physical or mental DISABILITY that affects the witness's reliability (Toohey v MPC), and severe short-sightedness is such a disability. Credibility in general (your pick) is the rule, not the exception, so it is too wide.

stem: A defendant is on trial for fraud. An employee was working for the company for which the defendant works and overheard the defendant making various false promises over the phone that are the basis for the fraud offence. The employee is a little concerned that they might lose their job if they testify against the defendant. The prosecution wishes to adduce the witness statement of the employee by reading it out in court. Can a statement by the employee be submitted as evidence instead?
correct: Yes, but only if can be established that the employee is being kept away from court through fear.
why: s 116(2)(e) CJA 2003: the statement of an identified witness who does not give evidence through FEAR is admissible with the court's leave (interests of justice, s 116(4)). The fear must be proved, not merely claimed. The overheard phone calls are not hearsay at all (the false promises ARE the fraud), so the employee's own evidence would be admissible. That is why both of your picks are wrong.

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for assault occasioning actual bodily harm on a victim and is raising the defence of self-defence. The prosecution case is that the defendant issued racially abusive tweets that the victim took offence at and, when the victim immediately went round to the defendant’s flat to complain, the defendant punched them in fury at being criticised. Is evidence of the abusive tweets likely to be admissible?
correct: Yes, as bad character that has to do with the offence.
why: Evidence 'to do with the alleged facts of the offence' falls OUTSIDE the statutory definition of bad character (s 98(a) CJA 2003). So no gateway is needed, and it is admissible if relevant: the tweets explain the victim's visit and D's motive. ⚠ KEY LOOKS WRONG: on s 98(a), option A ('not bad character evidence and has to do with the offence') is the accurate statement, and the key's 'bad character that has to do with the offence' contradicts itself. Your pick (D) is the test for 'important explanatory evidence' (s 101(1)(c)), which is only needed for evidence that IS bad character.

stem: A defendant is being tried for theft, the case being that the defendant has taken money from a charity for which the defendant volunteers as an accountant. The defendant attends court wearing a cross on the lapel of their jacket and carrying a rosary and, when giving evidence, she explains at length the work undertaken voluntarily for the charity. The prosecution has evidence that the defendant lost her job as a teacher for downloading indecent images of children. Is the evidence of the downloading of indecent images likely to be admissible as evidence correcting a false impression of honesty?
