correct: No, because the evidence would not correct any false impression that the defendant has given as to honesty.
why: s 101(1)(f) / s 105 CJA 2003: evidence correcting a false impression is admissible only if it has probative value in correcting THAT impression, and goes no further than necessary. Her evidence suggests honesty and piety. Downloading indecent images says nothing about dishonesty, so it does not correct the impression of honesty and would only be prejudicial.

stem: Two co-defendants are being jointly prosecuted for a robbery. Defendant A’s defence is that defendant B put them under pressure to commit the offence (the defence of duress). The prosecution has an unlawful undercover recording of defendant B threatening defendant A to force them to commit the offence. However, the prosecution has decided not to use the recording because it will almost certainly be subject to a successful application to have it excluded by defendant B. The recording has been disclosed to defendant A. Will defendant A be able to have the evidence admitted at trial?
correct: Yes and defendant B will not be able to have it excluded under Police and Criminal Evidence Act 1984 s 78.
why: s 78 PACE applies only to evidence 'on which the PROSECUTION proposes to rely'. It cannot be used to exclude evidence a co-defendant adduces (Lobban v R; R v Myers). Evidence obtained unlawfully is still admissible if relevant, so A can adduce the recording and B has no s 78 route to exclude it.

stem: A prosecution witness is 9 years old and a witness to a burglary. The child suffers from mental disabilities. How will the court determine the child's competence to give evidence?
correct: The witness is deemed competent unless they are unable to understand questions put in court and give understandable answers.
why: Competence (YJCEA 1999 s 53(3)): any witness is competent unless unable to (a) understand questions put to them as a witness and (b) give answers that can be understood. Age or disability alone does not matter. 'Solemnity of the occasion' and 'responsibility to tell the truth' (your pick and B) are the test for giving SWORN evidence (s 55), not for competence.

stem: A person is a complainant in a sexual assault case. There is no option for pre-trial cross examination. What special measures, by default, will be put in place for the person?
correct: The video interview will stand as evidence-in-chief, and cross- examination will take place behind a screen.
why: An adult complainant in a sexual case is automatically eligible for special measures (YJCEA s 17(4)). In the Crown Court their ABE video interview is admitted as evidence-in-chief unless that would not be in the interests of justice (s 22A). Without s 28 pre-recording, cross-examination happens at trial, and the default in the course materials is in court behind a screen (live link can be sought instead). Giving ALL evidence by live link (your pick) ignores the recorded interview.

stem: A defendant was refused bail at the first appearance and has now attended a second hearing, at which the magistrates’ court has adjourned the case for trial and refused bail. Can the defendant apply for bail again?
correct: Yes, but the magistrates do not need to hear arguments on facts and law in relation to bail unless there is a change in circumstances.
why: Bail Act Sch 1 Part IIA: at the hearing AFTER the first refusal, D may raise any argument. At later hearings, the court need not hear arguments of fact or law it has already heard, so a fresh application needs a change of circumstances or new considerations. D can also appeal to the Crown Court, but is not obliged to go there (your pick).

stem: A defendant has been charged with the murder of their partner following a heated argument. Their solicitor has noted substantial evidence to suggest the defences of diminished responsibility or loss of control will apply. The police will have to make a remand decision about the defendant. What advice should the solicitor give to the defendant about the likelihood of bail being granted by the police?
correct: Bail cannot be granted by the police because the defendant has been charged with murder.
why: A person charged with murder may be granted bail ONLY by a Crown Court judge (Coroners and Justice Act 2009 s 115). The police, and indeed the magistrates, have no power to grant it. So it is not a question of 'unlikely' (your pick): police bail is impossible.

stem: A defendant has been charged with common assault and criminal damage to the value of £2,500 (summary-only offences) following a dispute between neighbours. It is the first appearance and the defendant has been on bail so far. The magistrates are adjourning the case for trial and are considering bail. They decide there are substantial grounds for believing the defendant will continue to cause minor damage to neighbours’ properties. Are the magistrates entitled to refuse bail in this case?
correct: Not unless the defendant was on bail when the previous offences took place or has failed to surrender to custody or breached bail conditions.
why: These are summary-only IMPRISONABLE offences, so Bail Act Sch 1 Part IA applies. The grounds are narrower than for indictable offences: previous failure to surrender, the offence was committed while on bail (plus a risk of reoffending), breach of bail conditions, D's own protection, or a risk of offences causing injury or fear. A risk of further minor damage is not, on its own, a ground. Conditions (your pick) are irrelevant if no refusal ground exists.

stem: A defendant’s legal representative is seeking a representation order for their prosecution for criminal damage to the value of £120. The defendant has just started working as a solicitor. The defendant has no previous convictions and alleges that they have been wrongly identified as the offender. Assuming they pass the means test, which answer reflects the best appraisal of whether a representation order is likely in the defendant’s case?
correct: Because the defendant’s case may require expert cross-examination and because of a risk of potential loss of livelihood.
why: Interests of justice (Widgery criteria): a likely loss of livelihood (a new solicitor convicted of a dishonesty-type offence) and a need for skilled cross-examination (identification is disputed, so the eyewitnesses must be tested) both favour a representation order. D's premise (your pick) that a professional 'could represent themselves effectively' is wrong. The Widgery factor is whether D can conduct their own case, and testing identification witnesses needs expertise.

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for multiple counts of fraud in their capacity as a chairperson of a charity. The defendant is employed once a week at a primary school in a self-employed capacity as a supply teacher. They jointly own a house with their partner, subject to a large mortgage and with very little equity. They also have a very small amount of savings, in the hundreds of pounds. The defendant strongly denies the allegations of fraud and there is likely to be the need for a forensic accountant to establish the defence they want to advance. The defendant is seeking a representation order for proceedings in the Crown Court. What is the most likely outcome of such an application?
correct: The defendant will automatically pass the merits and will have to pass the means test subject to the issues of contributions.
why: Crown Court: the interests of justice (merits) test is AUTOMATICALLY satisfied for proceedings in the Crown Court, so D does not merely 'likely pass' (your pick). The means test still applies, and a Crown Court defendant may have to pay contributions from income and/or capital.

stem: A defendant’s solicitor is appearing in the Crown Court and making a response to an argument made by the barrister appearing on the other side about the evidence given by a professor. Which of the following would be the proper way of addressing and referring to these people as part of an argument?
correct: My learned friend has made a key point in relation to the professor’s evidence which Your Honour may think is.
why: Crown Court (circuit judge): 'Your Honour'. 'Your Lordship' is for High Court judges (and certain senior Old Bailey judges). Opposing counsel is 'my learned friend'. A witness is referred to by their title ('the professor'), not as 'the person'.

stem: A defendant is due to be tried at the Crown Court but has not appeared by the allotted time. What course of action can the judge take?
correct: The judge may proceed in the defendant’s absence.
why: Trial on indictment in D's absence is a DISCRETION (R v Jones [2002] UKHL 5), to be exercised with great caution: has D voluntarily waived the right to attend, can a fair trial still be had, and so on. It is never automatic either way. Hence 'may proceed', not 'cannot' or 'must' (your picks).

stem: The prosecution is making an opening speech in the prosecution of a defendant for robbery in a park late at night. Neither the victim nor another eyewitness have given particularly confident descriptions of the defendant, but their evidence is supported by fingerprint evidence and items found on the defendant when arrested soon after. How should the prosecution address the issue of identification during their opening speech?
correct: They may outline the case and the witnesses they will call, including the victim and other eyewitness but should remind the jury that they bear the burden of proof.
why: The prosecution opening outlines the case, the evidence and the witnesses to be called, including any eyewitnesses, however shaky. Weaknesses in identification are dealt with by a Turnbull direction, not by leaving witnesses out of the opening. It should also remind the jury that the prosecution bears the burden of proof.

stem: A defendant has been prosecuted for causing grievous bodily harm to a victim with intent and claims to have been acting in self-defence. The defendant’s lawyer put to the victim and other prosecution witnesses that the defendant was attacked but the witnesses do not accept this. The witness the defendant had hoped to call to support the defence account does not appear, but the defendant gives evidence explaining how the victim started the assault. Does the judge have to leave the issue of self- defence to the jury in these circumstances?
correct: Yes because the defendant has done enough to discharge an evidential burden of proof.
why: The judge must leave self-defence to the jury once there is SOME evidence of it, and D's own testimony is enough to discharge the evidential burden. The prosecution must then disprove it beyond reasonable doubt. Your D answer states that consequence, but the reason the issue goes to the jury is that the evidential burden has been met. Your A answer is simply wrong: D's own evidence suffices.

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for assault occasioning actual bodily harm following a fight with a victim. The case has finished and the magistrates have retired to consider their verdict. They agree that there is evidence that the defendant might have been acting in self-defence but one magistrate cannot decide whether they were or not, one thinks the defendant “probably was not” and the third member is sure that the defendant was not. What verdict should they enter?
correct: They must acquit the defendant.
why: Once self-defence is raised, the PROSECUTION must disprove it to the criminal standard. A conviction needs a majority of the bench to be SURE. Here only one justice is sure (one 'probably not' is not sure), so they must acquit. D does not have to prove anything, and the evidential burden was met because the bench accepted there was evidence of self-defence.

stem: A defendant is charged with common assault and appears in the magistrates’ court. The victim lives in the same flat hostel as the defendant and claims that the defendant hit them from behind following an argument in the shared kitchen. Two witnesses were also in the kitchen at the time, as was the defendant. He admits presence but denies assault, claiming that the allegation is fabricated. No identification procedure was conducted but the prosecution wants to ask the victim to point to the person in court who hit them. Should the defendant’s legal representative object to an in-court identification in this case?
correct: No, because a prior out-of-court identification would have served no useful purpose in proving or disproving the defendant’s involvement.
why: Code D 3.12: an identification procedure need not be held if it would serve no useful purpose, e.g. where it is not disputed that the suspect is already well known to the witness. The victim lives with D, and D admits being in the kitchen. The dispute is whether the assault happened (fabrication), not who did it, so a dock identification is not objectionable here.

stem: A witness is giving evidence against a defendant at trial for theft from the company they both work for. The defendant’s lawyer has accused the witness in cross-examination of making up the allegation against the defendant because the defendant, rather than the witness, got promoted to a senior role. At the close of the witness’ testimony, the prosecution applies to admit a diary entry the witness wrote prior to the promotion of the defendant in which they voiced their suspicions that the defendant was stealing from the company. Will the diary entry be admissible as evidence?
correct: Yes, because it is not a hearsay statement.
why: s 120(2) CJA 2003: where a witness is accused of RECENT FABRICATION, a previous consistent statement is admissible to rebut it, and becomes evidence of its truth. It must pre-date the alleged motive to fabricate (R v Oyesiku). ⚠ KEY LOOKS DOUBTFUL: such a statement is hearsay admitted by statute, not 'not hearsay'. Option C states the real condition (written before the witness learned of the promotion). The business-records route (your pick) is irrelevant.

stem: A defendant is being prosecuted for murder of a victim and is running the defence of loss of control. The defendant’s lawyers hoped to call a witness who was going to testify as to having been at the scene of the crime and having heard the victim say that the defendant was a “hopeless paedophile junkie”. By the time of trial, the witness cannot be found. The defendant has convictions for child sex offences and uses drugs. Can the witness’ statement be admitted as evidence?
correct: Yes, but only if they can show reasonably practical steps have been taken to find the witness.
why: s 116(2)(d) CJA 2003: the absent witness's statement is admissible if the witness cannot be found although such steps as are REASONABLY PRACTICABLE have been taken. 'Unavailable' alone (your pick) is too vague; the specific statutory condition must be shown. s 116 is available to the defence too. The victim's words are not hearsay, because they are relied on as the trigger for loss of control, not for their truth.

stem: An adult defendant is tried in the magistrates’ court for a low-level shoplifting offence and is convicted by a majority of justices two to one. How much should the justices disclose when revealing their verdict?
correct: They should give sufficient reasons to explain their decision.
why: Magistrates must announce their decision and, on conviction, give reasons sufficient to explain it (CrimPR; Art 6 ECHR; McKerry v Teesdale & Wear Valley JJ). A full reasoned judgment is not required. They should not reveal that the verdict was by majority. Giving reasons is mandatory, not optional (your pick).

stem: A group of three set designers work in partnership on projects for TV and film. On their last project, the production company shut down the production and kept some of their equipment and working materials. The designers want to issue a claim against the production company for unpaid fees and damages to compensate them for the loss of their property. The total value of the claim is approximately £70,000. How should the designers issue their claim?
correct: Send a claim form to the CIvil National Business Centre.
why: PD 7A: a County Court money claim issued on paper goes to the Civil National Business Centre, not to a local hearing centre. Money Claim Online (D) is only for a SPECIFIED sum under £100,000, and this claim includes unliquidated damages for the lost equipment. The defendant's location matters later, when the claim is transferred, not at issue.

stem: A surveyor served a defence relying on comparable sales data and a named estate agent report. Can the claimant obtain clarification and documents at this stage?
correct: They can serve a request for further information and obtain a copy of the report, but not any other documents.
why: Two separate tools. CPR Part 18 lets you request further information to clarify the defence. CPR 31.14 lets you inspect any document MENTIONED in a statement of case, so the named estate agent's report is covered. The underlying sales data was not specifically referred to, so it must wait for disclosure.

stem: A business that provides wedding venues has been served with a claim form and particulars of claim from a couple who were dissatisfied with the venue for their wedding. The defendant has acknowledged service but the deadline for service of the defence will be impossible for them to meet. There are 18 days left and the claimants have refused to agree any extension of time. What is the correct procedure for the defendant to ext defence?
correct: Issue and serve an application for an order to ext a witness statement explaining the reason further time is needed.
why: CPR 15.5: the parties may agree an extension of up to 28 days for the defence. Without that agreement, the defendant must apply to the court under Part 23: an application notice, supported by evidence (a witness statement explaining why more time is needed), served on the claimants. A consent order (your pick) needs consent, and the claimants have refused.

stem: A solicitor has been sued for professional negligence in relation to advice concerning a corporate transaction. It is alleged that, due to the negligent advice, an important element of the transaction was ineffective, causing substantial losses. The solicitor denies negligence, saying the client gave incorrect instructions. Alternatively, the solicitor claims the client was contributorily negligent because they did not read the assumptions contained in the advice before proceeding with the transaction. Which party bears the burden of proof concerning the alleged negligence of the solicitor?
correct: The client, because as claimant they bear the burden of proof on their case.
why: Whoever asserts must prove. As claimant, the client must prove its own case, i.e. that the solicitor was negligent. The solicitor bears the burden only on positive defences it raises, such as contributory negligence. But the question asks about the solicitor's negligence, which stays with the client. Option B is wrong because the claimant does not bear the burden on every issue.

stem: Three business partners run a firm of financial advisers as a general partnership. Two of the partners are in dispute with a parent of the other partner, who has received a substantial amount of financial advice and agreed to pay commercial terms. However, the parent is now unwilling to pay. The two partners intend to commence a claim against the third partner’s parent for unpaid bills, rendered over the last 3 years, in the sum of £25,000 plus interest. The two partners are individual claimants. The third business partner does not want to participate in the claim against their parent. Which of the following statements best describes how or if the proceedings should progress?
correct: The third business partner should be added as a defendant.
why: CPR 19.3: where a claimant seeks a remedy to which someone else is jointly entitled (here, a partnership debt), every jointly entitled person must be a party. Anyone who does not agree to be a claimant must be added as a DEFENDANT, unless the court orders otherwise. The claim continues; no permission is needed.

stem: A claimant has brought a claim against a surveyor, alleging negligence in relation to a property purchase. In the surveyor’s defence, they deny liability and raise various matters that were not addressed by the claimant in the particulars of claim. Does the claimant have to serve a reply?
correct: No, because a reply to a defence in not mandatory.
why: A reply is optional (CPR 15.8). A claimant who files no reply is NOT taken to admit the matters in the defence (CPR 16.7(1)). Your pick wrongly reverses this, and whether there is a counterclaim is beside the point. Only a defence to a counterclaim is compulsory.

stem: An individual resident in New Zealand has been served with a claim form and particulars of claim by a payday lending company in England. The claim alleges that they guaranteed the payment obligations of a family member under a loan agreement. The acknowledgment of service in the response pack confirms that the individual has 26 days from service of the claim form and particulars of claim to file an acknowledgment of service, a defence or admission form. The individual wishes to acknowledge service and indicate that they intend to defend the claim. When will the defence have to be filed?
correct: 40 days from service of the claim form and particulars of claim.
why: Service out of the jurisdiction (PD 6B table): the AoS period for New Zealand is 26 days. If an AoS is filed, the defence is due at the table period PLUS 14 days, i.e. 26 + 14 = 40 days from service of the particulars. The 14-day/28-day domestic rules do not apply.

stem: A claimant is pursuing a personal injury claim against their local council. They validly served a claim form on solicitors acting for the council by fax. The fax was transmitted at 4.45pm on Thursday. What is the deemed date of service of the claim form?
correct: Monday.
why: A claim form is deemed served on the SECOND BUSINESS DAY after the relevant step under CPR 7.5 is completed (CPR 6.14). For fax, the step is completing transmission: Thursday. Friday is business day 1 and Monday is day 2. The 4.30pm cut-off applies to other documents (CPR 6.26), not to the claim form.

stem: Two former business partners are in dispute concerning the allocation of money between them following the dissolution of their partnership. One of the business partners has issued a claim and the other has filed a defence. The defendant has said in their directions questionnaire that they would like to attempt to settle and has requested a 6-month stay of the proceedings for a mediation. The claimant has indicated they are willing to attempt to settle but opposes the 6-month stay. Is the court likely to grant the stay sought by the defendant?
correct: No, because the overriding objective requires that the court give directions to ensure the trial of a case proceeds quickly and efficiently.
why: The court can stay for ADR (CPR 26.5) and encourage it (Churchill v Merthyr Tydfil), but the overriding objective also requires cases to be dealt with expeditiously. A 6-month stay opposed by the claimant is disproportionate; a short stay or ADR direction is more likely. ADR is not a precondition to trial (C), and stays are not capped at one month (D).

stem: A taxi driver who lives and works in Torquay has been sued by the company for which they work for allegedly underreporting fares. The claim form was served by a process server at the taxi driver’s home. The particulars of claim was served 7 days later by post. The taxi driver has filed an acknowledgment of service with the court stating their intention to defend the claim in full. They also intend to counterclaim for sums they claim the company has unlawfully withheld from them. If they are found liable in the company’s claim, they will seek to set-off that sum against what is due to them from the company. By when should the defence and counterclaim be filed?
correct: Both within 28 days of the date of deemed service of the particulars of claim.
why: CPR 15.4: the defence is due 14 days after service of the PARTICULARS, or 28 days if an AoS is filed. The clock runs from deemed service of the particulars (served 7 days after the claim form here), not from the AoS or the claim form. A counterclaim filed WITH the defence needs no permission (CPR 20.4), so both share that date.

stem: A negligence claim has been brought against a small firm of architects in relation to a building project they designed for the claimant 4 years ago. The firm denies negligence and says they followed detailed measurements supplied by the building contractor by email. The claimant and the contractor allege that the first measurements were estimates and were superseded with exact measurements provided during several subsequent discussions with the firm. The individual architect that did the work is no longer with the firm. The firm has said they cannot provide inspection of the relevant meeting notes and working papers because they are no longer within the firm’s control - the only copies are on the personal laptop of their former colleague. How can the claimant seek inspection of relevant material on the laptop?
correct: Apply for an order against the individual architect for copies of the working papers and meeting notes.
why: Non-party disclosure (CPR 31.17): the court can order a non-party to disclose specified documents that are likely to support the applicant's case or adversely affect another party's, where necessary to dispose fairly of the claim. The order must be targeted: the working papers and meeting notes, not the whole laptop (disproportionate and intrusive). The architect's consent is not required.

stem: An individual that is resident in India has been served at their home with a claim form and particulars of claim. The claim alleges that they have breached the terms of an agreement to settle a previous claim. The individual denies the claim. A response pack is enclosed with the claim form and particulars of claim and indicates that the individual has 23 days from the date of service to respond. The individual intends to defend the claim but requires more time to prepare their defence. What should the individual include in the acknowledgment of service?
correct: State that they intend to defend the claim and provide an address for service in England and Wales.
why: The AoS simply states whether the defendant intends to defend all or part of the claim or to contest jurisdiction. A defendant served abroad must give an address for service in the jurisdiction (CPR 6.23). No reasons are given in an AoS. An extension is a separate matter: agreed with the claimant (up to 28 days, CPR 15.5) or sought from the court, not requested in the form.

stem: Two former business partners are in dispute concerning the allocation of profits between them. The claimant claims they are entitled to 75%. The defendant claims they agreed a 50:50 split. Both the claimant and defendant now operate independently in competing businesses. The defendant’s disclosure includes a series of emails from 6 months ago to former clients of the partnership, saying that everything had been shared 50:50 and the claim is motivated by spite. The defendant also wrote that the claimant was incompetent and had made serious mistakes for various previous clients. Both parties were cross-examined at trial about various documents that mentioned their profit share, including each of the defendant’s emails to the former clients. Judgment is awaited. The claimant wants to issue a claim against the defendant for defamation. Can the claimant use the emails for their defamation claim?
correct: Yes.
why: CPR 31.22: a disclosed document may be used only for the proceedings in which it was disclosed, UNLESS it has been read to or by the court or referred to at a hearing held in public, or the court or the disclosing party consents. The emails were put to the parties in cross-examination at a public trial, so the restriction has fallen away and no permission is needed.

stem: A shareholder in a company has issued an unfair prejudice claim against their fellow shareholders. They allege that the other shareholders have brought the company to the brink of collapse by diverting business worth £220,000 per year from 12 different customers to a competing company owned just by the other shareholders. The other shareholders deny this. The claimant seeks an order that the other shareholders buy them out, based on a fair valuation for their shares. A fair valuation will have to include an adjustment to compensate the shareholder for any business diverted away from the company by the other shareholders, to the extent that is established at trial. Which of the following would be an appropriate case management direction?
correct: A preliminary issue trial.
why: Whether the business was diverted at all is a discrete factual issue on which the valuation depends. Ordering it to be tried first as a preliminary issue avoids costly valuation evidence that may prove unnecessary, and fits the overriding objective. A 4-week disclosure deadline is unrealistic for 12 customers' dealings over years, and the claim is plainly multi-track.

stem: The parties to a civil claim have agreed, in an exchange of emails, that they need more time to complete disclosure. The current deadline is in 4 weeks, but they have agreed on an extension of time of 2 months. The order for directions did not specify any specific sanction for not complying with the disclosure deadline. The extension would not jeopardise any upcoming hearing. What must the parties do to make an extension of time effective?
correct: Nothing.
why: CPR 2.11: unless the rules or a practice direction say otherwise, parties may vary a time limit by written agreement. An email exchange is enough. Because no sanction attaches, CPR 3.8(4)'s 28-day cap does not apply, and no hearing is jeopardised. No consent order or application is needed.

stem: A claimant in civil proceedings has issued an application against the defendant for summary judgment. They believe the evidence in favour of their claim is overwhelming. What is the standard of proof necessary for the claimant to succeed on the application?
correct: The defendant has no real prospect of success.
why: Summary judgment (CPR Part 24): the court may give judgment against a defendant who has NO REAL PROSPECT of successfully defending the claim, where there is no other compelling reason for a trial. 'No reasonable grounds' (your pick) is the strike-out test under CPR 3.4(2)(a). The court does not decide the facts on the balance of probabilities at this stage.

stem: The parties to a county court claim concerning an allegedly defective engineer’s report on the strength of a building’s foundations are considering the possible directions for expert evidence from expert engineers. The case management conference is upcoming and the case will be allocated to the multi-track. The claimant argues that a single joint expert is appropriate. The defendant will ask the court for a direction that each side has their own expert. Which of the following statements best describes the likely approach of the court?
correct: A single joint expert because the case is of limited value and there is unlikely to be a range of expert opinion.
why: CPR 35.4/35.7 and PD 35: the court controls expert evidence and can direct a single joint expert even if a party objects. An SJE is favoured where the claim is of modest value and the technical issue is narrow, with little range of expert opinion. Every expert owes an overriding duty to the court (CPR 35.3), so that is no reason to prefer an SJE (your pick). Multi-track allocation does not automatically mean separate experts.

stem: During the process of reviewing material for standard disclosure, the defendant’s solicitor encounters an entry from the defendant’s electronic calendar. However, the file is corrupted and only shows the date but no other details. The date in question is significant to the case because the claimant alleges it is the date that the defendant contacted a third party and procured the third party to breach its contract with the claimant. The defendant does not recall the subject of the calendar entry. Is the calendar entry disclosable?
correct: No, because it is not relevant to the case.
why: Standard disclosure (CPR 31.6) covers documents a party relies on, or that adversely affect or support a party's case. An electronic calendar entry IS a 'document' (CPR 31.4). But a corrupted entry showing only a date reveals nothing about any issue, so it neither supports nor undermines either case. Speculation about what it 'might have contained' does not make it disclosable.

stem: The defendant to a civil claim is a small company with three employees. A customer has brought a claim for breach of contract concerning certain services provided by the defendant’s team over the last 5 years. The parties are preparing to undertake searches for potentially disclosable documents on their electronic devices. They have discussed a set of key word search terms and are largely agreed. However, the claimant has insisted that the defendant should search for and review all documents containing any part of the claimant’s name. The defendant objects because the parties have done business during the last 5 years in relation to eight large projects that are unrelated to the claim. How should the defendant proceed?
correct: Reject the further search terms.
why: Searches need only be reasonable and proportionate (CPR 31.7; PD 31B). Searching every document containing any part of the claimant's name would sweep in eight unrelated projects across the same 5-year period. That is disproportionate for a three-person company. A date limit (your pick) does not help, because the unrelated projects fall within the same 5 years.

stem: The parties to a civil claim are preparing for the case management conference. They both have hard copy documents and a number of electronic devices and are discussing how they might be searched. Which of the following documents are the parties required to complete before the case management conference?
correct: Disclosure report.
why: Multi-track: each party must file and serve a disclosure report (Form N263), describing what documents exist, where they are, and how they will be searched, at least 14 days before the first CMC (CPR 31.5(3)). The disclosure STATEMENT comes later, when disclosure is actually given. The electronic documents questionnaire is optional.

stem: The defendant in civil proceedings concerning a loan agreement is undertaking disclosure searches for relevant electronic documents on their company server. The search terms have been agreed with the claimant. The set of documents produced by the search includes a large subset of approximately 3,500 documents that are obviously unrelated to the issues in dispute. They are specialist files run through a piece of design software used by the defendant. All the documents in the subset have been captured by the same key word search term, used in those documents in an unrelated context. Which of the following statements describes the most appropriate next step in relation to this issue?
correct: Write to the claimant seeking their agreement to exclude the specialist file type.
why: PD 31B requires the parties to co-operate on electronic disclosure and to agree, or seek directions on, the scope of searches. The fix is to drop the irrelevant specialist FILE TYPE. The key word remains useful in other documents. Do it by agreement with the claimant, not unilaterally (your pick).

stem: The defendant to a civil claim for damages of £500,000 is undertaking disclosure. They have applied agreed search criteria and have a set of 400 electronic documents for manual review. The defendant’s solicitor has written to their opponent proposing that they use a technology-assisted review process to further reduce the documents that will require manual review. The process would involve machine-learning, whereby specialist software would learn from decisions of solicitors reviewing a subset of the documents and then prioritise those it considers most relevant. Documents that the software judges to fall below a pre-determined relevance threshold would not be manually reviewed. The claimant has objected to the proposal and the defendant has sought directions from the court. Is the court likely to approve the defendant’s proposal?
correct: No, because the number of documents does not justify an automated technology-assisted review process.
why: Technology-assisted review is accepted where it is proportionate (Pyrrho Investments v MWB), typically with very large document sets. 400 documents can easily be reviewed manually, so imposing TAR over the claimant's objection is not justified. Who pays for the software is irrelevant.

stem: A company has brought a claim for breach of contract against a supplier of bespoke software. The company alleges the software is incompatible with their existing systems. The supplier denies the claim, saying they complied with all the specifications agreed with the company. Shortly before the company and supplier made their agreement, there was a board meeting to review the draft contract. The company’s in-house counsel gave a short presentation about the parties’ rights and obligations under the draft contract and answered questions from the directors about liability if there was a problem in the future. The in-house counsel says the presentation and meeting minutes are privileged and therefore do not need to be disclosed. Are the documents likely to be privileged?
correct: Yes, because they are protected by legal advice privilege.
why: Legal advice privilege covers confidential communications between lawyer and client for the dominant purpose of giving or getting legal advice, and in-house counsel acting as lawyers count. Advising the board on the parties' rights and liabilities under a draft contract is legal advice. Litigation privilege does not apply (no litigation was in contemplation), nor does WP or common interest.

stem: The defendant to a civil claim arranged to meet an important witness to events relevant to their case, in the hope that the witness could provide them with helpful evidence. They met for lunch to discuss the matter. The defendant said the discussion was “off the record”. They then told the witness they were very worried about the case and explained the issues on which the witness would be able to provide useful evidence. They said that, without the witness’s evidence, they believed their defence would not stand up. The witness said they were not prepared to provide evidence and, if they did, it would not be helpful to the defendant’s case. The defendant is worried that the witness might be called by the claimant and divulge what was said by the defendant at the lunch. Are the defendant’s statements to the witness privileged?
correct: Yes, because the dominant purpose was obtaining evidence for the litigation.
why: Litigation privilege: communications between a party (or its lawyer) and a THIRD PARTY are privileged when litigation is in progress or reasonably contemplated and the dominant purpose is obtaining information or evidence for it (Waugh v BRB; SFO v ENRC). Privilege attaches to communications, so oral ones count. It does not matter that the witness refused to help.

stem: Three shareholders are defendants to a claim by another shareholder. The claimant alleges that the other shareholders have conspired to unfairly prejudice them. The first defendant has received a very positive legal opinion in which their solicitors say the claim is extremely unlikely to succeed. It also includes a summary of the first defendant’s account of relevant events, given to their solicitors. The first defendant printed copies of the opinion and left one on the desk of each of the other shareholders. They attached a note which read, “just between us, this case is over”. However, the first defendant misread a key element of the opinion. The summary of their account of events also contradicts the pleaded defence. The claimant wishes to rely on the opinion at trial but the defendants claim it is privileged. Which of the following statements best describes the claimant’s copy of the opinion?
correct: It is admissible.
why: The opinion started out legally privileged, but the first defendant left a copy on the desk of EACH of the other shareholders, and the claimant is one of them. Privilege depends on confidentiality, and voluntary disclosure to your opponent waives it. Common interest privilege covers sharing with co-defendants, not with the adverse party. So the claimant's copy is admissible.

stem: The parties to a civil claim are in discussions concerning additional directions for the attendance of certain witnesses at trial by video link. They are not yet agreed but are confident they can agree on the arrangements shortly. The parties would prefer to present the court with an agreed position and therefore wish to delay filing their pre-trial checklists for 10 days. What must the parties do to vary the date for filing their pre-trial checklists?
correct: Seek permission from the court to extend the deadline.
why: CPR 29.5 (multi-track): the parties cannot vary by agreement the date for returning the pre-trial checklist, or the CMC, pre-trial review or trial dates. They must apply to the court. The 7-day notification idea (your pick) has no basis in the rules.

stem: A claimant in a civil claim has applied for summary judgment. In their judgment on the application, the judge has commented that the claimant might well have a good claim but there is very important evidence from several witnesses that must be tested at trial. Therefore, summary judgment will not be ordered. No relevant offers to settle the application have been made and the court has made no criticism of either party’s conduct. Which of the following costs orders is the most likely to be made?
correct: Claimant to pay the defendant’s costs of the application.
why: Costs follow the event (CPR 44.2(2)). A summary judgment application that fails is a lost application, so the usual order is that the applicant (claimant) pays the respondent's costs of it, typically summarily assessed. 'Costs in the case' (your pick) fits applications where neither side clearly wins. The judge's remark that the claim may be good does not change who lost this application.

stem: The defendant in a civil claim made four specific disclosure requests of the claimant in correspondence. The claimant refused. The defendant then made an application and has succeeded in obtaining the first three of the specific disclosure orders sought, but not the fourth. The court is considering what order to make on costs. The claimant has presented a without prejudice save as to costs offer made by them the day after the application was served. In that offer, they said they would be prepared to settle the application by agreeing to the first three of the disclosure orders sought but not the fourth, and pay the defendant’s costs to that point, subject to assessment. Which of the following is the most likely approach of the court to the defendant’s costs of the application?
correct: Award the defendant their costs in relation to the successful parts of the application up to the date of the claimant’s offer, subject to assessment.
why: The court must consider any admissible offer when deciding costs (CPR 44.2(4)(c)). The day after service, the claimant offered exactly what the defendant ended up winning, plus its costs to date. The defendant should have accepted. So the defendant gets the costs of the successful parts only UP TO the offer, and nothing for pursuing the application after that point.

stem: A claimant has brought a claim for breach of contract, seeking damages of £25,000,000. They have been successful after a 4-week trial and were awarded damages of £20,000,000. The parties are preparing their costs arguments in advance of the consequentials hearing. Two weeks before trial, the defendant made a Part 36 offer, in a standard form, to pay £22,000,000. Which of the following statements best describes the CPR Part 36 consequences of the defendant’s Part 36 offer?
correct: No CPR Part 36 consequences.
why: In principle, a claimant who fails to beat a defendant's Part 36 offer pays the defendant's costs, plus interest, from the end of the relevant period (CPR 36.17(3)), which is your pick. The trap is TIMING. The offer was made less than 21 days before trial, so the 'relevant period' runs to the END of the trial (CPR 36.3(g)). The Part 36 consequences therefore never bite, although the court can still weigh the offer under its general discretion (CPR 44.2).

stem: A claimant who suffered an injury at work has brought a personal injury claim against their employer, claiming damages of £50,000. The case was filed on 10 November 2023 and is of moderate complexity. The claimant won £30,000 in damages. The claimant incurred £40,000 in legal costs and the defendant incurred £60,000. Under the fixed recoverable costs (FRC) regime for the Intermediate Track, how will the costs be managed for the claimant if they win?
correct: The claimant can recover costs up to the fixed amount prescribed by the FRC schedule for a moderate complexity case in the Intermediate Track.
why: Intermediate track (claims issued on or after 1 Oct 2023, worth £25,000–£100,000, trial of 3 days or less): costs are FIXED RECOVERABLE COSTS set by complexity band (CPR 45, Table 14). The winner recovers the fixed figure for its band, not its actual spend. So the claimant cannot recover the full £40k, and the defendant, as loser, recovers nothing.

stem: A civil claim has been allocated to the fast-track. The claimant has been successful at trial and the court has made an order for costs. The claimant’s total costs of the claim were £45,000. The court has not criticised either party’s conduct. Which of the following best describes the order the court is likely to have made in respect of the claimant’s costs?
correct: Awarded fixed recoverable costs for various stages of the case, including trial preparation and attendance, as outlined in the fixed recoverable costs schedule.
why: Since 1 Oct 2023, fixed recoverable costs apply to the WHOLE of a fast-track claim, stage by stage and by complexity band (CPR 45, Table 12): pre-issue, issue, trial preparation and trial. Fixed costs only for trial advocacy (your pick) was the old pre-October-2023 regime.

stem: A claimant is considering whether to bring a civil claim in the county court against a supplier, seeking damages of £90,000 for breach of contract. The solicitor has advised that the case is likely to be allocated to the intermediate track, based on complexity and value. The claimant wants to understand the cost implications, including how costs will be managed if they win or lose at trial. Which of the following statements best describes the costs position in such a case?
correct: The claimant may recover legal costs but only up to the fixed amounts specified by Civil Procedure Rules.
why: The core position on the intermediate track is that the winner recovers costs only up to the fixed amounts in CPR 45. Your pick is a real rule, but a secondary one: CPR 45.13 lets the court adjust FRC by 50% for unreasonable conduct. The question asks for the costs position overall. As often in your mistakes, you picked a true statement that is not the best answer to the question asked.

stem: A defendant is the respondent to an application by the claimant for an extension of time to complete disclosure. The claimant has issued the application notice and filed evidence explaining why further time is required. They have also served the application papers on the defendant. The defendant wishes to oppose the application. A 1-hour hearing has been listed for a date in 28 days. The court has not given any specific directions in relation to how or when the defendant should respond to the application. Which of the following statements best describes how the defendant should proceed?
correct: File and serve a witness statement containing their reasons for opposing the application as soon as possible.
why: PD 23A: a respondent who wants to rely on evidence must file and serve it AS SOON AS POSSIBLE, subject to any court directions. The '3 clear days' rule (your pick) is the minimum period for the APPLICANT to serve the application notice before the hearing (CPR 23.7). Turning up with a skeleton argument or objecting by letter is not enough.

stem: A tenant residing in a property in Southampton has issued a claim against their landlord for damages in relation to injuries suffered when a ceiling collapsed on them. The landlord considers the claim to be vexatious and is aware that the tenant has issued personal injury claims against other landlords in the past. The tenant has no material assets and is acting as a litigant in person. The landlord wishes to apply to the court for security for costs. The tenant has been asked to provide security voluntarily but has refused, without giving reasons. Is the landlord likely to obtain an order for security for costs?
correct: No, because there is not any relevant ground for security for costs that is satisfied.
why: Security for costs is available only on a listed ground (CPR 25.13(2)). Inability to pay costs is a ground only for a claimant COMPANY (or a nominal claimant). An impecunious individual resident in England and Wales is not caught. A 'vexatious' track record is dealt with by civil restraint orders, and refusing to give security voluntarily is not a ground.

stem: A decorator is the defendant to a claim for breach of contract and negligence. It is alleged that they failed to use weatherproof paint on the exterior walls of a garden centre. The garden centre has an email from a former apprentice to the decorator. In the email, the former apprentice says the decorator instructed them to buy non- weatherproof paint but prepare an invoice to the garden centre for the higher cost of weatherproof paint. The apprentice is now based overseas and has not provided a witness statement, nor do they intend to give evidence at trial. The decorator and another former apprentice have both provided witness statements denying all the allegations and they intend to give oral evidence at trial. The deadline for exchange of witness statements is tomorrow. What must the garden centre do to rely on the email from the former apprentice at trial?
correct: Serve a hearsay notice.
why: The apprentice will not give evidence, so the email is hearsay. To rely on hearsay at trial, a party must serve a hearsay notice (Civil Evidence Act 1995 s 2; CPR 33.2), normally when witness statements are exchanged. A notice to admit facts (your pick) only asks the other side to concede facts, and the decorator denies everything.

stem: An accountant has been appointed to act as an expert witness for the defendant accountancy firm in a civil claim concerning alleged professional negligence. The accountant is preparing their expert report. During one of their discussions with the solicitors acting for the defendant, one of the legal team told the accountant “in confidence” that they thought the defendant’s case could be doomed due to an important miscalculation shown in an email that had emerged from disclosure. The solicitor showed the accountant the email but said they were not sure the other side had noticed the point. The accountant did not ask anything further as the issue is not relevant to their report. Does the accountant have to include the damaging information in their expert report?
correct: No, because the solicitor’s statement was not a fact or instruction that is material to their expert evidence.
why: CPR 35.10(3): the report must state the substance of all MATERIAL instructions on which it is based. A solicitor's private remark about the case's prospects, on an issue outside the expert's remit, is neither a material instruction nor something the report relies on. The duty to the court relates to matters within the expert's expertise and instructions.

stem: Two business partners decided to have their dispute determined by arbitration. They agreed that there would be no option to challenge the award on any basis and the arbitrator should not provide reasons for the award. After the arbitration award is delivered, one of the business partners refuses to accept it. Which of the following statements best describes the status of the award?
correct: The award is binding but it can be challenged by an application to the court if there was some serious irregularity in the arbitration.
why: Arbitration Act 1996: a s 69 appeal on a point of law can be excluded by agreement, and agreeing to dispense with reasons counts as excluding it (s 69(1)). But a challenge for serious irregularity (s 68) and a jurisdiction challenge (s 67) are MANDATORY and cannot be excluded. So the award binds, subject to s 68/67.

stem: An ambulance driver, employed by the ambulance service, suffered serious injuries when they were involved in a collision when driving an ambulance. The collision was the fault of another driver driving dangerously. However, the driver’s injuries would not have been serious but for a defective seatbelt. The maintenance of the ambulance was outsourced to an independent company with a contract with the ambulance service. Is the ambulance driver likely to have a cause of action against the maintenance company?
correct: Yes, because the maintenance company would have a duty of care to a driver of the ambulance they maintain.
why: Donoghue v Stevenson: whoever maintains a vehicle owes a duty of care in negligence to people foreseeably endangered by poor work, obviously including its driver. A contract with the ambulance service does not confine the company's duties to its customer. Tort duties run alongside the contract. The dangerous driver's fault does not exclude the company's own liability.

stem: A company had a dispute with a supplier. They agreed terms of settlement, which included an obligation on the supplier to make a payment of £10,000 to the company by 1 October 2016. The terms of settlement were set out in a deed of settlement executed by the parties on 1 September 2016. The supplier did not make payment as agreed. What is the last date on which the company can issue a claim for breach of contract?
correct: 1 October 2028.
why: An action on a deed (a specialty) has a 12-year limitation period (s 8 LA 1980), running from when the cause of action ACCRUES. That is the breach, i.e. non-payment on 1 October 2016, not the date the deed was executed. So the last day is 1 October 2028.

stem: A person intends to bring a claim against their former solicitor for negligence. Three years ago, the solicitor advised them on a claim against another party but failed to advise them to issue a claim form before the limitation deadline, meaning the claim became time-barred. The person has just instructed a new solicitor to advise on the matter. Which of the following statements best describes the next step that should be taken?
correct: A preliminary notice should be sent, briefly outlining the grievance, and asking that the former solicitors notify their insurers.
why: Professional Negligence Pre-Action Protocol: the first step is a PRELIMINARY NOTICE, sent as soon as there is a reasonable chance of a claim. It outlines the grievance and asks the professional to notify its insurers (acknowledgment within 14 days). The letter of claim comes after that. Limitation (6 years from damage) gives time, so there is no reason to issue now.

stem: A company has sent a letter of claim to their former accountants, alleging negligence concerning the preparation of the company’s financial report 2 years ago. The solicitors acting for the accountants acknowledged the letter of claim within 21 days and sent a letter of response denying liability 4 months later. The letter of response was accompanied by a letter of settlement, written on a without prejudice basis. It includes a request for further information concerning the company’s alleged losses and a proposal of mediation following receipt of the further information. The company wants to press on with their claim without any further delay. Is the company’s intended next step consistent with the Pre-Action Protocol for Professional Negligence?
correct: No, because there should be a negotiation period ending 6 months from the letter of acknowledgment, before proceedings are commenced.
why: Professional Negligence Pre-Action Protocol: even after a denial in the letter of response, the parties should negotiate and consider ADR. Proceedings should not be issued until the negotiation period has ended, i.e. 6 months from the letter of acknowledgment. A response that is a month late does not let the claimant skip that period. The proposal to mediate points the same way.

stem: A company that develops computer software for medical research is in dispute with a competitor. They believe that the competitor has obtained a copy of their valuable intellectual property and is using it unlawfully to develop competing software. Which of the following is the most appropriate place to issue a claim?
correct: High Court, Chancery Division.
why: Intellectual property claims (copyright and software, confidential information, patents) belong in the Chancery Division of the Business and Property Courts, which hosts the IP List, the Patents Court and IPEC. King's Bench (your pick) handles general tort and contract. The Commercial Court is for trade and banking disputes.

stem: A breach of contract claim between two large banks has been issued in the Commercial Court. The claim is for damages in excess of £25 million and a final injunction. The claimant’s solicitors are preparing for a hearing of an application for an interim injunction. Where should the solicitors first look for guidance on the court’s requirements for the application hearing?
correct: The Admiralty and Commercial Courts Guide.
why: A claim in the Commercial Court is governed by the Admiralty and Commercial Courts Guide. The Circuit Commercial Court Guide is for the regional commercial courts, and the Financial List has its own guide for claims issued in that List. This claim is in the Commercial Court proper.

stem: A company has been served with a claim form. The particulars of claim was served separately, a week later, by first class post. The covering letter enclosing the particulars of claim was dated Friday and received on Saturday. The company needs to calculate when the defence is due by reference to the deemed date of service of the particulars of claim. What is the deemed date of service of the particulars of claim?
correct: Monday, because that is the next business day after the second day after posting.
why: For documents OTHER than the claim form (CPR 6.26), first class post is deemed served on the second day after posting if that is a business day, otherwise on the next business day after it. Posted Friday, the second day is Sunday, so it is deemed served on Monday. Actual receipt is irrelevant. 'Second business day' (your pick) is the claim form rule (CPR 6.14).

stem: A small business owner is in dispute with a key supplier based in North Wales. For commercial reasons, they have been reluctant to issue proceedings and have been engaged in ongoing pre-action correspondence and negotiations to try to resolve the dispute. The limitation period is approaching, and the business owner has been advised to issue their claim as soon as possible. They intend to serve the claim form by first class post. After issuing the claim, how long will the claimant have to serve the claim?
correct: The claim form and the particulars of claim will have to be posted by 12 midnight, 4 months from the date the claim form was issued.
why: CPR 7.5: the claim form must be served by completing the step (here, posting) before midnight on the calendar day 4 months after issue. Particulars served separately must follow within 14 days, but NO LATER than the latest time for serving the claim form (CPR 7.4(2)). Close to the deadline, both must be posted within the 4 months.

stem: A high net worth Spanish businessperson, resident in London, hired a PR firm on a 1 year renewable contract. However, after 2 months, they stopped paying the monthly fee and stopped all communications with the firm. The PR firm issued and served a claim form and particulars of claim by post at the businessperson’s London residence. The claim is for fees due for work undertaken and damages for lost profits regarding work that would have been undertaken had the contract run its agreed term. The claim was ignored. Therefore, the PR firm filed a certificate of service and a request for judgment with the court after the 14 day period for acknowledging service or serving a defence had passed. Which of the following statements best describes the order the court is likely to make?
correct: Judgment on liability and for the specific fees claimed, with directions for determination of damages and costs.
why: Default judgment by REQUEST (CPR 12.4) is available here: the defendant was served within the jurisdiction and none of the cases needing an application applies. For a specified sum (the unpaid fees), judgment is for that sum. For an unspecified sum (damages for lost profits), judgment is for an amount to be decided by the court, with directions. Postal service is valid without proof of actual receipt.

stem: A hairdresser in Derby has been sued for negligence because they applied the wrong product on a client’s hair, leaving the client with a portion of their head where hair will no longer grow. The client has issued a claim in the County Court for damages arising from negligence. The claim form has been served on the hairdresser by post. The claim form states that the particulars of claim are to follow. What is the next procedural step for the hairdresser?
correct: Nothing until the particulars of claim are served.
why: CPR 9.1(2): where the claim form says the particulars of claim will follow, the defendant need not respond to the claim until the particulars are served. The 14-day clock for the AoS or defence then runs from service of the particulars (CPR 10.3, 15.4).

stem: A surveyor is a defendant to a claim for negligence by a property investor. The claimant alleges that the surveyor gave them an unrealistically high valuation of £12 million for a commercial property. On the basis of the valuation, the investor acquired the property at auction for £10 million. However, when seeking to mortgage the property, two independent surveyors have provided valuations of £8 million and £8.5 million. The surveyor has just served their defence, in which they deny negligence and assert that they relied on “data from other sales of comparable properties in the area” and “a report by a leading estate agent in the area published 6 months before the valuation”. Which of the following statements best describes whether the claimant can obtain clarification of the basis for the defendant’s valuation at this stage of the proceedings?
correct: They can serve a request for further information and obtain a copy of the report, but not any other documents.
why: Two separate tools. CPR Part 18 allows a request for further information to clarify the defence. CPR 31.14 gives a right to inspect any document MENTIONED in a statement of case, and the estate agent's report is named. The comparable-sales data is only described generically, so the underlying documents must wait for disclosure.

stem: A specialist carpentry company has issued proceedings against one of its wood suppliers. The carpentry company alleges that wood supplied was not within the contractual specifications, was sub-standard, and products manufactured with it have warped, causing them to have to refund customers on a series of projects. The carpentry company claims damages, including for its lost profits. It does not have a specific figure at this stage but believes that its losses are likely to be between £60,000 and £80,000, once more customers seek refunds and the lost profits are calculated. The claim will be issued in the County Court. On the claim form, the company has to give a statement of value. What should the company put as the statement of value?
correct: “The claimant expects to recover more than £25,000, but not more than £100,000.”.
why: CPR 16.3(2): in the County Court, the claimant states the bracket it expects to recover in: not more than £10,000; more than £10,000 but not more than £25,000; more than £25,000 but not more than £100,000; more than £100,000; or that it cannot say. An expected £60k–£80k falls in the £25,000–£100,000 band. 'Less than £100,000' (your pick) is not one of the prescribed brackets.

stem: A 25% shareholder in a company is in dispute with the other three shareholders. The cause of action is unfair prejudice, and the claimant shareholder is seeking an order that their shares be acquired by the majority shareholders at a fair value. The claimant shareholder alleges that the other three shareholders unfairly prejudiced them by removing them as a director and generally excluding them from decision-making in the business, contrary to what was agreed when the company was established. The parties have completed disclosure and exchanged relevant documents. The defendants have disclosed a series of emails between them which show that they paid dividends to themselves but not to the claimant. This also would amount to unfair prejudice. Which of the following statements best describes how the claimant shareholder should pursue this issue?
correct: Seek consent or permission to amend their statement of case to add the unlawful dividends, because that is an additional fact on which the cause of action should be based.
why: After service, a statement of case can be amended only with the written consent of all other parties or the court's permission (CPR 17.1(2)). The unequal dividends are a new factual allegation, which must be PLEADED if the claimant is to rely on it at trial. Adding new facts to an existing cause of action still counts as an amendment.

stem: A claim has been issued in the County Court by an individual against their local car mechanic. The claimant alleges that the mechanic was negligent and irreparably damaged the engine of their limited-edition car. They claim damages of £20,000. The mechanic alleges that the engine had an undetectable manufacturing fault. The claim has been allocated to the fast track. Which of the following is a likely case management direction?
correct: Service of witness statements and expert evidence.
why: Fast track (PD 28): standard directions cover disclosure, exchange of witness statements and (limited) expert evidence. A disputed manufacturing fault needs an expert. Costs budgets (your pick) are a multi-track tool (CPR 3.12), and a fast-track trial lasts no more than 1 day.

stem: The carer of an elderly testator is an avid amateur actor and a member of the local amateur dramatic society. The carer visited their client daily and regularly spoke to them about the society and its financial struggles. The testator had never demonstrated any interest in theatre during their life. In their will, after some minor bequests to family, the testator left the residue of their estate on trust for the benefit of the local amateur dramatic society. The carer was one of the witnesses to the will. The testator’s family want to challenge the bequest to the dramatic society. Which of the following is the most accurate assessment of this situation?
correct: The family will need to demonstrate that the carer’s influence was sufficient to amount to coercion or pressure that overpowered the freedom of action of the testator.
why: In probate there is NO presumption of undue influence (that exists only for lifetime gifts). The challenger must PROVE coercion: pressure that overpowered the testator's free will (Wingrove v Wingrove; Hall v Hall). Persuasion and appeals to sympathy are lawful. The carer witnessing the will matters only for gifts to the carer or their spouse (s 15 WA 1837), and this gift is to the society.

stem: A testator has named their spouse, their 70-year-old uncle, and their 10- year-old child as the executors of their estate. Amongst the property being left in the will is the copyright of the testator’s books. Two years before the testator’s death, they and their spouse divorced. The testator executed a codicil to their will to confirm that their spouse would remain an executor to their will. Seven years after the execution of their will, the testator and their uncle were in a car accident, both dying at the scene. Which of the following statements accurately addresses the issue of the appointed executors to the will?
correct: The testator’s spouse can be an executor because the testator has demonstrated their intention for their former spouse to retain this role, despite their divorce.
why: s 18A WA 1837: on divorce, an appointment of the former spouse as executor takes effect as if they had died on the date of divorce, UNLESS a contrary intention appears in the will. A codicil executed after the divorce confirming the appointment shows that intention. One executor is enough; there is no two-executor minimum (your pick). The child (now 17) is still a minor and cannot take the grant, and the uncle is dead.

stem: A person has died and under the will appoints their neighbour as personal representative. The will states that everything must be divided equally between their nieces. The personal representative knows of only two living nieces and contacts them both. Several months after the estate is settled another niece comes forward seeking their share of the will. Would the neighbour be personally liable to the unpaid beneficiary?
correct: Personal representatives are personally liable to any unpaid beneficiary, even if it is not known when a distribution is made, unless they comply with s 27 of the Trustee Act 1925.
why: PRs are strictly and personally liable for misdistribution, even to a beneficiary they did not know about. Their protection is s 27 TA 1925: advertise for claims, wait at least 2 months, then distribute having regard only to the claims they know of. Without that (or a Benjamin order or insurance), ignorance is no defence (your pick).

stem: A solicitor is the executor of a person’s estate. The person died 3 months ago leaving their estate equally between a friend and their sibling. The friend went to Australia, and so far, attempts to trace them have failed. The executor has placed advertisements for claimants to the estate in the appropriate newspapers and waited 2 months. The executor has now paid all the debts of which they have knowledge. The person had an illegitimate child (aged 40) who is complaining that they should have been left something but so far has taken no legal steps to make a claim. The sibling wants the executor to distribute the entire estate to them. If the executor distributes the estate to the sister having waited 2 months, which of the following correctly states the protection offered by the advertisements?
correct: The advertisements will not protect the executor from liability to either the friend or the daughter.
why: s 27 TA 1925 protects only against claimants the PR has NO NOTICE of. The friend is a known, named beneficiary, so tracing problems call for a Benjamin order, insurance or a retention, not s 27. The child's potential Inheritance Act claim is known too. PRs are protected against that claim only if they distribute after 6 months from the grant (I(PFD)A s 20). So the adverts protect against neither.

stem: A person dies. The deceased’s will leaves their house (value £1m) to their sibling’s eldest child and their shares in a private company (value £1m) to their sibling’s second child. There is a pecuniary legacy of £1m to the deceased’s sibling. The deceased leaves the residue of their estate (value approximately £1m) to be divided equally between a named charity and their godchild. The deceased’s godchild dies before the deceased. The deceased is survived by their sibling’s two children and their sibling. There are unsecured debts of £20,000 to pay and a mortgage of £100,000 secured on the house. The will contains no directions as to the payment of debts or the payment of the mortgage Which of the following statements correctly sets out the legal position relating to the order in which assets will be taken to pay debts?
correct: The debts, excluding the mortgage, will be paid from the lapsed share of residue.
why: Mortgage: the charged property bears its own mortgage (s 35 AEA 1925), so the house passes subject to it. Unsecured debts follow the statutory order (AEA Sch 1 Pt II). FIRST comes property undisposed of by the will, which includes the godchild's LAPSED share of residue (a partial intestacy). Only then does the rest of the residue bear the debts.

stem: A person has died leaving an investment property to their first child, shares worth £100,000 to their second child and a legacy of £100,000 to their sibling’s child. The residue of their estate is left to their spouse. The first child (who is divorced) would like to pass the investment property to their only child but does not want to make a transfer of value for inheritance tax purposes or a disposal for capital gains tax purposes. They have already received rent from the property. The second child does not want the shares and wants their parent to have them. They have refused all dividends. Like their sibling, they do not want to make a transfer of value or a disposal. The child of the person’s sibling would like to give £50,000 of their legacy to their sibling. Like the person’s first child, they do not want to make a transfer of value or a disposal. Which of the following correctly states a method by which one of the beneficiaries can achieve their desired result?
correct: The child of the person’s sibling can vary the terms of the will in writing to give £50,000 to their sibling but they must include a statement of intent that there is to be no transfer of value or disposal.
why: s 142 IHTA / s 62(6) TCGA: a written instrument of variation made within 2 years of death is read back to the death for IHT and CGT ONLY if it contains a statement that those sections are to apply. A DISCLAIMER needs no such statement, but a gift cannot be disclaimed once a benefit has been accepted (the first child took rent). A disclaimed gift falls into residue; it does not go to the person of your choice. That is why your option D is wrong: a disclaimer does not need the statement.

stem: A deceased’s will leaves their estate equally between their two children (aged 20 and 25). All three are killed in a plane crash and there is no evidence as to the order of deaths. The spouse of the youngest child was pregnant with their first child at the time of the crash and subsequently gives birth to the child. The eldest child has no children. In addition to the grandchild, the deceased is survived by their spouse and their youngest child’s spouse. Which of the following statements correctly sets out those entitled to the deceased’s estate?
correct: The estate passes under the will and is divided equally between the estates of the dead children.
why: Commorientes (s 184 LPA 1925): where the order of deaths is uncertain, the YOUNGER is presumed to have survived the elder. Both children (20 and 25) are therefore treated as surviving their parent, so the gifts do not lapse. The estate passes under the will to the two children's estates equally, and the intestacy rules are not engaged.

stem: A solicitor is invited by the manager of a local care home to give an informative talk to the home’s elderly residents on the importance of making a will. The solicitor gives the talk to those residents who have expressed an interest in the subject matter and, in doing so, presents an even-handed and accurate explanation of the advantages and disadvantages of making a will. At the end of the talk the solicitor hands out leaflets advertising the will drafting services of the solicitor’s firm. The solicitor also offers to draw up a will there and then for any residents who would like the solicitor to do so. Which of the following best describes the consequences of the solicitor’s actions under the SRA Code of Conduct for Solicitors, RELs and RFLs?
correct: The solicitor is unlikely to have done anything wrong in giving the talk, but handing out the leaflets and then offering to draw up wills breaches the Code as unsolicited approaches to members of the public.
why: Code for Solicitors 8.9: no unsolicited approaches to members of the public to advertise legal services, other than general advertising. Giving an invited, balanced talk is fine. Handing out leaflets for the firm's will services AND offering to draft wills on the spot are BOTH direct approaches to these particular residents. The leaflets are a breach too (your pick missed that).

stem: A person dies. Their correctly executed will leaves their estate to be divided equally between their son, daughter, nephew and spouse. There are no substitutional gifts. The person’s son and nephew both die before them, each survived by one child. The person’s spouse and daughter both survive them. Their estate is £600,000 after payment of debts. Which of the following statements correctly states the way in which the woman’s estate will be distributed?
correct: The spouse and daughter each take £150,000 under the terms of the will. £150,000 passes to the child of the deceased son and the remaining £150,000 passes under the intestacy rules to the spouse.
why: s 33 WA 1837 saves a gift to the testator's CHILD (or other descendant) who predeceases leaving issue, so the son's quarter passes to his child. It does not save a gift to a NEPHEW, so that quarter lapses and passes under the intestacy rules. With spouse and issue, the spouse takes the statutory legacy (£322,000), which swallows the £150,000. So the spouse takes it all, not the spouse and daughter equally (your pick).

stem: A deceased’s will appoints their solicitor as their executor and trustee. The deceased leaves a shareholding to their sibling’s child (aged 35), a pecuniary legacy to their sibling’s other child, the residue to their second spouse for life and the remainder to their children (aged 24 and 26) equally. The deceased’s solicitor dies before the deceased. The deceased’s spouse dies one week after the deceased, appointing the spouse’s child from a previous marriage as the spouse’s executor. The deceased’s eldest child died one week after the deceased, appointing their spouse as their executor. Which of the following will have the best right to take a grant of representation to deal with the deceased’s estate?
correct: The deceased’s surviving child.
why: NCPR 1987 r 20 order of priority: executor first. The solicitor-executor is dead, so the right passes to residuary beneficiaries. Among those, a LIVING residuary beneficiary is preferred to the personal representative of a dead one. So the surviving child ranks ahead of the PRs of the spouse and of the dead child (your pick).

stem: In their will, a testator left their share of the family holiday house to their children.
