The testator co-owned this house with their sibling and they each used the property for 3 months of the year and then rented the property out for the remaining 6 months every year. The market value of the house is £400,000 and the testator owned a 40% share of the property. Which of the following is most accurate in assessing the inheritance tax due on this property?
correct: The market value of the house will be discounted by 10%.
why: When a deceased co-owned land with someone OTHER than a spouse, HMRC accept a discount on the value of the undivided share, reflecting how hard it is to sell or occupy part of a house. The standard figure in the course materials is 10%, not 15% (your pick). So it is 10% off the 40% share of £400,000.

stem: A deceased person’s estate consists of a family home worth £300,000, two cars worth £20,000 each, shares in a private company valued at £50,000 and a bank account with £75,000 of cash. The estate has been left to the testator’s children and the personal representatives are seeking advice as to how to pay the inheritance tax which is due on the estate. Which of the following best describes how inheritance tax may be funded?
correct: A bank loan may be taken out to cover the costs of inheritance tax.
why: IHT on non-instalment property is due when the IHT account is delivered, before the grant. PRs can fund it with a bank loan, the Direct Payment Scheme, insurance proceeds and so on. The Direct Payment Scheme is VOLUNTARY for banks: they may release funds directly to HMRC but are not obliged to (your pick). Land qualifies for the instalment option, so the house need not be sold.

No. A person must be living with the deceased during the whole of the 4-year period immediately before the death as the spouse, civil partner or same-sex partner of the deceased to be able to bring a claim. Yes. A person who was living with the deceased during the whole of the 6-month period immediately before the death as the spouse, civil partner or same-sex partner of the deceased may be able to bring a claim. Yes. A person who was living with the deceased during the whole of the 1-year period immediately before the death as the spouse, civil partner or same-sex partner of the deceased may be able to bring a claim. Yes. A person must be living with the deceased during the whole of the 2-year period immediately before the death as the spouse, civil partner or same-sex partner of the deceased to be able to bring a claim.
correct: The court will consider their age and the duration of the marriage, their contribution to the welfare of the deceased’s family, and the provision which might have reasonably been expected on divorce at the date of death.
why: I(PFD)A 1975 s 3(2): for a spouse, ON TOP of the general s 3(1) factors, the court considers the applicant's age, the duration of the marriage, their contribution to the welfare of the family (including looking after the home), and the 'divorce cross-check': what they would reasonably have received had the marriage ended in divorce. Moral obligation and the size of the estate (your pick) are GENERAL s 3(1) factors, not the extra ones.
question: The personal representative of an estate is in the process of paying the beneficiaries to a will. The deceased left their partner 2 years prior, but the parties never applied for a divorce. Which one of the following best describes the main EXTRA guidelines a court would consider for a surviving spouse?

stem: The personal representative of an estate is in the process of paying the beneficiaries to a will. The deceased had a child 23 years ago that had been left out of the will but has received £1,000 a month since birth. Which one of the following best describes the main guidelines a court would consider for a surviving child?
correct: The court would consider the financial resources and needs of the applicant, any other applicant, and any beneficiary (now or in the future), any moral obligation of the deceased to any applicant or beneficiary, the size and nature of the net estate of the deceased, the physical or mental disability of any applicant or beneficiary, and any other relevant matter, including the conduct of any person.
why: I(PFD)A 1975 s 3(1) general factors, applying to every applicant: (a)–(c) the financial resources and needs of the applicant, other applicants and beneficiaries; (d) the deceased's obligations and responsibilities; (e) the size and nature of the net estate; (f) any disability; and (g) ANY OTHER MATTER, including the conduct of the applicant or anyone else. Your pick stops at (f) and omits (g).

stem: A person dies leaving everything to their child, aged 30, and nothing to their spouse. The spouse wants to make an application to court for a share of the deceased’s estate, on the basis that reasonable financial provision has not been made for them. Which of the following correctly sets out the requirements for the spouse’s application?
correct: The spouse must show that reasonable financial provision has not been made for them.
why: A surviving spouse gets the higher 'surviving spouse standard': reasonable financial provision 'whether or not required for maintenance' (s 1(2)(a)). Everyone else gets maintenance only. Note: your answer is also a true statement, since claims must be made within 6 months of the grant (s 4), though the court can extend. The examiner wanted the substantive test that is special to spouses.

stem: A person is getting married. Their two parents, two surviving grandparents, future spouse and a friend want to give the person as much as possible to help pay for the wedding, without incurring a liability to inheritance tax. They have already used their annual exemption and have no assets eligible for any relief. Which of the following correctly states the maximum that can be given to the person?
why: Gifts in consideration of marriage (IHTA s 22): parent £5,000 each, grandparent £2,500 each, a party to the marriage £2,500, anyone else £1,000. So 2 × £5,000 + 2 × £2,500 + £2,500 (future spouse) + £1,000 (friend) = £18,500. Your £17,000 missed that the future spouse counts at £2,500 as a party to the marriage.

stem: liability and paid together. No, the capital gains tax should be drawn from any inheritance tax figure and paid accordingly. No, the beneficiaries should pay the capital gains tax from their respective shares.
why: The spouse exemption (IHTA s 18) is unlimited only where both spouses are UK-domiciled (since April 2025, long-term UK resident). Where the transferor is UK-domiciled but the recipient spouse is NOT, the exemption is capped at £325,000 (the nil rate band), unless the recipient elects to be treated as UK-domiciled (s 267ZA). So £325,000 is exempt, not all £500,000 (your pick).
question: A husband decides to give a gift to his wife of £500,000 for their 40th wedding anniversary. The husband lives in Oxfordshire while his wife is domiciled in Monaco. What portion of the £500,000 will be exempt from IHT?

stem: A client and their spouse attend a meeting with the client’s solicitor to change the client’s will, which was written following the death of the client’s first spouse. In the new will, the client changed their original bequest to leave their family home to their children from their first marriage and instead left the property to their second spouse’s children. The solicitor noted that their client seemed somewhat subdued during the meeting and their spouse seemed impatient for them to sign the revised clause. What is the most accurate interpretation of this situation?
correct: If the will was made under force or threat of force, it will not be regarded as an act of the testator and will not be admitted to probate without the direction of the court.
why: A will made under force, fear or threats (duress) is not the testator's own act and will not be admitted to probate. But that has to be PROVED. Mere suspicion, a subdued testator or an impatient spouse is not enough, so there is no 'always' or 'automatically' invalid. Actual violence is not required either.

stem: A testator urgently needs to find a second witness to attest to their signature in their will. The primary beneficiary of the will is the testator’s only sibling. Which of the following would be the best choice as a second witness?
correct: The testator’s neice who is illiterate.
why: s 15 WA 1837: a gift to a witness, or to a witness's SPOUSE, is void (the will itself stays valid). So neither the sibling nor the sibling's spouse (your pick) should witness: the main gift would fail. A witness must be able to SEE the signing, so a blind witness is out (Re Gibson), and a parent with dementia may lack the capacity to attest. An illiterate witness is fine and can sign with a mark.

stem: A testator prepared a handwritten will but the day before they were due to execute the will, they fell down the stairs and broke both of their wrists. The testator’s two neighbours were asked to witness the will. Being unable to write because of their injuries, the testator asked the first witness to sign the will on their behalf, which they did and then immediately left. When the second witness arrived, the testator then added their thumb print as confirmation of their mark on the document in front of the second witness, who then signed the document as well. The second witness was not shown the contents of the will. Which of the following is the most accurate account of this situation?
correct: The will is invalid because the testator did not sign the document in front of both witnesses at the same time.
why: s 9 WA 1837: another person may sign FOR the testator, in their presence and at their direction (so E is wrong). But the signature must be made or acknowledged in the presence of TWO witnesses present AT THE SAME TIME. The first witness left before the second arrived, so that never happened. Witnesses need not read the will, and need not sign in each other's presence.

stem: An accountant makes a will which leaves everything to their spouse, with a substitutional gift to their sibling’s child to take effect if their spouse predeceases them. Five years later, the accountant and their spouse divorce. The accountant subsequently dies and is survived by their former spouse, sibling, and sibling’s child. The accountant had no children, and their parents died before them. The accountant’s family are unsure as to the effect of their will. Which of the following best states the legal position with respect to the will?
correct: The will is valid despite the divorce – the residuary gift to the spouse fails, and the residue will pass under the substitutional gift in the will to the sibling’s child.
why: Divorce does NOT revoke a will (only marriage does). Under s 18A WA 1837 the former spouse is treated as having died on the date of the divorce. So the gift to the spouse fails, and a substitutional gift conditional on the spouse 'predeceasing' takes effect. The residue goes to the sibling's child under the will, not on intestacy (your pick).

stem: A widower is consulting a solicitor about their deceased spouse’s will. The will was made on 4 December 2015 and leaves everything to the deceased's sibling. The widower and the deceased married on 12 January 2020. A line has been drawn through each page of the will and the words “This is revoked” are written across the top of the will, in the deceased's handwriting. The deceased is survived by the widower and their child, who is aged 18 months. The deceased has an estate capable of passing by will of £200,000. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the deceased’s will? (Note: For this question, see also 13.4.2.1 in the manual.)
correct: The will is revoked and the widower will take the whole estate under the intestacy rules.
why: Marriage revokes a will (s 18 WA 1837) unless it was made in contemplation of that marriage. The 2015 will was revoked by the 2020 marriage. (Crossing out and writing 'revoked' is not a valid revocation anyway: s 20 needs destruction or a duly executed document.) On intestacy with a spouse and issue, the spouse takes the statutory legacy of £322,000, which exceeds the £200,000 estate. So the widower takes everything and the child nothing (your pick split it).

stem: A person makes a will appointing their two siblings as executors. When the person dies, the eldest sibling is working abroad. The eldest sibling has informed the person’s various banks of their death but says that they will find it difficult to do anything else and wishes to renounce probate. The youngest sibling has not done anything in relation to the administration of the estate. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the appointments in the will?
correct: The youngest sibling can renounce probate but the eldest sibling cannot.
why: An executor who has INTERMEDDLED, i.e. acted in the administration (here, dealing with the deceased's banks), has accepted the office and can no longer renounce. Power can be reserved instead. The younger sibling has done nothing and is free to renounce. Your pick reverses who can renounce.

stem: Ten years ago, a person makes a will appointing as executors their spouse, their 15-year-old child and their accountant. When the person dies this year, they had been divorced from their spouse for 8 years, their child is 25, and their accountant is 70 and says that they do not wish to act as executor. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the appointments in the will?
correct: The appointment of the spouse fails but the child can take a grant of probate alone and the accountant can renounce.
why: The former spouse's appointment fails: s 18A WA 1837 treats them as having died on divorce. The child's appointment is valid even though they were a minor when the will was made. What matters is capacity when the grant is taken, and at 25 they can act alone. The accountant has not acted, so can renounce. A single executor is enough.

stem: A person leaves their shareholding in a company to be divided equally between their child, their sibling’s eldest child and their sibling’s eldest grandchild. The person’s child dies before them, leaving a child who is living at the person’s death. The sibling’s eldest child survives the person. The sibling’s other child had three children when the will was made but the oldest one died before the person, leaving two children surviving. Which of the following statements correctly states the legal position in relation to the gift of the shareholding?
correct: The one-third share left to the person’s child takes effect as a gift to the person’s grandchild.
why: s 33 WA 1837: a gift to the testator's own CHILD (or remoter descendant) who dies before the testator leaving issue passes to that issue, unless the will shows a contrary intention. So the child's third goes to the testator's grandchild instead of lapsing. s 33 does not help the sibling's line.

stem: A purchaser wished to buy a painting by a famous and sought-after artist, who was a distant relative. They did not know much about art, but they knew what they liked when they saw it. The purchaser registered their interest with an art dealer who said they had a painting by the artist for sale. The purchaser asked if the painting was genuinely by the artist, making it clear they would not purchase unless it was by their relative. The art dealer took all reasonable steps to verify the painting and confirmed that it was genuine. The purchaser bought the painting for £8,000. Eighteen months ago, the purchaser discovered the painting was a very good forgery and worth about £150. When they bought the painting, works by the artist were selling for £20,000 and the price has remained stable. Ignoring interest, what is the amount of damages the purchaser can claim?
why: This is a vitiating-factors (misrepresentation) question. The dealer took all reasonable steps, so the misrepresentation was INNOCENT and s 2(1) MA 1967 damages are defeated (reasonable grounds for belief). s 2(2) damages in lieu need rescission to still be available, and it is barred by lapse of time: the purchaser has done nothing for 18 months since discovering the truth (Leaf v International Galleries). Result: £0. ⚠ CAVEAT: the purchaser's 'I won't buy unless it's genuine' looks like Bannerman v White, which would make it a TERM. Breach-of-contract damages would then be £20,000 − £150 = £19,850 (your first answer). The key follows the misrepresentation analysis, so know both routes.

stem: An interior designer borrowed £5,000 from their restaurateur cousin to assist in setting up an interior design business. In return, the interior designer agreed to repay the restaurateur as soon as possible and to assist them in redecorating the interior of one of their restaurants. When the restaurant opened there was a lot of favourable publicity, especially with regard to the new décor and business boomed. The interior designer’s business also benefited from being showcased in the restaurant. The interior designer now tells the restaurateur they consider the design work for the restaurant is equivalent to £5,000, so they do not intend to repay the loan. Can the restaurateur recover the money?
correct: Yes, there is a claim because this is not a social arrangement.
why: Family arrangements are presumed NOT to be intended to create legal relations (Balfour v Balfour). But a business loan between relatives, given to set up a business, rebuts that presumption: it is a commercial deal. Consideration is also present, but the live issue raised by 'cousins' is intention to create legal relations. Your pick is true but does not answer the question asked.

stem: A painter abandons a decorating contract halfway through after taking a deposit. What is the legal position?
correct: The homeowner does not have to pay on a quantum meruit basis for the work as it is only partial performance.
why: A painter who ABANDONS an entire contract cannot recover for partial performance (Cutter v Powell; Sumpter v Hedges). A quantum meruit is available only if the homeowner FREELY accepted the part-performance, and having the work in your own home and needing to finish it is not free acceptance.

stem: A department store ordered boxed chocolates to sell in its store. It was listed as a written term of the contract that the chocolates be packaged in the store’s own- brand packaging, as the store famously only sells own- branded products. Once delivered it was discovered that the chocolates were instead in packaging representing the manufacturer’s brand. The manufacturer claims the packaging detail was only a warranty and the store can still sell the goods. The department store says it was obviously a condition and they cannot sell the goods. What is the likely legal position?
correct: The clause will be held to be a condition of the contract.
why: The parties expressly made own-brand packaging a written term, and its importance was obvious (the store sells ONLY own-brand goods). That shows they intended it as a CONDITION, so any breach allows rejection (Bunge v Tradax; Lombard v Butterworth). The innominate 'substantial benefit' analysis (Hong Kong Fir, your pick) is the fallback only where the parties' intention about the term's status is unclear.

stem: A shareholder is the sole owner of a company. They also own a piece of land. They require some building work to be done on the land, and their company entered into a contract with a builder to carry out some work on the land. The company failed to pay the builder and the builder tried to claim payment from the shareholder on the basis of unjust enrichment. Can the builder succeed?
correct: No, because the shareholder was not party to the contract.
why: Unjust enrichment cannot be used to sidestep the contractual allocation of risk. The builder chose to contract with the COMPANY and must look to it for payment, even though the shareholder's land was improved (MacDonald Dickens & Macklin v Costello). So no claim against the shareholder. (Unjust enrichment is NOT confined to void contracts, so B is wrong.)

stem: A shop owner orders some bread to sell in their delicatessen. They tell the baker it is vital the bread is made with organic flour as the delicatessen only sells organic products. The baker assures the shop owner they will only use organic flour. However, the written order document, as drawn up by the baker, does not specifically mention the word “organic”. What is the legal status of the requirement/specification?
correct: It was a term of the contract due to the expressed importance of the specification.
why: A pre-contract statement becomes a TERM where the recipient made clear it was vitally important and they would not contract without it (Bannerman v White). The contract can be partly oral, or the assurance can operate as a collateral contract. Leaving it out of the baker's written order does not reduce it to a mere representation (your pick).

stem: A company tendered for and obtained a contract to build an exclusive development of "mock Tudor executive style houses". The contract was valued at £200 million. Site clearance work commenced, and the company acquired the materials and the equipment necessary to complete the project within the 18-month time limit. After one week of clearance work, a bone was found and sent for examination. It was identified as an extremely rare Elaphrosaur neck bone. The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) have placed a six-month nature conservation order on the site to allow excavation. The company wish to terminate the contract. Do they have grounds?
correct: No, the order by the DCMS does not frustrate the contract.
why: Frustration requires the contract to become impossible or RADICALLY different from what was agreed (Davis Contractors v Fareham UDC). A 6-month suspension within an 18-month project is delay and inconvenience, not a radical change. The contract is not frustrated (your pick), so terminating would itself be a repudiatory breach.

stem: The owner of a country pub orders a new garden wall to be built in the same colour stone as the pub. However, once the wall is built, it is apparent that the shade of stone is a bit darker. The owner wants the wall completely rebuilt at a cost of £10,000 even though it has not adversely affected their business and a local estate agent says it has only affected the value of the property by about £2,000. Which of the following measure of damages is the court most likely to award?
correct: Expectation loss.
why: Ruxley Electronics v Forsyth: where the cost of cure (£10,000 to rebuild) is out of all proportion to the benefit, the court awards the DIMINUTION IN VALUE (around £2,000) as the expectation measure, possibly plus loss of amenity. It does not award cost of cure (your pick).

stem: A manufacturer makes environmentally friendly cars. In August last year, the manufacturer entered into a 5-year contract to supply cars to a car dealer. The dealer placed an initial order for 1,500 cars to be delivered within 12 months. The order was accepted. The agreed terms included a minimum retail price of £15,000 for the cars, as well as a clause stating that for every car that is not delivered within 12 months, the manufacturer will pay the dealer £8,000. The manufacturer delivers only 1,000 cars within the relevant 12-month period and it is clear that they will not fulfil the contract. What option best describes the legal position?
correct: The dealer can claim £8,000 for each car that has not been delivered.
why: Under Cavendish v Makdessi, a clause is a penalty only if it imposes a detriment out of all proportion to a legitimate interest. With a £15,000 minimum retail price, £8,000 per undelivered car is a plausible estimate of the dealer's lost margin and business interest. So it is an enforceable liquidated damages clause, and the dealer claims £8,000 per car.

stem: A couple agreed to purchase an old sailing boat, called “The Wendy”, towards which they had developed a strong emotional attachment, having passed by it on romantic walks together over many years. Their intention was to sail around the world in the boat and then write a book about their adventures. By the time they concluded the purchase contract and raised the money for the purchase, the seller had changed their mind and refused to hand over the boat. The couple are devastated about not being able to complete their trip in “The Wendy”. What would be the most appropriate remedy?
correct: They can ask for specific performance of the contract as the boat is classed as unique goods.
why: Specific performance is available where damages are inadequate, typically for unique goods (SGA 1979 s 52; Behnke v Bede Shipping: a ship). 'The Wendy' is unique to the couple. Damages for disappointment (your pick) are only awarded where the contract's object is pleasure or peace of mind (Jarvis v Swans Tours; Farley v Skinner), and they would not get them the boat.

stem: A personal assistant works for a high-profile politician. The personal assistant is offered a large sum of money by a newspaper to publish their memoirs when they leave their employment. The politician finds out and applies for an injunction, citing the confidentiality clause in the personal assistant’s contract of employment with the politician. Can the confidentiality clause be enforced against the personal assistant?
correct: Yes, because it is a term of the personal assistant's contract.
why: An express confidentiality clause in the employment contract is enforceable, and the court can grant an injunction to restrain a THREATENED breach before any publication (quia timet). The employee's intention to publish is the threat. There is no need to wait for an actual breach (your pick).

stem: A parent verbally agreed to indemnify their child's business debt with a large supplier. The child is unable to pay the debt and the parent has refused. What is the legal position?
correct: The parent is legally obliged to pay the debt as they provided the indemnity.
why: An INDEMNITY creates a PRIMARY, independent liability, and unlike a guarantee it need not be evidenced in writing (s 4 Statute of Frauds 1677 applies only to guarantees). So the oral indemnity binds the parent directly. Having to sue the principal debtor first (your pick) is a guarantee concept.

stem: A manufacturer of garden sheds and a supplier of timber agreed verbally with a supplier that the supplier would supply it with the “most optimum timber available at the going rate”. Two weeks later, the manufacturer requested an initial quantity of timber from the supplier, but the supplier advised it was unable to supply any timber to the manufacturer, as the supplier had just agreed to an exclusivity deal with another garden shed manufacturer. What advice would you give to the manufacturer?
correct: There is no contract as the “most optimum timber” is too vague.
why: Certainty of terms: 'the most optimum timber available' is too vague to identify what must be supplied, so there is no binding contract (Scammell v Ouston). A price at 'the going rate' could be filled in by SGA s 8 (a reasonable price), but the subject matter cannot be. So there is no claim for breach (your pick).

stem: A famous opera singer misses the first night of a series of six concerts they are contracted to appear in, but says they are available for the other five nights. However, their failure to attend on the first night has impacted ticket sales for the remaining nights. The concert organiser refuses to pay the opera singer anything at all. What is the legal position?
correct: The opera singer should be paid nothing at all, as attendance on the first night is fundamental and was a condition of the contract.
why: Poussard v Spiers: a singer's failure to appear on OPENING night broke a CONDITION, entitling the organiser to terminate. Compare Bettini v Gye, where missing rehearsals was only a warranty. The first night is fundamental to a run of shows. It is an express condition, not an 'implied term' (your pick), and substantial performance does not apply.

stem: A customer phoned a local dealer and explained that they wanted a cheap, reliable and economic car. It was very important to them that the car was as fuel efficient as possible. The dealer told them they had a second-hand Kia Rio in their price range that "would be just the ticket". The dealer said it was a "great little runner and will do 50mpg easily". The customer bought the car for £5,000 but after a few weeks found that it stalled a lot and was not doing more than 35mpg. The customer took it back to the dealer where they fixed the stalling fault. However, after another six months the car was not achieving more than 38mpg and was costing substantially more to run than the person budgeted for. Can the customer bring any action against the dealer?
correct: No, because although there were actionable misrepresentations the person affirmed the contract by accepting the repairs and continuing to use the car.
why: Accepting repairs and continuing to use the car can AFFIRM the contract and bar RESCISSION (Long v Lloyd). ⚠ KEY LOOKS DOUBTFUL: affirmation bars rescission only. It does NOT bar DAMAGES for misrepresentation under s 2(1) MA 1967. The '50mpg' claim by a dealer is an actionable misstatement of fact (with the dealer's expertise behind it), so your answer C (an actionable misrepresentation about mpg) is arguably correct. Learn the distinction: affirmation kills rescission, not damages.

stem: A developer wishing to build a new shopping centre needs to buy a small terrace of three houses to clear the site. The developer approaches the homeowners with an offer and two of them accept. The third homeowner rejects the offer, saying the only way they are leaving the house is “in a pine box”. The developer says, “If that is what it takes, it can be arranged”. The developer tells the homeowner they have a week to think about it. When the developer returns the resident says they do not have much of an option so they will take the money and they sign a written agreement to this effect. Two months after the sale, the homeowner discovers the development is not going ahead as the council have revoked planning permission. The houses are still standing. The homeowner wishes to return to their former home. What is the likely outcome in contract?
correct: The resident can elect to have the contract set aside.
why: Duress to the person (a threat of violence, 'it can be arranged') makes a contract VOIDABLE, not void (Barton v Armstrong). The threat need only be A reason for entering it. The homeowner can elect to rescind: only 2 months have passed, there is no affirmation, and the houses still stand. A lawful alternative offer does not cure an illegitimate threat (your pick).

stem: A first-time church attender was so struck by the message, they decided to formally join the church as a member. The minister explained that the church asked for a "faith commitment" from its members. In addition to giving money, members were expected to work for the church in their homeless hostel and their behaviour was closely controlled. The church attender had an inheritance of £100,000. They decided to give £20,000 to the church immediately and changed their will to leave the rest to the church. The church attender worked for the church until they became ill and were taken home by their parents to recuperate. After several years away from the church, the church attender decided they needed a proper job and a place of their own. They changed their will and asked for their money back. Will the church have to return the money?
correct: No, there was presumed influence under a protected relationship. The person's gift was not valid. However, lapse of time means rescission is not possible.
why: Allcard v Skinner: a religious superior and devotee is a relationship of PRESUMED undue influence, so the gift was voidable. But the donor waited YEARS after leaving the church's influence before asking for the money back. Laches and acquiescence bar rescission, so the church keeps the £20,000. (The will is simply changed.) Your pick ignored the delay bar.

stem: A bride lost one of a pair of unique, hand-crafted earrings. They wished to wear the earrings as part of their wedding outfit. The earrings had great sentimental value, as they were a present from the bride's grandparent on their 18th birthday. The bride contacted a jeweller, whose reputation rested on the production of exclusive handmade individual jewellery, to see if they could make a replacement. The bride was told that if they sent the earring the jeweller would try to make another to match it. The bride did so, enclosing a note saying “Thank you for agreeing to make an identical earring to match that which is enclosed. Please invoice me on completion." Unfortunately, when the earrings arrived, they did not match each other, and the bride felt they could not wear them for their wedding. Can the bride repudiate the contract?
correct: Yes, because the breach of contract goes to the root of the contract.
why: Supplying an identical earring was the whole point of the contract, so a mismatched one is a breach going to the ROOT of the contract. It is a breach of condition, and the bride can repudiate. 'Deprived of substantially the whole benefit' (your pick) is the Hong Kong Fir test for INNOMINATE terms, which is the wrong route where the term is plainly essential.

stem: A decorator enters a contract with a homeowner to redecorate their flat. The contract price is £2,000 and a deposit of £500 was paid to the decorator on the day the contract was made. The decorator spends two days removing woodchip wallpaper from the walls and the ceilings. At the end of the second day the homeowner says: "I’ve changed my mind and will do the work myself. I’d like my money back please". What can the decorator recover at common law?
correct: The homeowner has prevented the decorator from performing the contract and should pay the decorator on a quantum meruit basis.
why: When one party's repudiation PREVENTS the other from completing, the innocent party can claim a quantum meruit for work done (Planché v Colburn) or damages. Expectation damages would be the lost PROFIT, not the whole £2,000 fee (your pick), because the decorator saves the cost of doing the rest. They cannot insist on finishing either, because the job needs the homeowner's cooperation (White & Carter).

stem: A painter enters a contract with a homeowner to paint their flat. The contract price is £3,000 and a deposit of £600 was paid to the painter on the day the contract was made. The painter spends the first day stripping off all the old paint. The painter is then offered a more lucrative job elsewhere and abandons the current job. The homeowner is obliged to find an alternative painter to finish the work. Which of the following options best describes the legal position?
correct: The homeowner does not have to pay on a quantum meruit basis for the work as it is only partial performance.
why: An entire contract abandoned halfway: the party in breach recovers nothing for partial performance (Cutter v Powell; Sumpter v Hedges). A quantum meruit (your pick) needs the other party's FREE acceptance of the partial work, and a homeowner left with half-stripped walls has no real choice. The contract is not divisible, and the painter has left, so this is an actual repudiation, not an anticipatory one.

stem: The Law Society has produced a statement of best practice for conveyancing. It contains a set of steps to follow when acting in the sale and/or purchase of a home for an owner occupier. What is this statement of best practice called?
correct: The Law Society Conveyancing Protocol.
why: The Law Society Conveyancing Protocol sets out best-practice steps for residential sales and purchases, and Conveyancing Quality Scheme firms must follow it. The Formulae (A, B, C) are only the procedures for exchanging contracts by telephone. The Code for Completion by Post covers postal completion.

stem: A couple are purchasing a property and have instructed a solicitor who notes from the Property Information Form that the seller built a garage at the property 8 years ago. The solicitor has received the local search result which reveals that the property is not listed and that no planning permissions relating to this property. Should the buyers be concerned about the lack of planning permission?
correct: No, because the time limit for enforcement action for lack of planning permission passed 4 years ago.
why: Planning enforcement limits (TCPA 1990 s 171B): for breaches substantially completed BEFORE 25 April 2024, operational development (building a garage) could be enforced against only within 4 years. The LURA 2023 10-year rule applies only to later breaches. A garage built 8 years ago became immune 4 years ago. Enforcement is never unlimited (your pick), although listed building enforcement has no time limit.

stem: A solicitor has exchanged contracts for a company client on the purchase of a commercial unit with a registered title. Completion is not due to take place for another 3 months. What should the solicitor do to protect their client’s contract?
correct: Register a notice on the seller’s title at HM Land Registry.
why: On exchange the buyer has an estate contract. For REGISTERED land it is protected by entering a notice (agreed or unilateral) on the seller's title. A C(iv) land charge is the unregistered-land equivalent. Insuring (your pick) protects the BUILDING, not the CONTRACT. That is your recurring trap: a true step that does not answer the question asked.

stem: A seller and a first-time buyer exchanged contracts for the sale of the th seller’s residential property using the Standard Conditions of Sale (5 edition – 2018 revision) (the Standard Conditions) unamended. The seller is moving into rented accommodation. The buyer delayed sending the balance due for completion to their solicitor and as a result the completion funds were not received by the seller’s solicitor until 3.45pm on the contractually agreed completion date. Is there any contractual significance to the fact that the funds were not received until 3.45pm?
correct: Yes, because this amounts to delayed completion and the seller is entitled for compensation for delay under the contract.
why: SCS 6.1.2: if completion money arrives after 2pm, completion is treated as taking place on the NEXT working day for the purposes of compensation for late completion (SC 7.2: interest at the contract rate). The seller had moved out, so the vacant-possession exception (6.1.3) does not apply. The delay is not 'trivial' (your pick), but it does not justify rescission either.

stem: Two solicitors acting for a seller and a buyer respectively exchanged contracts regarding the sale and purchase of a freehold residential dwelling. The seller and the buyer had both agreed to complete on the th 26 of next month. The solicitors used the contract incorporating the th Standard Conditions of Sale (5 edition – 2018 revision) (the Standard Conditions). The solicitors exchanged contracts on the telephone at 4.45pm and in their haste, both forgot to insert a completion date on their respective parts of the contract. Do the Standard Conditions assist?
correct: The Standard Conditions do assist and provide that, in the absence of insertion of the completion date, completion will take place 20 working days from exchange of contracts.
why: SCS 6.1.1: if no completion date is agreed, completion is 20 WORKING DAYS after the date of the contract. Time is not of the essence. The contract remains valid, so no re-exchange is needed. 10 working days (your pick) is the period for a notice to complete (SC 6.8).

stem: No one, the property will pass to the Crown.
correct: A chronological list of the unregistered title documents forming the epitome, together with a photocopy of those documents attached.
why: An epitome of title is a chronological LIST of the documents making up the unregistered title, with PHOTOCOPIES of each attached. The originals are handed over on completion. 'At least 15 years old and does not cast doubt on the title' (your pick) describes a good ROOT of title, not the epitome.
question: A solicitor is acting for a client who is selling land with an unregistered title. The solicitor has received the title deeds from the client and is about to prepare an epitome of title. Which of the following statements best describes an epitome of title?

stem: A solicitor is acting for a client who is purchasing a property with the aid of a mortgage from a bank which subscribes to the UK Finance Mortgage Lenders' Handbook (Handbook). Which one of the following is one of the requirements set out in the Handbook?
correct: The solicitor must raise appropriate searches and enquiries on the property being purchased.
why: The UK Finance Mortgage Lenders' Handbook requires the conveyancer to make the searches and enquiries a prudent conveyancer would make (Part 1). It says nothing about who signs the contract (your pick), which Formula is used, or how the deposit is held. AML checks are on the conveyancer's own client, not the seller.

stem: A solicitor is acting for a client who is selling land with an unregistered title. The solicitor has received the title deeds from the client and is about to prepare an epitome of title. Which of the following statements best describes an epitome of title?
correct: A chronological list of the unregistered title documents forming the epitome, together with a photocopy of those documents attached.
why: An epitome of title is a chronological schedule of the title documents with PHOTOCOPIES attached. Originals stay with the seller's solicitor until completion, when they are handed over. So 'the original listed documents' (your pick) is wrong. Official copies (B) are for registered land.

stem: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a property with an unregistered title. The solicitor investigates the title when the contract pack is received. The solicitor notes that the only documents listed on the epitome of title are two conveyances on sale. The solicitor also notes that the epitome indicates that the original documents will not be handed over on completion and that only photocopies of the two conveyances are available. What is the significance of the fact that only photocopies are available?
correct: A photocopy of a document is not a good link in the chain of title and is not acceptable to HM Land Registry on first registration.
why: On first registration HM Land Registry needs the original deeds or properly certified copies. A plain photocopy is not a good link in the chain of title. The epitome says the originals will NOT be handed over, so asking for an undertaking to hand them over (your pick) misses the point. The defect is that the copies cannot prove the title.

stem: A tenant took a 6-year lease of a factory unit 4 years ago but has not paid the rent for 6 months. The landlord drafted the lease themselves and they did not include a forfeiture clause in the lease. The landlord now wants to end the lease due to the tenant’s default. Which of the following statements best describes the landlord's position as to non-payment of rent and their wish to end the lease?
correct: The landlord cannot bring the lease to an end but can sue for non- payment of rent.
why: There is no implied right of forfeiture for breach of covenant. Forfeiture needs an express forfeiture clause or a lease drafted as a condition. Without one the landlord cannot end the lease and must sue for the rent (or, for commercial premises, use CRAR). Quiet enjoyment is the TENANT's protection.

stem: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a property in Wales which has had a large extension added to it by the seller. The property is an old cottage, but the buyer was relieved to find out that it is not a listed building. The solicitor has received the result of the local search and notes that the property does not benefit from a planning permission. The seller indicated on the Property Information Form that the extension was completed 2 years ago. How long does the local authority have to take enforcement action?
correct: 2 years.
why: In WALES the planning enforcement limit for operational development is still 4 years from substantial completion. The 2024 LURA change to 10 years applies only in England. The extension was completed 2 years ago, so the authority has 2 more years to act. Your answer gave the total period (4 years) instead of the time remaining.

stem: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a residential dwelling in England. The solicitor has received the contract pack and reviews the documentation. The solicitor notes that the seller has indicated on the Property Information Form that they subdivided a single dwelling house into two separate dwelling houses 6 years ago. The solicitor’s local search has revealed no planning permissions relating to the property. The solicitor raised enquiries in response to which the seller confirmed that no external building work of any sort was involved in the conversion to two separate dwellings. Is the lack of planning permission a concern?
correct: Yes, the conversion to two dwellings is a material change of use and the local authority has 4 years to take enforcement action.
why: Subdividing one dwelling into two is a material change of use (TCPA s 55(3)(a)). For breaches before 25 April 2024 the limit was 4 years (the change to use as a single dwellinghouse, s 171B(2)). The 10-year LURA period (your pick) only covers later breaches. ⚠ KEY LOOKS DOUBTFUL: the conversion was 6 years ago, so a 4-year period has already EXPIRED. On these facts option E (no longer enforceable) is the logically correct answer. Learn the rule: 4 years for pre-25-April-2024 breaches, 10 years after.

stem: A VAT registered development company built a factory unit 2 years ago. A buyer has been found and has agreed to purchase the factory unit for £550,000. The buyer is not registered for VAT. What is the VAT position regarding this transaction?
correct: VAT is payable on the purchase price at the rate of 20%.
why: The freehold sale of a NEW commercial building (less than 3 years old) is compulsorily standard-rated: 20% VAT. Zero-rating (your pick) applies to new residential buildings. Whether the buyer is VAT-registered does not change the rate. It only means the buyer cannot recover the VAT.

stem: A limited company has recently completed the purchase of a freehold shop in a shopping precinct. The limited company borrowed £100,000 from a bank which will take a first legal charge over the title to the property. The limited company made up the balance of the purchase price of £47,000, which was paid from a recent sale of a company asset. How much stamp duty land tax (SDLT), if any, will be payable?
why: SDLT on NON-residential property: 0% up to £150,000, 2% to £250,000, 5% above. SDLT is charged on the whole consideration (£100,000 loan + £47,000 = £147,000), however it is funded. That is below £150,000, so the tax is £0. Your figures applied residential bands or the wrong total.

stem: A person has sold an investment property which they owned. For the entire period of their ownership, the property was rented out to tenants. The person took the advice of their accountant and is aware that they have capital gains tax (CGT) of £7,800 to pay to HM Revenue & Customs (HMRC). Their sale completed 10 days ago. Is there a relevant CGT deadline with which the person must comply?
correct: The person must report and pay the CGT to HMRC within 50 days.
why: Disposals of UK residential property: CGT must be reported and paid within 60 days of COMPLETION (since 27 October 2021). Completion was 10 days ago, so 50 days remain. Your answer gave the full period instead of the time left.

stem: The owner of a row of shops in a precinct has agreed to sell the shops and has instructed their solicitor. A number of the shops will be sold subject to existing tenancies, and the seller and the buyer need to discuss the transaction with their respective accountants to agree the VAT position. Which of the following is the most appropriate form of contract?
correct: A contract incorporating the Standard Commercial Property Conditions.
why: Commercial sales, especially with tenancies and VAT to sort out, use the Standard Commercial Property Conditions (SCPC, 3rd edition, 2018 revision), which deal with VAT, tenancies and apportionments. The SCS (5th edition) are for residential sales. 'Standard Commercial Conditions of Sale' (your pick) does not exist.

stem: A solicitor has been instructed by a company client regarding the sale of freehold commercial premises which the company purchased in 2017. The property is in mortgage to a bank which has a first legal charge against the property. The company’s solicitor is obtaining their clients title to the property to enable the solicitor to draft the contract. How will the solicitor deduce title to the property?
correct: The solicitor will obtain official copies of the title from HM Land Registry.
why: Bought in 2017, the title is REGISTERED (compulsory registration has applied everywhere since 1990), so the seller deduces title with OFFICIAL copies from HM Land Registry ('office copies' is the old name). Lenders no longer hold deeds for registered land, and abstracts and epitomes are for unregistered titles.

stem: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a property and has carried out the title investigation. The solicitor has carried out a full land charges search and has noted that there is a C(i) entry on the land charges search result. Which document in the epitome of title explains this entry?
correct: A mortgage deed.
why: Land charge class C(i) is a PUISNE MORTGAGE: a legal mortgage of unregistered land not protected by deposit of the title deeds. So the document behind it is a mortgage deed. Easements (your pick) are registered as D(iii) (equitable easements).

stem: A solicitor is acting for the buyer of a property and has carried out the title investigation. The solicitor has carried out a full land charges search and has noted that there is a D(ii) entry on the land charges search result. Which document in the epitome of title explains this entry?
correct: A conveyance.
why: Class D(ii) is a RESTRICTIVE COVENANT created after 1925 (other than between landlord and tenant). Covenants like that are usually imposed in a CONVEYANCE. A licence (your pick) is not an interest in land and is never registrable.

stem: A married couple are purchasing a residential property and have instructed their solicitor who has submitted the pre-contract searches. The couple went back to view the property yesterday and are concerned to see that the local villagers were having a May Day festival on the open grassland which the couple thought forms part of the garden of the property. One of the local villagers told the couple that the villagers had a right to have festivals and gatherings on the land. How will the solicitor acting for the couple determine whether the villagers have a right to use the land?
correct: The solicitor will carry out a common’s registration search.
why: A commons registration search (CON29O optional enquiry 22) shows whether land is registered common land or a town or village green, which is where locals' rights to hold festivals would show up. An index map search (your pick) only shows registered titles and pending applications.

stem: A person has instructed their solicitor to act in relation to the purchase of a property. Last year, the seller built a large annex to provide additional living space built in the back garden. The solicitor has received the local search result which has revealed that the property is in a conservation area. The local search has revealed no planning permissions relating to the property. The person is concerned that the local authority can take enforcement action regarding lack of planning once their purchase completes. Is the person right to be concerned about the lack of planning permission?
correct: Yes, planning permission was required for the annex and the local authority could take enforcement action against the person.
why: In a CONSERVATION AREA, permitted development rights for outbuildings and annexes are restricted, so planning permission was needed. Built last year, it is well within the enforcement period. Enforcement runs with the LAND, so the new owner is exposed even though they did not do the work. Building regulations (your pick) are a separate regime, and the question asks about planning.

stem: An unmarried couple are purchasing a property to live in and have instructed a solicitor to act for them on their purchase. Their solicitor is also acting for their building society which is lending them 80% of the purchase price. The solicitor has received the mortgage offer and has sent a report to the couple and has explained that they are taking out a mortgage which requires them to have an investment plan in place to pay off the capital sum borrowed at the end of the term. Which mortgage product is the couple taking out?
correct: An interest-only mortgage.
why: With an INTEREST-ONLY mortgage, the monthly payments cover interest only and the capital is repaid at the end from a separate investment vehicle (an endowment policy, ISA, pension, etc.). An endowment mortgage (your pick) is just one TYPE of interest-only mortgage. The question describes an investment plan generally, so the answer is the category: interest-only.

stem: Two business partners purchased a freehold shop together five years ago. They contributed equally to the purchase price and both appear on the title as registered proprietors. They initially agreed to hold the beneficial interest as joint tenants. They have received tax advice and now wish to bring the joint tenancy to an end, but wish to remain co-owners. How can the business partners give effect to the tax advice?
correct: The joint tenancy in equity must be severed and a form A restriction placed on the proprietorship register.
why: A legal joint tenancy can NEVER be severed (s 1(6) and s 36(2) LPA 1925). The trustees always hold the legal estate as joint tenants. Only the EQUITABLE joint tenancy can be severed, turning them into tenants in common in equity. That is then protected by a Form A restriction on the PROPRIETORSHIP register.

stem: An unmarried couple (A and B) are splitting up. The house, which they have lived in as their home, is owned in the sole name of A. B did not contribute to the purchase price of the property. B is worried that A might sell the house and want B to move out. Which of the following statements best describes B’s legal position?
correct: B should remain in occupation of the property but does not have an interest that is capable of protection.
why: B is not on the title, made no financial contribution and is not married to A. So B has no beneficial interest and no statutory home rights: FLA 1996 home rights (a Class F charge for unregistered land, or a notice for registered land, your pick) are only for spouses and civil partners. Occupation alone gives nothing capable of protection.

stem: A lawyer is acting for a client who is selling their house. The title to the seller’s house is registered at HM Land Registry. The seller is not retaining any land. Which document will transfer the legal title of the house from the seller to the buyer on completion?
correct: A transfer of whole.
why: For a REGISTERED title, the legal estate passes by a transfer (form TR1, a transfer of WHOLE where no land is retained), completed by registration. A conveyance (your pick) is the unregistered-land document. A transfer of part (TP1) is used when the seller keeps some land.

stem: A seller has agreed to sell their house and garden. On the day of completion, the buyer attends the property to find the seller removing the plants and shrubs from the garden. When asked what they were doing, the seller told the buyer that they wanted them for their new garden. Is the seller permitted to remove the plants and shrubs?
correct: No, because the plants and shrubs form part of the surface of the land and are included in the sale.
why: Plants and shrubs growing in the soil are part of the land ('quicquid plantatur solo, solo cedit') and pass with it unless the CONTRACT expressly excludes them. The facts give no such exclusion. Merely listing them on a fittings and contents form (your pick) does not help unless that form is part of the contract.

stem: A landowner wishes to sell their farm but discovers that their unregistered title deeds have been lost. The landowner consults their lawyer for advice and is told that the lawyer can make an application for registration at HM Land Registry, based on lost title deeds. What class of title is the land registry likely to grant?
correct: Possessory title.
why: If the title deeds are lost, the applicant cannot prove a documentary title, so HM Land Registry will usually grant POSSESSORY title, based on the applicant's possession. It can be upgraded to absolute later (after 12 years, or once the title is proved). Qualified title (your pick) is for a SPECIFIC identified defect.

stem: A landlord and tenant have entered into a lease of commercial premises which includes a landlord covenant to maintain the exterior structure of the building, within which the demised premises are situated, including the roof, external walls and foundations. The tenant is concerned because the roof is leaking which could cause damage to the tenant’s belongings contained in the demised premises. The tenant does not have any spare financial resources and wants the roof to be fixed as soon as possible. Which of the following statements best describes the most appropriate course of action for the tenant?
correct: The tenant could pursue the landlord for an order for specific performance.
why: A landlord's covenant to repair is a positive obligation, so the remedy that COMPELS the work is specific performance (Jeune v Queens Cross Properties). An injunction (your pick) restrains or orders specific acts but is not the standard tool for enforcing a repairing covenant. The tenant cannot fund the repairs, so self-help set-off (D) is unrealistic, and damages come too late.

stem: Two landowners own adjoining pieces of land. Title to both pieces of land is unregistered. They agree that one will grant the other a right of way over their land to gain access to the public highway. They enter into a deed of easement. One party forgot to sign the deed and the other party signed it but their signature was not witnessed. The landowner with the benefit of the right of way exercised the right for four years, until the neighbouring landowner said that they could no longer exercise the right of way. Which of the following statements best describes the position of the landowners in relation to the right of way?
correct: A legal right has not been created but a right in equity has arisen, which should be protected by registration of a D(iii) land charge.
why: A legal easement needs a valid deed (signed by the grantor and witnessed). This one was not validly executed, so the right can exist only in EQUITY. In unregistered land, an equitable easement is protected by a D(iii) land charge. D(ii) (your pick) is for RESTRICTIVE COVENANTS.

stem: A couple buy a property together and their lawyer advises them to hold the beneficial interest as tenants in common. Which of the following best describes how their beneficial interest should be protected on the register of title?
correct: A restriction in the Proprietorship Register.
why: A beneficial tenancy in common is protected by a Form A restriction in the PROPRIETORSHIP register. It ensures any sale is to at least two trustees so the beneficial interests are overreached. A notice in the charges register (your pick) protects third-party burdens such as easements, covenants and leases.

stem: A registered proprietor with title absolute has granted a 15-year lease by deed. How will the tenant’s lease be dealt with by HM Land Registry upon receipt of the tenant’s application for registration?
correct: HM Land Registry will register the title to the lease with title absolute.
why: A lease of more than 7 years is substantively registrable (LRA 2002 s 27(2)(b)). Because the landlord's freehold is registered with absolute title, the landlord's right to grant the lease is guaranteed, so the lease gets ABSOLUTE leasehold title. Good leasehold (your pick) is for when the superior title is not available to the Registry.

stem: A buyer completed the purchase of a piece of land with unregistered title last month. Which of the following statements best describes when the legal title will be transferred to the buyer?
correct: Legal title passes upon completion.
why: For UNREGISTERED land, the legal title passes on COMPLETION by the conveyance. Completion triggers compulsory first registration, which must be applied for within 2 months or the legal title reverts to the seller (LRA 2002 ss 6–7). 'Passes on registration' (your pick) is the rule for dispositions of land that is ALREADY registered (s 27).

stem: A person’s parents have agreed to lend them £30,000 to assist with developing their business. The parents want to ensure that the £30,000 is repaid to them at some point in the future. The person does not own any business assets but does own a home, which is registered at HM Land Registry in the person’s sole name. What legal advice should the parents receive, regarding their wish to recover the money lent to the person?
correct: The parents should take a legal charge over the person’s home and register it on the charges register of the person’s title.
why: Security for the loan comes from a LEGAL CHARGE over the home, registered in the CHARGES register (where mortgages are entered). The property register (your pick) describes the land and its benefits, such as easements.

stem: “A legal mechanism by which if the buyer of land pays the purchase money to two or more trustees, the interest of any behind-the-scenes beneficiary transfers from the land to the proceeds of sale, that is, the money.” What legal process does the above describe?
correct: Overreaching.
why: Overreaching (LPA 1925 ss 2, 27): if the purchase money is paid to at least TWO trustees (or a trust corporation), the beneficiaries' interests detach from the land and attach to the proceeds of sale, so the buyer takes free of them. Overriding interests (your pick) are a quite different concept: unregistered interests that bind a buyer of registered land.

stem: 12 months ago, a homeowner borrowed £80,000 from a bank to build an extension at their property. The loan is secured by a second legal charge on the charges register of the homeowner’s title. The mortgage contained a clause requiring repayment of the capital after six months. The homeowner defaults on three monthly repayments. Can the bank exercise a power of sale over the property?
correct: Yes, provided that six months have elapsed since the homeowner entered into the mortgage.
why: The statutory power of sale ARISES (LPA s 101) once the mortgage money is due, i.e. once the legal date for redemption (here 6 months) has passed. It becomes EXERCISABLE (s 103) when, for example, interest is more than 2 months in arrears, which three missed payments satisfy. A second mortgagee can sell subject to the first charge and does not need to join the first mortgagee (your pick).

stem: The registered proprietor of a property has taken a shortcut to the public highway by walking through their neighbour’s field for the last seven years. The neighbour sent a letter asking the registered proprietor to stop walking through their field but the registered proprietor is sure that their property has a right of way over the field. How would a right of way appear on the neighbour’s title?
correct: A notice on the charges register.
why: An easement is recorded on BOTH titles. The BENEFIT appears on the dominant land's PROPERTY register, and the BURDEN appears as a NOTICE on the servient land's CHARGES register. The question asks about the NEIGHBOUR's (servient) title, so it is the charges register. Your pick (property register) is the dominant-title answer.

stem: The person has no legal right to use the driveway but has acquired a right to use it by licence. The person has a prescriptive right to use the driveway.
correct: The landowner cannot create the rights before the sale because there will not be a dominant and servient tenement in separate ownership.
why: An easement needs a dominant AND a servient tenement in DIFFERENT ownership or occupation (Re Ellenborough Park). Splitting your own title does not create two owners, so you cannot grant an easement to yourself. The rights must be created in the transfer of part on the sale (grant and reservation). Your pick restates a Re Ellenborough condition, which is true, but it does not answer whether this can be done BEFORE the sale.
question: A landowner wants to sell part of their land for development. To ensure that the sale proceeds smoothly, the landowner wants to subdivide the title to the land and to enter into a deed specifying the rights of access to the property before it is sold. Which answer best describes whether the landowner can achieve their aim?

stem: A bank has agreed to lend a farmer £100,000 for their business. The farmer owns 110 acres of farmland, the title to which is unregistered. The bank will take a first legal charge over 20 acres of the farmer’s land. How will the bank’s interest be protected?
correct: The transaction will trigger first registration of the 20 acres of land and the charge will be protected by a notice on the charges register.
why: A first legal mortgage of unregistered land triggers compulsory first registration (LRA 2002 s 4(1)(g)), but only of the land actually CHARGED, here the 20 acres. The bank's charge is then entered as a registered charge in the CHARGES register. The other 90 acres (your pick) stay unregistered.

stem: For the past 22 years, a person has driven over their neighbour’s driveway to get to the public highway. The person’s title does not contain reference to the use of their neighbour’s driveway. Over the years, the person has asked their neighbour if they can continue to use the driveway and has made a few payments towards the upkeep of the driveway. The neighbour has just sold their land and the new owner has told the person that they cannot use the driveway any more. Which of the following statements best describes the person’s legal position?
correct: The person has no legal right to use the driveway and has not acquired a right to use it by prescription.
why: Prescription needs use 'as of right': without force, secrecy or PERMISSION (nec vi, nec clam, nec precario). Asking permission and contributing to upkeep makes the use permissive (a licence), so no easement arose (your pick). A licence is personal and does not bind the new owner, who can end it.

stem: The tenant of an office block wants to sell the residue of the lease of the premises. The tenant’s lawyer tells them that there is a qualified covenant against assignment contained in the lease. What is the effect of this clause?
correct: The landlord can only withhold their consent to assignment if it is reasonable to do so.
why: A QUALIFIED covenant (no assignment without consent) has implied into it that consent is not to be UNREASONABLY withheld (LTA 1927 s 19(1)(a)). LTA 1988 s 1 adds that the landlord must respond within a reasonable time and give written reasons. Your pick (a written request) is procedure. The question asks for the covenant's EFFECT.

stem: A seller has exchanged contracts to sell a property. There is a large shed in the back garden which is bolted to a concrete slab in the garden. On the day of completion, the buyer arrives at the property to discover that the seller has removed the shed and has tidied up the concrete slab and filled in the holes. The buyer tells the seller that they were expecting the shed to be left at the property. The seller tells the buyer that they were allowed to remove the shed. Is the seller correct?
correct: No, because the shed is bolted to the land and is thus a fixture which will pass with the sale of the land.
why: Fixtures pass with the land; chattels do not. The test is the degree and PURPOSE of annexation (Holland v Hodgson; Elitestone v Morris). A shed BOLTED to a concrete slab is a fixture and must be left. A shed resting on its own weight would usually be a chattel. Concrete foundations are not required (your pick), and filling in the holes does not cure the removal.

stem: A teacher who is unable to drive as they suffer from epilepsy (which they have suffered from since being a child) has applied for a job at a private school. At the initial interview, the teacher was asked if they had a valid driving licence as the school prefers to hire staff with a driving licence and who own a car due to the school’s remote location. The teacher does not have a driving licence and, after explaining to the school why they do not have a driving licence, they were not invited to the second interview. Has the school acted in a discriminatory way towards the teacher?
correct: Yes, because this treatment could fall within the definition of prohibited conduct in respect of the teacher’s epilepsy.
why: Epilepsy is a disability. Rejecting the teacher because they cannot drive is unfavourable treatment because of something ARISING from the disability (EqA 2010 s 15). A blanket licence requirement is also a PCP that may be indirect discrimination (s 19). Either way it is prohibited conduct unless the SCHOOL proves the treatment was a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim. That is far from obvious for a teaching job, and reasonable adjustments apply. Your picks assumed the justification was already made out. The school was told, so lack of knowledge is no defence either.

stem: A software engineer and an administrator have been professional colleagues for a long time. The administrator identifies as part of the lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender (LGBT) community and has been open about it. Lately, the administrator has noticed that the software engineer is making rude comments about the administrator in relation to sexual orientation. The software engineer has also posted some pictures of LGBT persons on the office fridge and wrote offensive words on it. Which of the following provides the best explanation of the software engineer’s behaviour?
correct: The software engineer’s behaviour is harassment because the software engineer’s conduct is linked to the administrator’s sexual orientation and affects the administrator’s dignity.
why: Harassment (EqA 2010 s 26) needs: (1) unwanted conduct, (2) RELATED to a protected characteristic, (3) with the purpose or EFFECT of violating dignity or creating an intimidating, hostile, degrading, humiliating or offensive environment. Your pick stops at element (2). Victimisation is about detriment for doing a protected act, such as complaining.

stem: A solicitor acts for a client in relation to the acquisition of a private limited company. Two days before the transaction is due to complete, the solicitor suspects that the client will be using the transaction to launder money. The solicitor reports this to the nominated officer who makes a suspicious activity report to the relevant authority. What action should the solicitor now take?
correct: Proceed with the transaction only after receiving authorisation from the relevant authority.
why: After a SAR, the solicitor needs 'appropriate consent' (a DAML) before doing the prohibited act (POCA ss 328, 335). Silence for 7 WORKING DAYS (not 3, your pick) is deemed consent. A refusal triggers a 31-day moratorium. Telling the client about the SAR is tipping off (s 333A), so A and B are wrong too.

stem: A solicitor recently acted for an existing client in the purchase of property. The client had previously deposited two significant cheques into the firm’s client bank account on an alleged purchase of a new development site to cover the deposit and legal fees for the transaction. On both occasions, after 2 weeks, the client instructed that the development has fallen through, and so will not proceed any further and instructed the firm to return the money, less an amount for its fees. On completion of the recent purchase, the client instructs the solicitor to transfer the house to a relative of the client. What should the solicitor do?
correct: The solicitor will commit an offence under the Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 if they act on the client’s instructions.
why: Repeated aborted deals with money refunded through client account, followed by a transfer to a relative, are classic laundering red flags. POCA offences (ss 327–328) are committed with KNOWLEDGE OR SUSPICION; actual knowledge (your pick) is not required. Acting on the instructions without an authorised disclosure and consent would be 'arranging'.

stem: A solicitor is instructed on the purchase of company shares. The solicitor discovers that a colleague in the firm has been instructed by the same client in respect of an investigation by the Italian tax authorities into certain of the client’s business activities in Italy, which are alleged to amount to tax fraud. The solicitor makes an authorised disclosure to the firm’s nominated officer. The nominated officer does not go on to make a suspicious activity report to the National Crime Agency. Forty-eight hours later, having heard nothing from the nominated officer, the solicitor buys the shares on the client’s behalf. Is the solicitor likely to have committed the offence of “arranging” under Proceeds of Crime Act 2002 s 328?
correct: Yes because the solicitor did not have appropriate consent to proceed with the purchase of the shares.
why: The s 328 defence needs an authorised disclosure AND 'appropriate consent' before acting. Consent from the nominated officer can only be given after a SAR and NCA consent, or once 7 working days pass without refusal. Buying the shares after 48 hours of silence, without consent, is the offence. Your pick blames the missing SAR, but the solicitor's own failure is acting without consent. Foreign tax fraud is still criminal conduct (s 340), so D is wrong.

stem: A client has sold their 40% shareholding in X PLC (an unlisted company) for £5m to a company incorporated in the British Virgin Islands which already holds 10% of the voting shares in X PLC. A solicitor’s firm is dealing with the negotiation of the terms on which the sale will be concluded. The client wants advice about tax efficient investments for the proceeds. Can solicitor’s team arrange this disposal and provide the investment advice without being authorised by the FCA?
correct: Yes, the solicitor may act on the client’s instructions without breaching the law.
why: Selling shares can be a regulated activity, but the 'sale of a body corporate' exclusion applies where the shares disposed of, together with those the buyer already holds, carry at least 50% of the voting rights: 40% + 10% = 50%. Generic advice about tax-efficient TYPES of investment is not 'advising on investments', which must relate to a particular investment. So no FCA authorisation is needed for either.

stem: A firm of solicitors is considering providing financial services to its clients. The firm intends to offer a full range of financial options, including shares, debentures, insurance, and pensions. The firm is not authorised by the Financial Conduct Authority (FCA). Clients will be billed separately for legal and financial advice. Which of the following best represents the firm’s options?
correct: If the firm fails to obtain authorisation at all and carries out a regulated activity regulated under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000, this will involve the commission of a crime, and any contract made, for example, with a client, will be unenforceable.
why: Carrying on a regulated activity without authorisation or exemption breaches the general prohibition (FSMA s 19). It is a CRIMINAL offence (s 23), and agreements made in breach are UNENFORCEABLE against the client (ss 26–27). A firm genuinely within the Part 20 professional-firms exemption commits no offence (your pick says it would).

stem: A solicitor acted for an offshore registered investment company. The solicitor provided legal advice on a series of transactions that later turned out to have been used to finance money laundering. The solicitor did not directly facilitate or become involved in the transactions themselves. The solicitor believed at the time that the advice was to further a legitimate purpose. Accordingly, no disclosure was made. Which of the following best describes the solicitor’s position?
correct: The solicitor may have committed a “failure to disclose” offence but can rely on the “reasonable excuse” defence, as they were misled.
why: 'Arranging' (s 328) requires actual KNOWLEDGE OR SUSPICION, which is subjective. The solicitor genuinely believed the purpose was legitimate, so there is no s 328 offence (your pick wrongly includes it). Failure to disclose (s 330, regulated sector) has an objective limb ('reasonable grounds' to suspect), so it may be committed, subject to the reasonable excuse defence.

stem: An experienced solicitor in a firm specialising in family law is advising a client who has just obtained a substantial settlement in a divorce. The client wishes to purchase a property with part of the settlement and will need a mortgage. The client also wishes to invest the rest of the settlement and asks the solicitor for advice on investing in company stock and shares. The solicitor has experience in providing this type of advice. Can the solicitor provide the services requested by the client within a divorce matter?
correct: The solicitor can provide the service requested as they fall within the exemption in the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000.
why: SRA-regulated firms may carry on certain regulated activities without FCA authorisation under the Part 20 FSMA exemption for professional firms (with the SRA Financial Services (Scope) Rules). The activity must arise out of, and be incidental to, their legal services, with fees accounted for to the client. This is not about 'competence' (your pick): the solicitor is experienced in this work.

stem: A 70-year-old retiree wants to study a philosophy degree. The university admissions department wants to reject the retiree’s application because they believe the retiree is too old. Can the university reject the retiree’s application?
correct: The university cannot reject the retiree’s application because of the retiree’s age as this would constitute direct discrimination.
why: Refusing because someone is 'too old' is less favourable treatment BECAUSE OF age, which is direct discrimination. ⚠ NOTE: age is the one protected characteristic where direct discrimination CAN be justified as a proportionate means of achieving a legitimate aim (EqA s 13(2)), so your answer B states a real rule. A bare belief that someone is too old for a philosophy degree could never meet that test, which is why the key says the university cannot reject.
