stem: After completion of the sale of 40% shareholding in an unlisted company, the client tells their solicitor that they need to transfer the proceeds into a limited company, for which they will pay for all of the shares, but they will be held in the names of close friends. The client wants the solicitor to arrange a suitable structure. The client says the purpose is that they now want to keep their affairs as private as possible. The solicitor has no reason to believe that the client is under any financial pressure and are working under the supervision of a partner with experience of setting up nominee arrangements. Should the solicitor discuss this with any compliance officer(s)?
correct: No. There are no circumstances requiring the attention of the compliance officer.
why: Nominee shareholdings are not inherently suspicious. The client gives a plausible privacy reason, has no financial pressure, and the work is supervised by an experienced partner. Without actual knowledge or suspicion of laundering, nothing needs to go to the MLRO or compliance officer. The ordinary risk-based CDD continues (your pick treats nominees as automatically suspicious).

stem: A couple is going through divorce proceedings, and they have a 12-year- old child of the marriage. One day, the mother takes the child from school with the intention to take the child to another country. The father wants to apply for prohibited steps order. Is legal aid available in this case?
correct: Yes, legal aid is available and there is no need to pass the means test.
why: Most private family law left legal aid scope after LASPO 2012, but cases to prevent child ABDUCTION are an exception. In the course materials, legal aid is available in child abduction cases WITHOUT a means test. Your pick ('all children cases') is too wide: ordinary child arrangements disputes are out of scope.

stem: A veterinarian has been charged with fraud and the trial will take place in the Crown Court. The veterinarian is currently unemployed but is married to a teacher who is in full time employment. Will the veterinarian’s partner’s income be considered when calculating eligibility for legal aid?
correct: Yes, partner’s gross income will be added to the veterinarian’s income.
why: In criminal legal aid means testing, a partner's income is AGGREGATED with the applicant's (unless the partner has a contrary interest, e.g. as victim or witness). Your pick ('considered') is substantively right too. The key is simply more precise: the partner's gross income is ADDED to the applicant's.

stem: An energy company hires a law firm on a private retainer agreement. The st retainer agreement states that the law firm is to be paid £5,000 on the 1 calendar day of the month. Last month, the law firm contacted the energy company and explained that due to a high demand in their services by the energy company, the retainer fee has been used up and that the energy company needs to pay an additional sum of £2,000 for the services received. Can the law firm charge the energy company the extra fees?
correct: The law firm can charge extra fees depending on what the retainer agreement says.
why: Fees depend on the contract. Whether the firm can bill beyond the monthly retainer turns on what the retainer agreement says (e.g. a cap, or extra work at hourly rates), together with the duty to give clients the best possible costs information (Code 8.7). Your pick assumes extra work automatically justifies extra fees.

stem: A law graduate wants to help a friend and make a representation in the friend’s defence at the magistrates’ court. The law graduate is not a member of the SRA. Would this representation be permitted?
correct: Yes, if the court has given permission.
why: Rights of audience are a reserved legal activity (LSA 2007 s 12 and Sch 2). But Sch 3 exempts a person whom the court GRANTS a right of audience for the particular proceedings. So the friend can represent with the court's permission. Your pick ignores that exemption.

stem: An accountant is a former employee at a law firm and has made an official complaint under the Equality Act 2010. The complaint relates to some of the accountant’s former colleagues who made rude remarks about the accountant’s turban (something the accountant wears due to his Sikh religion) during a lunch meeting. Several weeks after lunch meeting (and after the official complaint was made), the accountant was excluded from some meetings, and subsequently was unable to be part of an important case. Has the accountant’s employer acted unlawfully?
correct: Yes, because the employer is acting in this way because of the accountant’s protected act.
why: Victimisation (EqA s 27): subjecting someone to a detriment BECAUSE they did a PROTECTED ACT (bringing a complaint under the Act). Exclusion from meetings and cases after the complaint fits. Your pick ('a breach of the EqA') is too vague: you need to name the specific prohibited conduct.

stem: The judge at the Court of Appeal (Civil Division) needs to apply the Social Services Act 1988. Section 5 of the Act refers to “family”. When applying the literal rule, the judge is faced with an absurd outcome that does not fit the current case.Which is the next step that the judge needs to take?
correct: The judge should apply the golden rule.
why: Statutory interpretation: when the literal rule produces an ABSURD result, the GOLDEN rule lets the court modify the meaning to avoid the absurdity (Adler v George; Re Sigsworth). The mischief rule (Heydon's Case, your pick) is a separate approach asking what defect the Act was meant to cure. It is not the step that follows absurdity.

stem: A Member of Parliament (MP) has recently introduced a private memberʼs bill in the House of Commons.What stages does the Bill need to go through to become law?
correct: The Bill needs to go through three readings and a committee stage at the House of Commons and the House of Lords and then receive the Royal Assent.
why: Every bill, including a private member's bill, goes through first reading, second reading, committee stage, report stage and third reading in BOTH Houses, then receives Royal Assent. No government approval is required (your pick), although without government time few PMBs succeed.

stem: A person made an application for judicial review on the grounds of Human Rights Act 1998. The person alleges that the Disability Act 2001, which requires disabled individuals not to leave the house unless they are accompanied, is in breach of the Convention rights. The court has found the Disability Act incompatible with the Convention. Which of the following remedies is the court likely to award in this case?
correct: Declaration of incompatibility.
why: Courts cannot quash or disapply an ACT of Parliament. If primary legislation cannot be read compatibly (HRA s 3), the court can only make a DECLARATION OF INCOMPATIBILITY (s 4). The Act stays in force until Parliament acts. Quashing orders (your pick) are for secondary legislation or executive decisions.

stem: The Protection of Birds Bill has been introduced in Parliament and has not reached its Third Reading. The opposition party has suddenly realised that the Bill does not address some issues in relation to environmental protection and wishes to add those the Bill during this stage.Can the opposition party raise this issue at the Third Reading stage?
correct: No, because during the third reading new additions to the Bill are not permitted.
why: Third reading in the Commons is a final debate on the bill as amended. No substantive amendments are allowed. New provisions must be added at committee or report stage. Scrutiny happens at every stage, but not by adding new content at third reading (your pick).

stem: permitted. Yes, because new amendments to the Bill are permitted at any stage. No, because the opposition parties are not permitted to question Bills. Yes, because Bills can be scrutinised at any of the three reading stages.
correct: The judge aims to see what issue of the old law the new law was aiming to resolve.
why: The mischief rule (Heydon's Case) asks what the common law was before the Act, what MISCHIEF (defect) the old law did not cover, and what remedy Parliament adopted to cure it. The judge reads the provision to suppress that mischief. Reading for 'the intention of Parliament' (your pick) is too general, since every rule claims to do that. The specific feature of the mischief rule is looking at the problem in the OLD law.
question: A judge at the High Court is applying the Family Act 1999. Before this Act, the area was governed by common law. Interpreting section 6, the judge struggles with what 'parent' means and uses the mischief rule. What does the judge aim to do by using this approach?

stem: The newly elected Prime Minister is told that some of the royal prerogative powers are exercised by the Prime Minister. The Prime Minister cannot understand this, since they always thought that prerogative powers are those exercised by the Monarch. Which of the following statements best explains the operation of the royal prerogative?
correct: Most of the royal prerogative powers are exercised by the government of the day.
why: By convention, most prerogative powers (e.g. treaties, deployment of the armed forces, appointments) are exercised by the GOVERNMENT of the day, through ministers, not by the Prime Minister personally (your pick). A few personal prerogatives, such as Royal Assent and appointing the PM, remain with the Monarch, exercised on advice.

stem: Recently the government has enacted new legislation. The newly enacted Social Activities Act does not allow individuals to meet in public places. The Act has been approved by both Houses of Parliament and received the Royal Assent. The citizens are upset about this new law and wonder if the judiciary would be able to annul the Act.Which of the following statements best describes the power that the judiciary has in relation to annulling Acts of Parliament?
correct: The Judiciary cannot annul any law passed by Parliament.
why: Parliamentary sovereignty: no court can annul or strike down an Act of Parliament. The HRA 1998 preserves this: the most a court can do is a declaration of incompatibility (s 4), which does not affect validity (your pick). 'Rule of law' arguments do not give the courts a power of annulment either.

stem: The Supreme Court has been asked to make a ruling on the validity of the Special Measures Act 2019, which put many restrictions on individual freedoms and is considered highly controversial.Which of the statements below, correctly identifies the powers of the Supreme Court to make a ruling on the validity of an Act?
correct: No court has the power to rule on the validity of an Act of Parliament if the Act was enacted in accordance with the correct procedure.
why: Under parliamentary sovereignty and the enrolled bill rule (Pickin v British Railways Board), no court, including the Supreme Court, can rule an Act invalid if it was passed in the proper form. Incompatibility with Convention rights leads only to a s 4 declaration. Your pick combined two contradictory statements.

stem: The Government has been told that certain judges at the High Court have been acting unprofessionally and making public comments in relation to some of the cases involving judicial review. The Government wants to remove these judges form their posts.Which of the following correctly describes the process of removal of High Court judges from office?
correct: A resolution of both Houses of Parliament is needed to remove a High Court judge.
why: High Court (and Court of Appeal) judges hold office during good behaviour. They can be removed only by the Monarch on an ADDRESS presented by BOTH Houses of Parliament (Senior Courts Act 1981 s 11(3)). The Lord Chancellor (your pick) has no power of removal, only disciplinary functions with the Lord Chief Justice.

stem: An accountant and a friend got into a verbal argument at their local pub. At one point, the accountant said something to the friend, which made the friend punch the accountant in the face. The accountant’s cheek was bruised as a result. Police have been called to the scene and the friend has been arrested and charged with battery. Which court will deal with the friend's case?
correct: Since the friend is charged with battery, it will be dealt with by the Magistrates’ Court only.
why: Common assault and battery are SUMMARY-ONLY offences (CJA 1988 s 39), so they are tried in the magistrates' court only. There is no election for Crown Court trial (your pick), which exists only for either-way offences.

stem: A grandparent purchased a brand-new car for a grandchild. After 18 months, the grandparent paid to replace the rear nearside tyre, because it had a puncture. Unfortunately, the replacement tyre was defective and caused a blowout on the motorway. The grandchildʼs car collided with the centre reservation and was written off. The grandchild was unharmed. Does the grandchild have a claim in negligence against the manufacturer of the tyre?
correct: Yes, but not in respect of the replacement tyre.
why: A manufacturer owes a duty to the ultimate consumer (Donoghue v Stevenson), so no contract is needed. But damage to the defective product ITSELF (the tyre) is pure economic loss and irrecoverable in negligence (Murphy v Brentwood; Aswan Engineering). Damage to OTHER property (the car) is recoverable. Your pick reverses this. (CPA 1987 s 5(2) similarly excludes loss of the product itself.)

stem: An airport worker negligently pulls an aeroplane too close to an exit tunnel, causing damage to the tunnel, resulting in significant delays to passengers arriving at the airport. One affected passenger is on a plane that lands at 5am, but they are not able to disembark until 10.30am. They had intended to drive their family straight home from the airport. However, as a result of the delay, the passenger has no option but to stop and buy their whole family breakfast before they make the journey home. Can the passenger recover the cost of the breakfast from the airport worker and/or the relevant employer?
correct: No, because there is no property damage or personal injury.
why: The breakfast is PURE ECONOMIC LOSS: the passenger suffered no personal injury and no damage to their own property. It is generally not recoverable in negligence (Spartan Steel v Martin). Foreseeability (your pick) is not the issue. Even foreseeable economic loss is excluded absent a special relationship.

stem: Frustrated after an argument with their neighbour, a teenager picks up their neighbour’s sledgehammer and smashes their neighbour’s car windscreen with it. However, the sledgehammer is defective and snaps in the middle on impact, causing the teenager to fall into the broken glass. The teenager suffers severe cuts to their hands and face. What advice would you give to the teenager about a possible claim in negligence against the manufacturer of the sledgehammer?
correct: You cannot sue the manufacturer because you were engaged in illegal activity.
why: Illegality (ex turpi causa): the teenager was injured in the course of committing criminal damage, and the claim arises directly from that crime, so the court will refuse to allow it (Patel v Mirza; Gray v Thames Trains). Cuts from a snapping hammer are plainly foreseeable (your pick), and no contract or ownership is needed in negligence.

stem: A customer has found a decomposed snail in their bottle of fizzy pop and suffered physical and psychiatric harm as a result. Which statement best describes the legal position on the issue of breach of duty in a claim by the customer against the manufacturer of the product for common law negligence?
correct: The court will presume that the manufacturer breached its duty.
why: A snail in a sealed bottle 'speaks for itself': the court INFERS (presumes) a breach of duty, and the manufacturer must rebut it by showing it took reasonable care (res ipsa loquitur; Grant v Australian Knitting Mills). It is a rebuttable presumption, not an automatic finding that the snail 'amounts to' breach (your pick).

stem: A solicitor specialising in litigation is asked to act for a client who wishes to sue a company for a substantial amount of money. The case, if successful, would also generate bad publicity for the company. The solicitor holds a significant number of shares in the company concerned. Which one of the following statements best describes whether the solicitor can act for the client?
correct: No, because the solicitor cannot act with independence and so the solicitor must therefore decline to act.
why: A substantial shareholding in the company being sued gives the solicitor a personal interest in the outcome: an own-interest conflict (Code 6.1), which also compromises independence (Principle 3). There is no consent route for own-interest conflicts, so the solicitor must decline. Not being a director (your pick) does not remove the conflict.

stem: A homeowner notices that a neighbour’s tree is overhanging their garden. What advice would you give to the homeowner?
correct: Chop the overhanging branches and throw them back over the boundary.
why: Abatement: a neighbour may cut back overhanging branches up to the boundary without notice. That is self-help for nuisance and encroachment, and it is cheap and proportionate. The cuttings still belong to the tree owner, so they should be offered back, hence 'throw them back over' (Mills v Brooker). An injunction (your pick) is disproportionate for a simple overhang, and poisoning the tree would itself be actionable.

stem: A tenant finds that their neighbour is regularly playing loud music in the middle of the night. They ask the neighbour to stop, but the disturbance continues. Which one of the following statements best describes whether it is likely that the tenant could obtain an injunction to prevent the neighbour from playing the music?
correct: Yes, because damages would not be an adequate remedy.
why: For a continuing nuisance, an injunction is the usual remedy because damages are inadequate for ongoing night-time disturbance. But it is EQUITABLE and discretionary (Coventry v Lawrence; Shelfer), never 'as of right' (your pick).

stem: A patient with a mental illness is refusing a blood transfusion because they believe that the blood in the hospital has been poisoned by aliens. However, they urgently need a life-saving operation, and the operation will not be possible without a blood transfusion. The consultant assures the patient that they will not give them a blood transfusion, but then does so once the patient is under general anaesthetic. Can the patient or their representatives recover damages from the consultant in the tort of battery?
correct: No, because the defence of necessity will apply.
why: Capacity is decision-specific (MCA 2005 ss 2–3). A delusion that the blood is poisoned by aliens prevents the patient from using and weighing the relevant information, so they lack capacity to refuse. Treatment in their best interests is then lawful under necessity / MCA s 5 (Re F). Contrast Re C: a patient WITH capacity can refuse even irrationally, and treating them anyway would be battery (your pick).

stem: A rally car driver invites a friend to join them in their rally car for a spin around a track on their own private land. The rally car driver has been drinking, and the friend is aware of this. Whilst racing round the track together, the rally car driver takes a turn too quickly. The car flips over, causing the friend to suffer a fractured skull. What advice would you give to the friend?
correct: The driver may escape all liability for negligence, on the grounds that you consented to the risk of harm.
why: Volenti non fit injuria: knowingly riding with a drunk driver can be consent to the risk (Morris v Murray). On a public ROAD, RTA 1988 s 149 bars volenti for passengers, leaving only contributory negligence (Owens v Brimmell, your pick). But this is a private track, so s 149 does not apply and volenti can defeat the claim entirely.

stem: A vaccine has been produced to protect humans against a new virus. The manufacturer of the vaccine uses new technology in the creation of the vaccine, and it passes the necessary safety checks before being released to market. The manufacturer has made significant profits from sales of the new vaccine. After the vaccine has been in circulation for several months, it becomes clear that the vaccine has a dangerous side effect which is caused by the new technology. Many patients who have received the vaccine suffer this side effect. Can the patients sue the manufacturer for product liability?
correct: No, because the technology was new, and the defect could not reasonably have been identified.
why: CPA 1987 imposes strict liability, so 'reasonable care' (your pick) is no defence. But s 4(1)(e) gives the DEVELOPMENT RISKS defence: the state of scientific and technical knowledge when the product was supplied did not allow the defect to be discovered. New technology with an unknowable side effect fits that defence. Medicines are covered by the CPA.

stem: "I leave the residue of my estate on trust to be divided between such of my living descendants as my trustees in their absolute discretion may decide." Which of the following is the most accurate in relation to this clause?
correct: This is a discretionary trust so the trustees should apply the any given postulant test to the potential beneficiaries before disposing of the trust property.
why: 'As my trustees in their absolute discretion may decide' makes this a DISCRETIONARY trust. The certainty-of-objects test is McPhail v Doulton's 'is or is not' (any given postulant) test: can it be said of any person that they are or are not in the class? A complete list (your pick) is the FIXED trust test (IRC v Broadway Cottages).

stem: A settlor wants to create a trust over £500,000 to benefit their descendants equally. Which of the following best describes this trust?
correct: This is a fixed trust for a class of objects which will require the trustees to identify all potential beneficiaries and establish conceptual certainty of the class of descendants.
why: 'Equally' makes this a FIXED trust: each beneficiary's share depends on how many there are. So the trustees must be able to draw up a COMPLETE LIST (IRC v Broadway Cottages), which needs conceptual certainty of 'descendants' plus evidential certainty. The 'any given postulant' test (your pick) is for discretionary trusts.

stem: A person and their partner bought a house together. The person provided the deposit of £80,000 from the sale of their previous house, but the mortgage and title were registered in both names as joint owners, as they intended it to be a shared family home. The relationship broke down 5 years later and now the person’s partner is claiming that they are entitled to an equal share of the property. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this situation?
correct: If joint owners do not have a common intention to equally share ownership from the start, or if their common intention to share ownership changed over time, it may be possible to rebut the presumption of equal shares.
why: Joint legal owners of a family home are presumed to be joint beneficial owners in EQUAL shares (Stack v Dowden). That presumption can be rebutted by showing a different common intention, judged holistically on the whole course of dealing, and the intention may change over time (Jones v Kernott). Registration alone is not conclusive (your pick), and unequal deposits alone do not rebut it.

stem: A person and their partner live together in the house that the person bought before they met. Only the person’s name is on the title but, in the 10 years the couple have lived together, the partner, who is a builder, has looked after the house and carried out and paid for all the repair work, including adding a new kitchen and bathroom. The couple do not have any children, but they have two dogs and the person’s partner has looked after the dogs and paid for their upkeep and vet’s bills. The relationship has broken down and the person is arguing that they are the sole owner of the property and their partner is not entitled to any beneficial share. What would be the best analysis in this circumstance?
correct: Courts will adopt a holistic approach in determining whether the non- legal owner has contributed sufficiently to acquire a beneficial interest in the property.
why: Sole legal owner: the non-owner must show a common intention constructive trust (common intention plus detrimental reliance). The court looks HOLISTICALLY at the whole course of dealing (Stack v Dowden; Jones v Kernott; Abbott v Abbott). Rosset's narrow focus on direct contributions to the price has been doubted. No single factor, including paying for repairs or improvements (your pick), is automatically enough.

stem: A person intends to transfer their beneficial ownership of shares in their company for the benefit of their child. The person declares a bare trust in their own favour, with the bank as their trustee. The person then phones the trustee and instructs them to transfer title of the shares to the person’s child. The child dies the day after the phone call and has left their entire estate to their child, who wants to know if the shares are included in the estate. Which of the following offers the best outcome for the grandchild in these circumstances?
correct: Where the beneficial owner orally instructs the legal owner to transfer the shares to a third party, with the intention that the beneficial interest will also pass, the transfer of the legal title takes the equitable title with it and an oral instruction is sufficient.
why: Vandervell v IRC: where an absolutely entitled beneficiary directs the bare trustee to transfer the LEGAL title to a third party, intending the beneficial interest to pass with it, s 53(1)(c) LPA does not apply. No writing is needed. Your picks treat it as a separate disposition of the equitable interest, but the equitable interest travels with the legal title.

stem: A person makes an oral declaration that they are holding their house on trust for their child. Which of the following is the most accurate interpretation of this situation?
correct: A declaration of a trust of land must be manifested and proved in some writing and signed by the person able to declare the trust, so this oral declaration of a trust will be valid but unenforceable in court.
why: s 53(1)(b) LPA 1925: a declaration of trust of LAND must be manifested and proved by writing signed by the person able to declare it. This is an evidential requirement, so the oral declaration is VALID but UNENFORCEABLE until there is writing. No deed is needed to declare a trust (your pick): a deed is needed to transfer a legal estate.

stem: A person wishes to set up a trust for their three children and wishes to appoint five people to the role of trustee. The trust includes a portfolio of shares and several interests in land. Will the person be able to appoint the five trustees?
correct: Yes, there are no restrictions as to the number of trustees that may be appointed.
why: ⚠ KEY LOOKS WRONG. Where a trust includes LAND, the number of trustees is capped at FOUR (s 34(2) Trustee Act 1925; s 34(2) LPA 1925: the legal estate cannot be held by more than four). If more are named, the first four able and willing to act are the trustees. Your answer (C) states the law correctly. There is no cap for trusts of pure personalty (e.g. shares only), and charitable trusts are exempt.

stem: Two trustees decide to invest £100,000 in cryptocurrency. Neither trustee knows very much about cryptocurrency. The trust portfolio mainly consists of investments in land, as well as a large share portfolio in FTSE 100 index companies. The £100,000 is lost very quickly and the beneficiaries are furious. Which elements of the standard investment criteria have potentially been breached by the trustees?
correct: The duty to take advice, the suitability of the investment and diversity.
why: Trustee Act 2000: the standard investment criteria (s 4) are SUITABILITY and DIVERSIFICATION, and s 5 imposes a duty to take proper ADVICE. A speculative, unadvised crypto bet breaches all three. Ethical considerations (your pick) are not part of the standard investment criteria. Trustees must act in the beneficiaries' financial interests (Cowan v Scargill).

stem: A solicitor trustee acts as the sole trustee of a trust. The solicitor’s partner in the firm also acts for a company that has approached the trust about purchasing a parcel of trust land. The solicitor trustee has consulted an agent who states that the offer is more than generous. Can the solicitor trustee continue to provide services to the trust?
correct: Yes, if the solicitor trustee gets informed consent of all the clients under para 6.2.
why: Para 6.1 (your pick) is an OWN-INTEREST conflict (solicitor vs client), which is absolutely prohibited. That is not this case: the clash is between two CLIENTS (the trust and the buyer company), which is governed by para 6.2. Para 6.2 allows acting only with informed consent of all clients AND where there is a substantially common interest or they are competing for the same objective, with safeguards. (In practice a straightforward sale is hard to fit within those exceptions. The examiner's point is 6.2, not 6.1.)

stem: A trustee was appointed by their best friend 15 years ago. The trust instrument contained a clause exempting the trustee from liability for a breach of trust. The trustee has regularly breached their duties to the trust and made several large personal profits. Will the exemption clause protect the trustee?
correct: Making of personal profits would be a breach of fiduciary duty and the exemption clause would not apply.
why: Armitage v Nurse: a trustee exemption clause can exclude liability even for gross negligence, but never for ACTUAL FRAUD or dishonesty (the irreducible core of the trust). Repeated breaches to make personal profits breach the fiduciary no-profit rule and are dishonest, so the clause does not protect the trustee. Your pick states the reverse.

stem: The trustees of a trust have made several negligent investments over a 10-year period. The beneficiaries are unhappy about the handling of the trust and wish to bring a claim against the trustees for breach of trust due to negligence and the trustees profiting personally from the trust property. Can the beneficiaries bring a claim against the trustees for breach of trust across the 10-year period?
correct: The beneficiary could only bring a claim for breach of trust over the last 6 years.
why: Limitation Act 1980 s 21(3): the general limit for breach of trust is 6 YEARS from the breach, so negligent investments older than 6 years are time-barred. ⚠ CAVEAT: under s 21(1) there is NO limit for fraud, or for recovering trust property (or its proceeds) that the trustee has converted to their own use. Claims for the trustees' personal profits from trust property may not be barred. The key's flat '6 years' covers the negligence claims.

stem: A client has ordered and paid for 20 bottles of cabernet from a local vineyard. Before the wine can be delivered, the vineyard goes into liquidation. Amongst the remaining assets is a warehouse holding 500 bottles of cabernet, including those which would have been sent to the client. Which of the following statements is most accurate in relation to this scenario?
correct: Certainty of subject matter requires that tangible assets belonging to a trust must always be segregated from other homogenous tangible assets and clearly identifiable.
why: Certainty of subject matter for TANGIBLE goods requires them to be SEGREGATED from the bulk (Re London Wine; Re Goldcorp). 20 bottles out of 500 unsegregated bottles cannot be held on trust, so the client gets no beneficial interest and no priority (your pick). Hunter v Moss (no segregation needed) is confined to intangibles such as shares. (Any sale-of-goods co-ownership claim under SGA s 20A is a separate, non-trust route.)

stem: A client intends to leave the following property on trust to benefit their five children: shares in three different companies, a collection of 20 rare coins, two Rembrandt paintings, a reasonable income to support their youngest child through university and the residue of their estate. Which of the following is most likely to be considered sufficiently certain as the subject matter of a trust?
correct: A reasonable income to my youngest child until they reach the age of 25 years.
why: Re Golay: 'a reasonable income' is certain enough, because the court can quantify it objectively. '10% of my shares' (your pick) fails: the shares are in THREE different companies, so you cannot tell which shares. 'Ten of my coins' fails as unsegregated tangibles (Re London Wine), 'the bulk of my estate' fails (Palmer v Simmonds), and 'my favourite' is uncertain without a selection mechanism.

stem: A will includes the following clause: “I leave £100,000 to my company directors to hold on trust for such of the employees and ex-employees of my company and their friends and relatives, in such shares as my trustees shall in their absolute discretion decide.” Which statement is true in relation to this bequest?
correct: The trust will be invalid because “friends” is not conceptually certain in relation to discretionary trusts.
why: Discretionary trust: every class must satisfy the 'is or is not' test (McPhail v Doulton). 'Relatives' passes (Re Baden (No 2)). 'FRIENDS' is conceptually uncertain for a discretionary trust; Re Barlow allows it only for individual gifts or conditions. One conceptually uncertain class defeats the whole discretionary trust, and there is no severance doctrine to cut 'friends' out (your pick).

stem: A person wants to donate £500,000 to the private school at which they studied. The school charges tuition fees of £25,000 per year. The person is seeking advice as to whether this would be considered a charitable bequest. Which of the following interpretations is most likely in this case?
correct: This is a valid charitable trust for the advancement of education. It must demonstrate that it meets the requirements of the public benefit test.
why: Education is a charitable purpose (Charities Act 2011 s 3(1)(b)), but there is NO presumption of public benefit (s 4(2)). A fee-charging school must SHOW public benefit, including more than token provision for those who cannot pay the fees (R (ISC) v Charity Commission). Fees do not automatically disqualify it. 'Only a section of the public' (your pick) is not the issue.

stem: A client was buying a new house and, on the morning of completion, their solicitor phoned to say there would be a slight delay with the transfer of funds from the party buying the client’s old house and so they would be short £50,000 to complete their purchase, triggering a late fee of £5,000. In breach of trust, the client decided to withdraw £50,000 from the family trust fund, of which they were a trustee, confident that they could repay the money quickly. The client transferred the money to the solicitor, who was surprised, but decided not to question the good luck. The solicitor was having technical problems with their client account, so they placed the money into their personal account. Which of the following best identifies the potential ethical and conduct issues in this scenario?
correct: The solicitor is potentially liable for both accessory liability and recipient liability for the breach of trust. The solicitor’s conduct and honesty fell below what a reasonable person would have expected of a person with the solicitor’s knowledge and experience. By placing the money in their personal account, the solicitor breached the Code of Conduct by beneficially holding client money.
why: Two routes of liability. ACCESSORY (dishonest assistance): the solicitor's turning a blind eye is dishonest by the objective standard, applied to someone with a solicitor's knowledge (Royal Brunei v Tan; Ivey). RECIPIENT (knowing receipt): putting the money into a PERSONAL account is beneficial receipt, with knowledge making retention unconscionable (BCCI v Akindele). It is also a conduct breach (client money). Your pick covered only accessory liability.

If joint owners do not have a common intention to equally share ownership from the start, or if their common intention to share ownership changed over time, it may be possible to rebut the presumption of equal shares. The person has contributed more to the purchase price and therefore would be entitled to a greater share of the value of the property following the sale.

question: A person and their partner live together in the house that the person bought before they met. Only the person's name is on the title but, in the 10 years the couple have lived together, the partner (a builder) has looked after the house and carried out and paid for all the repair work, including a new kitchen and bathroom, and has looked after and paid for the couple's two dogs. The relationship has broken down and the person argues they are the sole owner. What would be the best analysis?

stem: A person convinced their partner to sell the large house their partner had inherited and move in with them. The person promised that, even though the house was in the person’s name, the partner could share it with them. The partner sold their inherited property at less than its market value because the person wanted the partner to move in immediately and help look after the person’s young children. After living together for 10 years, helping to raise the children and contributing to the upkeep of the person’s house, the partner has now been told by the person to move out of the house as they met someone else. Property prices have gone up significantly in the last 10 years and the partner can no longer afford to buy another house in the area. Which of the following is the best response in this situation?
correct: The partner could show that they had relied on the person’s assurances to their detriment and it would therefore be unconscionable to allow the person to deny their interest.
why: Express common intention constructive trust: an express assurance of sharing ('you can share it'), RELIED ON to the partner's DETRIMENT (selling her own house at an undervalue, moving in, raising the children), makes it unconscionable for the owner to deny her an interest (Grant v Edwards; Eves v Eves). Proprietary estoppel (your pick) might also be argued, but the court awards the minimum equity needed. There is no automatic 'right to live there for life'.

stem: There are two trustees managing an estate. The trust arose three years ago. So far, the beneficiaries of the trust have received no financial benefits from the trust and have received no information from the trustees. Which of the following duties may the trustees have breached?
correct: The duty to provide accounts and information and the duty to distribute to the correct beneficiaries.
why: Trustees must keep and provide ACCOUNTS and information to beneficiaries, and must DISTRIBUTE to the right beneficiaries in accordance with the trust. Three years with no information AND no distribution suggests breach of both duties, not just the information duty (your pick). Nothing suggests secret profits or a fair-dealing problem.
